en: The Hundred and One Karmavācanās of the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Command.
At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. He addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

“From this day forward, O bhikṣus, whenever anyone comes seeking [ordination]—one who is well-versed in the Dharma and Vinaya and desires to go forth and receive full ordination—the ācārya and upādhyāya should grant them the going forth and the full ordination.”
At that time, the bhikṣus did not know how many ācāryas and how many upādhyāyas there were.
The Buddha said:
“There are five kinds of ācāryas and two kinds of upādhyāyas. What are the five kinds of ācāryas? First, the ācārya of the ten precepts;
second, the ācārya who instructs in private; third, the ācārya of the ritual (karmavācanā); fourth, the ācārya of dependence (niśraya); and fifth, the ācārya who teaches the recitation.”
What is meant by a *daśa-śikṣāpada-ācārya*?
It refers to one who bestows the three refuges and the ten precepts (*śikṣāpada*).
What is meant by a *raho’nuśāsaka-ācārya*?
This refers to interrogating [the candidate] in a secluded place regarding obstructing dharmas.
What is a *karmācārya*? It is one who performs the formal ritual procedure (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).
What is meant by an ācārya as a basis for dependence?
It refers to depending upon someone for even a single night’s stay.
What is meant by an ācārya who teaches recitation?
This refers to teaching the recitation of even a single four-line gāthā.
What are the two kinds of upādhyāyas?
First, one who shaves the hair, grants ordination, and bestows the ten precepts; second, one who grants full ordination (upasampadā).
As the Blessed One has said,
"The preceptors and others should grant him the going forth, the reception of the precepts,
and full ordination," the bhikṣus did not know how they should grant the going forth and full ordination.
The Buddha said:
"Whenever anyone wishes to seek ordination, they should go to a teacher according to their preference. The teacher must then inquire about all obstructing conditions (*antarāyika-dharma*).
If the candidate is entirely pure, the teacher may accept them according to his own inclination."

Once they have been accepted, he grants them the three refuges along with the five precepts, thereby establishing them in the discipline of an upāsaka. Regarding this term "protection" (*hṛ*), the Sanskrit is *saṃvara*, which is translated as "guarding" or "protection."
By receiving the protection of the precepts through taking refuge, one ensures that one does not fall into the three miserable realms (*apāya*).
The older term "vinaya" (律儀) is a literal translation; it means the ritual procedures of the *dharma*.
If one were to use only the term "protection" (*raksā*), I fear students might not understand the full significance; therefore, both terms are retained.

The *Viniścaya-śāstra* has already been translated as "protection" (*gū*), which refers to the unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) that constitutes the essence of the precepts; it should be conferred in this manner.
First, after instructing the one seeking to go forth to perform prostrations, they should squat with palms joined before their preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and be taught to speak these words:
"O Ācārya, please attend to me!"

I, [Name], from this day forth until the end of my life, take refuge in the Buddha, the most honored among two-legged beings; I take refuge in the Dharma, the most honored among those free from desire; I take refuge in the Saṃgha, the most honored among assemblies.
Thus he said three times.
The preceptor said: "Oṃ vīra."
The translation says "good" (hǎo), or alternatively "so" (ěr).
This also carries the meaning of "skillful means" (upāya); for this reason, the holy teaching serves as a skillful means capable of leading one toward nirvāṇa and the place of peace and security.
[The interlocutor] replied: "Svāsti."
"Translated as 'good,' this same procedure applies whenever a formal act (*karmavācanā*) is concluded or when a matter is announced at any time.
If one does not speak thus, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma."

Whether in Sanskrit or Chinese, the subsequent texts merely say "good" or "virtuous," all of which may be understood accordingly. Or it is said that the later phrasing is the same as the former; next, the five precepts (*śikṣāpada*) are conferred, and the instruction says: "Follow my words."

"In accordance with the sacred teachings and traditional lineage, one should receive the words for the precepts exactly as the teacher recites them. If there is no teacher to speak them, one may directly ask, 'Are you able?
The matter of the precepts is not trivial; it does not permit haste. 'Ācārya, please attend to me!'"
Just as the noble Arhats, for as long as life lasts, do not kill living beings, do not take what is not given, do not engage in sexual misconduct, do not speak falsely, and do not drink intoxicants.

I, [Name], from this day forth until the end of my life, shall refrain from taking life, refrain from taking what is not given, refrain from sexual misconduct, refrain from false speech, and likewise refrain from drinking intoxicants; these are my five precepts of training, which are the precepts studied by the noble Arhats, and I shall train in them, practice them, and maintain them accordingly.
Thus he says three times:
"May the Ācārya bear witness that I am an upāsaka who has taken refuge in the Three Jewels and received the five precepts."
The Master said, "Very well. He replied:
"Excellent.
Next, he requested that Upādhyāya be translated as "Preceptor" (親教師); to call him "Upādhyāya" is merely the colloquial usage of the West and is not the formal, canonical term.
However, the Sanskrit originals of all the sūtras and vinayas read "upādhyāya.
The instruction states:
"'Ācārya' is translated as 'Preceptor' (軌範師); [O] Preceptor, please attend to me!"
I, [Name], now request the venerable Ācārya to be my Upādhyāya; may the venerable Ācārya act as my Upādhyāya.
Because the venerable Ācārya acts as my Upādhyāya, I shall go forth into homelessness.
Thus it is said three times.
The subsequent words are the same as before; upon reaching the third repetition, one should say:
"Because Upādhyāya [is so called] due to the status of the Preceptor (upādhyāya), the word is repeated for that reason."
Next, one bhikṣu should be requested to act as the proclaimer to the assembly; he should ask the preceptor:
"Have all obstructing factors been inquired about?
To which he should reply: [Yes].
"Once asked. If one asks, it is well;
if one makes a formal announcement without having asked, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
Next, he shall inform the assembly; all members of the Saṃgha must gather, or he shall go from room to room to notify them.
Then, leading him into the midst of the assembly, he shall pay his respects. Standing before the elder (sthavira), crouching with palms joined, he shall speak as follows: “Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This person, so-and-so, seeks to go forth from the householder’s life under the venerable monk so-and-so; he is still a layman with unshorn hair and wishes to go forth and receive full ordination (*upasampadā*) within this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya to become a bhikṣu. If this person, so-and-so, having shaved his hair and beard and donned the dharma-robes, gives rise to right faith and leaves the home for the homeless life—with so-and-so as his preceptor (*upādhyāya*)—would the Saṃgha grant so-and-so the going-forth?
"This is merely a formal announcement (*jñapti*) of the matter, not a formal motion (*karmavācanā*). When the assembly has made this single announcement, they all say:
'If he is completely pure, he should be granted ordination.'"
"If everyone asks, it is well;
if they do not ask, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
Next, he requested a bhikṣu to shave his hair, and the bhikṣu shaved it all off, whereupon the man later regretted it."
The Buddha said:
"One should leave a small amount of hair on the crown of the head. He asked:
"Have you removed your topknot? If he says, "No."
To one who says this, one should say: "Go as you wish. If they say:
Regarding the instruction "Remove," it means they should be shaved.
Next, provide them with a bath; if it is cold, give them warm water, and if it is hot, give them cold water.

Next, when providing her with a lower garment (*nivasana*), one must examine her; for there may be the fear that she is rootless (*amūlaka*), possesses both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*), or has incomplete organs.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu examined her while naked, which caused her to feel shame. The Buddha said:
"One should not examine her while naked. When providing her with the lower garment, you should look discreetly so as not to let her perceive it."

Next, having bestowed the plain cloth and instructed him in its acceptance upon the crown of his head, and having dressed him in the robes, the preceptor should request a bhikṣu to grant him the śrāmaṇera vows. Once he has been instructed in the ritual of prostration, he should squat with palms joined before the two masters and be taught to speak these words:
"The two masters should sit close together, and you, disciple, should grasp the corner of the Preceptor’s saṃghāṭī."
Beholding the Western Quarter, may the Ācārya bear this in mind:

I, [Name], from this day forth until the end of my life, take refuge in the Buddha, the most honored among two-legged beings; I take refuge in the Dharma, the most honored among those free from desire; I take refuge in the Saṃgha, the most honored among assemblies.

That Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Lion of the Śākyas, the Great King of the Śākyas, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—once he has gone forth into homelessness, I shall follow him and likewise go forth.

I have already discarded the appearance and deportment of a layperson and now accept the form and characteristics of one who has gone forth. For the sake of this matter, I shall state the name of my preceptor; the name of my preceptor is [Name].
Thus he spoke three times.
The Master said:
"Excellent."
He replies, "Excellent.
Next, he confers the ten precepts (śikṣāpada), instructing him as follows:
"Follow my words. "Venerable Ācārya, please attend to me!

Just as the noble Arhats, for as long as they live, abstain from taking life, abstain from stealing, abstain from sexual misconduct, abstain from false speech, abstain from drinking intoxicants, abstain from singing, dancing, and music, abstain from perfumes, garlands, and unguents, abstain from sitting or lying on high or large beds, abstain from eating at improper times, and abstain from accepting or keeping gold and silver; [so shall I likewise abstain]."

I, [Name], from this day forth until the end of my life, shall not kill living beings, shall not steal, shall not engage in sexual misconduct, shall not speak falsely, shall not drink intoxicants, shall not engage in singing, dancing, or music, shall not use perfumes, garlands, or cosmetics, shall not sit on high or large beds, shall not eat at improper times, and likewise shall not accept or possess gold and silver.
"These are my ten precepts of training.
These are the precepts of training for all the noble Arhats; I shall train in them, practice them, and uphold them.
Thus he says three times.
"May the Ācārya bear witness: I am a śrāmaṇera; for a certain reason, I shall state the name of my Upādhyāya, whose name is [so-and-so]."
The Master said, "Very well. He replied:

"Excellent! You have now successfully received the ten precepts. You should make offerings to the Triple Gem, attend upon your two teachers, study and recite the sūtras, diligently cultivate the three types of action, and do not be negligent."

"If one has reached the age of twenty, they may be granted full ordination (*upasampadā*). The preceptor should seek for them the three robes and an alms bowl, a water-strainer, and bedding; he should also invite the *karmavācanā* master, the private instructor, and enter the ordination platform together with them."

Once the assembly of bhikṣus has gathered—whether it be a group of five or a group of ten—they shall cause the candidate for ordination to bare the right shoulder and remove their leather sandals, requiring each person to perform three prostrations of respect.
However, there are two kinds of reverence:

the first refers to the "five wheels" touching the ground—namely, the forehead wheel, the two palms, and the two knees; the second refers to holding the teacher’s calves and feet with both hands while walking along behind him.
Once one has paid respect to one [of them], one should request the *upādhyāya*.
Whether he was previously the *upādhyāya* or the *ācārya*, he should be addressed by that title at the appropriate time.
If one was not previously one of the two teachers,
one should say: "Venerable Sir," or say:
"Venerable Sir," if one is requesting a preceptor (ācārya), it should be done in this manner.
One should maintain proper deportment and speak these words:
"Venerable Upādhyāya, please attend to me!
I, [name], now request the Venerable Upādhyāya to be my Upādhyāya; may the Venerable Upādhyāya act as my Upādhyāya."
"Because the preceptor acts as preceptor, you shall receive full ordination; this refers to the one who was previously the preceptor for the ten precepts.
Thus it is said three times, with the subsequent words being the same as before.
Then, in the midst of the assembly before the preceptor, the preceptor shall bestow the three robes upon him and instruct him as follows:
"O Upādhyāya, please attend!..."
"I, [Name], this saṃghāṭī—translated as 'double-layered robe'—I now maintain; it has already been made into a finished garment and is for my use.
Thus he says three times; the rest is the same as before.
"Venerable Upādhyāya, please attend to me!
I, [name], this uttarāsaṅga—translated as the 'upper robe'—I now formally accept and maintain; it has been completed as a finished garment and is for my personal use."
Thus he says three times, the subsequent words being the same as before:
“Venerable Upādhyāya, please attend to me!
I, [name], am now taking formal possession of this *antarvāsaka*—translated as ‘inner garment’—which has already been made into a finished robe; it is for my personal use.”
Thus he spoke three times, and the subsequent words were the same as before.
If it is an item that has not yet been washed or dyed, nor cut into pieces, such as silk or cotton cloth used provisionally to count as a robe, one should maintain its status in this way:
"O Upādhyāya, please attend to me!..."
I, [Name], now take formal possession of this robe; it shall be made into a nine-panel *saṃghāṭī* robe with two panels long and one short.
Provided there are no obstacles, I shall wash, dye, cut, and sew it; this is what I shall use.

Thus he spoke three times, and the subsequent words were the same as before; all other rules for wearing robes should be understood accordingly, as detailed in the notes on the five robes of the nuns below.
Next, one may hold up the bowl to present it to the entire assembly, fearing that it might be too small, too large, or of an improper color such as white.
If it is of good quality, the assembly will all say: "A fine bowl."
If one does not speak thus, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
Thereafter, one should hold [the bowl] with the left hand, open the right hand to cover the mouth of the bowl, and instruct as follows:
"O Upādhyāya, please attend to me!"
"I, [Name], this pātra is the vessel of the Great Sage; it is a vessel for alms-gathering. I now accept and maintain it for the purpose of eating food.
Thus one says three times, and the subsequent words are the same as before.
Next, he should be placed where he can see [the assembly] but not hear it, and instructed to stand with palms joined in single-minded devotion toward the community.
The *karmavācanā* master should then ask the assembly:
"Who has been previously invited?"
"You should instruct such-and-such a person in a secluded place.
The one who accepts the request replies:
"I am such-and-such a person."
Next, one asks:
"You, [Name], are you able to instruct [Name] in private, acting as his upādhyāya? He should respond:
“I am able. Next, the *karmavācanā* is performed;
the preceptor should recite the *jñapti*:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, [Name], is able to instruct [Name] in a secluded place; [Name] shall be his upādhyāya."

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha grant its permission that the Saṃgha now appoint the bhikṣu [Name] as the instructor in private; he shall provide instruction to [Name] in a secluded place, with [Name] acting as the upādhyāya.
"Thus it is declared.
Next, the preceptor leads the candidate to a secluded place; once he has instructed him to pay homage, he crouches with palms joined and speaks these words:
"Venerable one!..."

Listen: this is the time for you to speak with sincerity, the time for you to speak the truth. I now have a few questions for you; you should respond with a fearless mind, saying "it exists" if it exists, or "it does not exist" if it does not, and you must not speak falsely.
"Are you a man? He replied, "I am."
"Are you twenty years of age? He replied, "I am."
"Are your three robes and alms bowl complete? He replied, "They are."
"Are your parents still living?
If he says, "They are," [one should ask further].
When [the teacher] asks, "Have you been permitted to go forth?
he replies, "I have been permitted."
If he says, "He is dead," there is no need to ask further.
"Are you not a slave? Are you not a royal minister?
Are you not a person who has committed poison-murder for the royal family?"
"Are you not a thief? Are you not a eunuch? Have you not defiled a bhikṣuṇī?"
"Have you not killed your father?
Have you not killed your mother? Have you not killed an Arhat?"
"Are you not one who has caused a schism in the Saṃgha?
Are you not one who, with an evil mind, has shed the blood of a Buddha?
Are you not a follower of a non-Buddhist path?"
[The Buddha] asked this outsider, "Are you not one who has gone over to the non-Buddhist paths?
[The candidate replied that he had] previously left the home life but returned to the non-Buddhist paths, and now comes once again: "Are you not one who dwells as a thief [in the Saṃgha]?"
"Are you not living apart? Are you not one with whom one does not live together?
Regarding those who have previously committed a grave offense: "Are you not a magically conjured being?"

"Are you not in debt? If he says, "I am," [the preceptor asks: "What is it for? If he says, "It is for this," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it after receiving the full ordination, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it even after receiving the full ordination," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of labor or service, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of labor or service either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it through the favor of a donor, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it through the favor of a donor either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of medicine, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of medicine either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of clothing, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of clothing either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of food and drink, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of food and drink either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of bedding and seating, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of bedding and seating either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of a vehicle, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of a vehicle either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of a boat, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of a boat either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of a field, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of a field either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of a house, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of a house either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of a shop, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of a shop either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of a storehouse, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of a storehouse either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of a treasury, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of a treasury either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of a granary, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of a granary either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of a garden, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of a garden either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of a forest, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of a forest either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of a mountain, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of a mountain either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of a river, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of a river either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of a pond, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of a pond either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of a well, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of a well either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of a spring, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of a spring either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of a stream, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of a stream either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of a lake, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of a lake either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of a marsh, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of a marsh either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of a meadow, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of a meadow either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of a pasture, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of a pasture either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of a herd of cattle, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of a herd of cattle either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of a herd of horses, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of a herd of horses either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of a herd of elephants, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of a herd of elephants either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of a herd of sheep, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of a herd of sheep either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of a herd of goats, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of a herd of goats either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of a herd of poultry, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of a herd of poultry either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of a herd of pigs, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of a herd of pigs either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of a herd of dogs, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of a herd of dogs either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of a herd of cats, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of a herd of cats either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of a herd of monkeys, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of a herd of monkeys either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of a herd of deer, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of a herd of deer either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of a herd of wild boars, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of a herd of wild boars either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of a herd of wild asses, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of a herd of wild asses either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of a herd of wild oxen, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of a herd of wild oxen either," [the preceptor] should say, "If you can repay it by means of a herd of wild sheep, then you may receive the full ordination. If he says, "I cannot repay it by means of a herd of wild sheep either," [the pre
To such a person, one should ask:
"After you have received full ordination (*upasampadā*), will you repay that debt?
If they say:
If one says, "I can," that is good.
However, if one says:
"‘I cannot’ means:
‘You may ask him; come only if he grants permission.
‘Have you not already gone forth [into homelessness]?’"
If he says, "No," that is well.
As it is said:
"I once went forth into homelessness.
[The teacher asks: "Have you not committed any offense among the four *pārājika* defeats?"
"Did you properly relinquish the precepts when you returned to lay life?
He replied, "I committed a grave offense."
"Go as you please. Or if he says: "There is no offense."
If they say, "It is well," one asks:
"What is your name?"
“I am named [Name]. “What is the name of your upādhyāya? He replies:
"I have come for a certain purpose to state the name of my upādhyāya; the name of my upādhyāya is so-and-so.
"Furthermore, you should listen!
Within the body of a man, there are such diseases as these:"

That is to say: leprosy, goiters, scabies, sores, vitiligo, skin diseases, hairlessness on the head, malignant ulcers, downward discharges, tumors, dropsy, coughing with wheezing, labored breathing, dryness of the throat, fainting spells, insanity, pallor of complexion, hiccups and vomiting, various hemorrhoids, ringworm, swelling of the feet, spitting of blood, carbuncles, diarrhea, high fever, pain in the ribs, aching and distress in the bones and joints, as well as various types of malaria, disorders of wind, bile, and phlegm, the three humors combined, chronic fevers, possession by spirits, deafness, blindness, muteness, stunted growth, lameness, and missing limbs or joints—do you not have any such diseases or other ailments?
He replied, “No. [The preceptor] said, “Listen, you, so-and-so!
"Just as I now question you in this private place, so too shall the bhikṣus question you in the midst of the great assembly.
In that setting, with a mind free from fear, you should answer truthfully—saying 'it exists' if it exists, and saying 'it does not exist' if it does not."
"You stay here for now; do not come until you are summoned.
The preceptor proceeds halfway along the road, stands before the assembly, and should speak these words:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
That so-and-so has already been formally instructed by me in private; I have questioned him regarding the obstructing dharmas, and so-and-so acts as his preceptor (upādhyāya).
Shall he be permitted to come?
The entire assembly said, "If he is pure, he should be summoned. It is well if they all say this;

if they do not, one commits an offense against the Dharma (vyatikrama). The five-day altar site (*pañcarātra-maṇḍala*) is established in a secluded place within the monastery, occupying only the size of a single chamber. On all four sides, it is built up with bricks to a height of two feet, with a foundation five inches high on the inner edge. Monks sit upon it. In its center is a small *caitya* as tall as a person, with a small door opened at its side to allow for entry and exit.

The person seeking to receive the precepts stands outside the altar, while the officiating teacher (karmadāna) questions them in a screened location so as not to allow the assembly to see; this differs from the local custom where everyone remains within the ordination platform (sīmāmaṇḍala) for all to witness together, which completely contradicts the principle of maintaining privacy during the screening.

Once the inquiry regarding obstructing factors has been completed, the person may be instructed to stand apart outside the altar. The preceptor then proceeds halfway along the path and announces it from afar to the assembly for their knowledge; this is what constitutes the formal announcement (*jñapti*), and it is fundamentally not a formal ritual motion (*karman*). Having personally witnessed this practice in the West, those who hear of it should harbor no doubts.
One should summon him from afar.
Once he has arrived among the assembly, have him squat before the presiding elder with palms joined.
After he has paid his respects, he should request the full ordination (*upasampadā*), instructing him to speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
I, [Name], now for a specific reason shall state the name of my upādhyāya; I seek to receive full ordination from my upādhyāya, [Name]."
I, [Name], now request from the Saṃgha the full ordination (upasampadā). For a specific reason, I shall state the name of my preceptor (upādhyāya); [Name] is my upādhyāya.
May the virtuous Saṃgha grant me full ordination; may they receive and rescue me, and instruct me out of compassion for me.
May those who are compassionate do so out of pity.
Thus he says three times.

Next, he is led before the *karmavācanā* master; using a brick or an object wrapped with straw to support the heels of both feet, he crouches with his ten toes planted on the ground and joins his palms.
The *karmavācanā* master should perform a single formal motion (*jñapti*) and inquire regarding the obstructing factors:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This person, so-and-so, seeks to receive full ordination from the preceptor, so-and-so."
This person, [Name], now requests from the Saṃgha the full ordination (upasampadā), with [Name] acting as preceptor (upādhyāya).

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and they grant permission, may the Saṃgha allow me to interrogate this person, [Name], regarding all obstructing dharmas (antarāyika-dharma), with [Name] acting as preceptor.
"Thus it is announced.
Next, the obstructing dharmas are to be inquired about, as should be understood from above.
Next, the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) is performed:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This person named [Name],
seeking full ordination from the upādhyāya named [Name],
is a male who has reached twenty years of age and is fully equipped with the three robes and the alms bowl."
So-and-so declares himself to be pure and free from all obstructing dharmas.
This So-and-so now requests from the Saṃgha the full ordination (upasampadā), with So-and-so as his preceptor (upādhyāya).

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha grant permission: the Saṃgha now confers full ordination upon [Name], with [Name] acting as the preceptor (upādhyāya).
The motion is thus made.
Next, the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is performed: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
This person, [Name], seeks to receive full ordination from the preceptor, [Name].
This man is twenty years of age; he possesses the three robes and the alms bowl; [Name] himself declares that he is pure and free from all obstructing conditions.
This person, [Name], now requests from the Saṃgha the full ordination (upasampadā), with [Name] as his preceptor (upādhyāya).
The Saṃgha now grants the full ordination to [Name], with [Name] as his preceptor.
If the venerable ones consent to granting full ordination to [Name] with [Name] as the preceptor (upādhyāya), let them remain silent; if they do not consent, let them speak.
This is the first *karmavācanā*.
Thus it was said three times:
"The Saṃgha has already conferred full ordination upon so-and-so, with so-and-so as preceptor; the Saṃgha has granted its consent, as indicated by its silence; thus do I now uphold this."
"When the ritual procedure is completed, one should immediately measure the shadow.
When the bhikṣu stepped upon it, the shadow moved past him. The Buddha said:
"One should use a *śaṅku* (measuring rod) to measure it."
They all did not understand what was meant by the "measuring square" (*śaṅku*).
The Buddha said:
"Take a fine tally about two feet long, break off four finger-widths at one end, and set it upright in the sun to measure the length and shortness of its shadow; this is called the measuring square."
Each shadow measured by a single *śaṅku* is designated as "one person"; when this shadow is just four finger-widths long, one observes that the shadow of one's own body resembles the body itself.
If there are increases or decreases, one should reflect accordingly; thus the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"Regarding the shadow of one or two persons, people in the past were all unaware of it."
When the measurement of the shadow is completed,
one should inform them, saying: "You received full ordination before the meal, or after the meal when the shadow was this long—
whether it was one finger-breadth, two finger-breadths, one and a half persons, two persons, three persons, and so forth."
If it is at night, or if it is daytime with shadows, one may estimate and inform them accordingly, specifying whether it is the first watch, midnight, or until daybreak, and so forth.
"Subsequently, you should inform them of the distinctions regarding the seasons.
They did not know how many seasons there were.
The Buddha said:
"There are five distinctions of time:
first, winter; second, spring; third, the rainy season; fourth, the final period; and fifth, the long period."
Regarding the winter season, it consists of four months, namely from the sixteenth day of the ninth month to the fifteenth day of the first month.
Regarding the spring season, it likewise consists of four months, namely from the sixteenth day of the first month to the fifteenth day of the fifth month.
Regarding the "rainy season," it lasts for one month, specifically from the sixteenth day of the fifth month to the fifteenth day of the sixth month.
Regarding the "concluding period," it refers to the single day and night of the sixteenth day of the sixth month.

Regarding the phrase "for a long period," it refers to three months minus one day and one night; that is, from the seventeenth day of the sixth month to the fifteenth day of the ninth month. This is the essential rule for the Saṃgha in the Western Regions (India). If one does not understand this, they are not a bhikṣu. However, because this has not been translated until now, those who hear of it fail to realize its meaning.

This means that the esoteric teachings of the Buddha’s school differ from the secular; if one were to go to a foreign land and fail to understand them when questioned by others, everyone would laugh at one. This is not like the practice in China, which merely records the months.
"Next, you shall be instructed in the four reliances (*catur-śaraṇa*). 'Listen, [Name]!

These four reliances are what has been known and seen by all the World-Honored Ones, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas; they have declared these to be the reliances for those bhikṣus who have received full ordination (*upasampadā*), namely: relying on this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya to go forth, receive full ordination, and achieve the state of a bhikṣu.'"
What are the four? "Listen, [Name]!
First, rag-robes (*pāṃśukūla*): these are pure objects that are easy to obtain."
"Relying upon this, a bhikṣu goes forth and receives full ordination within the sublime Dharma and Vinaya, thereby attaining the nature of a bhikṣu.
You, [Name], from this day forward until the end of your life, will you take delight in sustaining yourself with rag-robes?"
He replied, “I am delighted. [The Buddha said:

“If you obtain long-term benefits such as silk, plain cloth, strips of fabric, small or large cloaks, light gauze, ramie cloth, or various other items; or if you further obtain pure robes, whether received from the community or from an individual—will you accept these things accordingly and know the proper measure in their use?”
He replies, "I accept it. [The preceptor] says, "Listen, you, so-and-so!..."
Second, one always begs for food; this is pure food that is easily obtained.
By relying on this, a bhikṣu goes forth and receives full ordination within the sublime Dharma and Vinaya, thereby perfecting the nature of a bhikṣu.
"Venerable [Name], from this day forth until the end of your life, will you take delight in supporting yourself by constantly begging for alms?
He replies, "I shall take delight in it."

"If one obtains long-term benefits such as rice, congee, or drinks; whether it be a meal offered in the order of the Sangha, a separate invitation for a meal, the regular food of the Sangha, or *nidda* (translated as 'constant offering')—where a specific donor provides money or goods to the Sangha to establish an inexhaustible fund for food, ordering that the community daily prepare fine meals to provide for one person, continuing as long as the sun and moon endure without interruption."

In the western regions, these are common within monasteries, yet the people here have neither heard of nor know them. It is well to provide food offerings, even if it be only milk; on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month, if you obtain pure food—whether from the community as a whole or from an individual—you may accept such things as they come to you. Do you understand how to receive and consume them with moderation?
He replies, "I accept it. [The preceptor says: "Listen, you, so-and-so!
Third, the bedding under a tree is a pure object that is easy to obtain.
By relying upon this, a bhikṣu goes forth and receives full ordination within the sublime Dharma and Vinaya, thereby becoming a bhikṣu.
"O [Name], from this day forth until the end of your life, do you take pleasure in supporting yourself by spreading out bedding under trees?
He replies, "I take pleasure in it."
"If you obtain long-term benefits such as rooms, pavilions, or dwellings in caves, thatched with grass or covered with boards, which are fit for walking meditation;

or if you further obtain pure locations, whether received from the community or from an individual—should you accept such things according to your needs, and do you know how to use them with moderation?"
He replies, "I accept it. [The preceptor says: "Listen, you, so-and-so!
4. Regarding discarded medicines: these are pure substances that are easily obtained.
By relying on these, a bhikṣu goes forth and receives full ordination within the sublime Dharma and Vinaya, thereby attaining the nature of a bhikṣu.
"O [Name], from this day forth as long as you live, do you take delight in sustaining yourself with discarded medicine? He replies, "I do."

"If one obtains long-term benefits such as ghee, oil, honey, molasses, or medicinal substances consisting of roots, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth—whether they be 'more-medicine' (yāvad-ūpika), seven-day medicine, or lifetime medicine—"
If you further obtain pure medicines—whether obtained from the community or from an individual—will you accept them as appropriate and consume them with moderation?
He replied, "I accept it.
Next, the four *pārājika* (defeats) were proclaimed:

"Listen, [Name]! There are these four dharmas which the World-Honored Ones—the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas—knowing and seeing, have declared to be dharmas of defeat for bhikṣus who have received full ordination."

Among these four, if a bhikṣu commits any one of them, at the very moment of such transgression, he is no longer a bhikṣu, no longer a śramaṇa, and no longer a son of the Śākyas; he loses his status as a bhikṣu.
This leads to falling away, extinction, and the cessation of saṃsāra; having been overcome by others, one cannot be recovered.
It is like cutting off the head of a tāla tree, which can no longer grow or increase in height; so it is with the bhikṣu.
What are the four? Listen, [Name]!

These World-Honored Ones, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, through their knowledge and vision, have by means of immeasurable methods censured all sensual desires. They have declared that desire is defilement, desire is moisture, desire is attachment, desire is domesticity, desire is a fetter, and desire is indulgence in pleasure; they are to be severed, to be vomited out, to be weary of, to be extinguished, and they are matters of darkness.
"You, [Name], from this day forward, you must not casually look upon women with a defiled mind, much less engage in unchaste acts with them.
Venerable one!"
As the Blessed One has said:

"If a bhikṣu, having received the training rules together with other bhikṣus, does not relinquish those training rules and, while his training is weak, does not declare it himself, should perform an impure act—the method of sexual intercourse—even with an animal; regarding such a matter, if the bhikṣu commits it, at that very moment he is no longer a bhikṣu, no longer a śramaṇa, no longer a son of the Śākya; he has lost the nature of a bhikṣu."
"You will thus fall away and be lost in saṃsāra; overcome by others, you cannot be recovered.

From this day forward, regarding these sensual dharmas, you must not intentionally transgress them. You should give rise to weary detachment and guard against them with earnestness; conceiving a sense of dread, examine them closely and practice diligently, remaining heedful.
"Are you able to refrain from doing this? He replied, "I shall not."

“Listen, [Name]! These World-Honored Ones, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as they know and see, have by means of immeasurable methods censured taking what is not given, and have praised and extolled the excellence of abstaining from taking what is not given.”

"You, [Name], from this day forth, shall not intentionally steal even so much as a grain of hemp or chaff belonging to another without it being given, let alone five *māṣakas* or more than five *māṣakas*. In the various Vinaya schools of the West, this term is used consistently for the purpose of interrogation; they sever the grave offense based on this, rather than using the term 'five coins' (*pañca-kārṣāpaṇa*)."

These are cowrie shells; eighty shells are reckoned as one *māṣa*, totaling four hundred shells in all. Only when they are simultaneously removed from their place does it constitute the offense of theft; originally, this was not based on the value of money.
If one were to translate this as "five coins," it would entirely deviate from the original text.
Therefore, I have retained the Sanskrit term; its various applications and restrictions are explained extensively elsewhere.
Venerable One!
As the Blessed One said:

"If a bhikṣu, whether in a village or in a secluded place, takes with a thieving mind an object not given by another; at the time of such theft, if a king or a minister should seize him, or kill him, or bind him and banish him, or reprove him, saying: 'Ho, man!'"
"You are a thief! You are deluded and ignorant to commit such theft!

Regarding such a matter, if a bhikṣu commits it, at that very moment he is no longer a bhikṣu, no longer a śramaṇa, and no longer a son of the Śākya; he loses the nature of a bhikṣu, falls away, is cut off from the cycle of saṃsāra, is overcome by others, and cannot be recovered.

"From this day forward, you must not intentionally commit the offense of stealing the Dharma. You should cultivate a sense of weary detachment, guard it with earnestness, give rise to a mind of dread, examine yourself with clarity, and practice diligently without negligence."
"Are you able to refrain from doing such things? He replied, "I will not."

“Listen, [Name]! These World-Honored Ones, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as they know and see, have by means of immeasurable methods censured the taking of life, and have praised and extolled the excellence of abstaining from taking life.”
"From this day forth, you, [Name], must not intentionally take the life of even a mosquito or an ant, much less a human being or a human fetus.
Venerable one!"
As the Blessed One said:

"If a bhikṣu should intentionally, with his own hand, take the life of a human being or a human fetus—whether by handing over a knife, or taking up a knife himself, or seeking one who holds a knife; or whether he encourages death or praises death, saying: 'O man!'"
"What use is this sinful, burdensome, and impure evil life?
You had better die now; death is superior to life.

Following his own thoughts, he uses various words to exhort and praise [the person] so as to induce death. If that person dies because of this, then regarding such a matter, the bhikṣu who committed it ceases to be a bhikṣu, a śramaṇa, or a son of the Śākyas at the very moment the act is performed. He loses the nature of a bhikṣu; he has fallen, been extinguished, and cut off from saṃsāra, overcome by another, and cannot be recovered.

"From this day forward, you must not intentionally commit this act of killing; you should cultivate revulsion for it, guard against it with earnestness, examine it with discernment, practice diligently, and remain heedful."
"Are you able to refrain from doing such things? He replied, "I shall not."

"Listen, [Name]! These World-Honored Ones, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, through immeasurable gateways, have condemned false speech as they know and see it; they praise and extol the excellence of abstaining from false speech."
You, [Name], from this day forward, even in jest, you should not intentionally speak falsehoods, much less claim to possess superhuman qualities when you do not actually have them.
"Venerable ones!
As the Blessed One has said:

'If a bhikṣu, being actually without knowledge and without thorough knowledge, knows for himself that he has not attained the state of a superior person, nor the peaceful, noble, and sublime realization, wisdom, vision, and dwelling in bliss, yet says: "I know; I see. "
At another time, whether questioned or unasked, desiring to purify himself, he speaks thus:
"I truly did not know and did not see, yet I said I knew and I saw; it was a false and deceptive lie."
Excluding those with overweening pride, some say:
"I have realized the principle of the Four Noble Truths," or they say:

“Devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits come to converse with me; I have attained the perception of impermanence and other such notions, as well as the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations.
I have realized the fruits of the four noble stages.”

If a bhikṣu commits such an act, at the very moment it is done, he is no longer a bhikṣu, no longer a śramaṇa, and no longer a son of the Śākya; he loses his status as a bhikṣu. He has fallen, been extinguished, and perished from the cycle of saṃsāra; he is overcome by others and cannot be recovered.

"From this day forward, you must not intentionally commit the offense of lying; you should cultivate weary detachment from it, guard against it with earnestness, examine yourself with diligence, and practice with heedfulness."
"Are you able to refrain from doing this?
He replied, "I shall not do it."
"Next, the four kinds of practices that a śramaṇa ought to perform shall be explained: 'Listen, [Name]!

These four kinds of practices that a śramaṇa ought to perform were taught by the World-Honored Ones, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, according to what they know and see, for the sake of those bhikṣus who have received full ordination.'"
What are the four? Listen, [Name]!

From this day forward, if others revile you, you should not revile them in return; if others are angry with you, you should not be angry in return; if others are insolent toward you, you should not be insolent in return; if others strike you, you should not strike them in return. When such disturbances arise, are you able to restrain your mind and refrain from retaliating?
He replied, "I do not report it. [The preceptor] said, "Listen, you, so-and-so!
Previously, you set your mind upon a specific hope, thinking thus:
"When shall I be able to go forth and receive full ordination within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya of the World-Honored One, thereby attaining the status of a bhikṣu?"

"You have already left the household life and now received full ordination (upasampadā). You have obtained excellent and lawful preceptors (upādhyāya) and instructors (ācārya), and the Saṃgha, acting in harmony, has performed the formal act of the fourfold proclamation (jñapti-caturtha-karman), with the wording free from error and perfectly well-established."
Just as other bhikṣus, even those who have completed a hundred years of summer retreat, must train in what is to be learned, so too must you train;
and that which you study, they likewise study. You share the same training rules and recite the same Prātimokṣa Sūtra together with them.

From this day forward, you should give rise to a heart of reverence toward this place and must not feel weary or detached. You should regard your preceptor as a father, and the preceptor should likewise regard you as a son. Until life ends, you should serve and nourish him, tending to his illness, looking after one another with mutual inquiry, and giving rise to a heart of compassion until old age and death.

Furthermore, toward fellow practitioners of the holy life—whether seniors, equals, or juniors—one should always give rise to respect and reverence, following their example with diligence. One should dwell together with them in recitation, study, and meditation, cultivating all manner of wholesome deeds.

Regarding the aggregates, bases, elements, the twelve links of dependent origination, the ten powers, and other such dharmas, one should seek to understand them thoroughly. One must not cast off the yoke of virtue, remain free from all indolence, and strive to attain what has not been attained, to realize what has not been realized, and to manifest what has not been manifested, until finally reaching the fruit of arhatship and ultimate nirvana.

I have now presented for you the general outline of the essential matters in brief; regarding those things not yet known, you should consult the two teachers, as well as your fellow students, friends, and associates.
"Furthermore, when the *Poṣadha-sūtra* is recited during the half-month, you should personally listen to and receive it.
In accordance with the teachings, apply yourselves diligently to practice. Then he spoke a verse, saying:
“You have fully received the śīla within the most excellent teaching;
you should uphold it with a sincere heart, for an unimpeded body is difficult to obtain.”
"One of upright appearance has gone forth; one who is pure has received full ordination.
These are the words spoken by those who speak truth, known by the Perfectly Awakened One.
"You, [Name], have now completed your full ordination. Do not be negligent; you must reverently practice and uphold it."
"Let him go ahead. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-ekottara-karmavastu*, Fascicle One.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-ekottara-karmavastu*.
Fascicle Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Command.
At that time, the Venerable Upāli requested of the World-Honored One, saying:
“Venerable Sir! As the Blessed One has said:
‘Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, by her affection for and delight in the Eight Rules of Respect, has indeed become a renunciant, received full ordination, and attained the status of a bhikṣuṇī.’”
"O Virtuous One! How should the rest of the community of bhikṣuṇīs proceed?
The Buddha told Upāli:
“Other bhikṣuṇīs who have already left the household life but have not yet received full ordination (upasampadā) should perform their duties according to the usual sequence.

If there is a woman living as a layperson who resolves to seek renunciation, she may go at her own convenience to a bhikṣuṇī, who should then inquire about all obstructing factors (antarāyika-dharma).”
If one is fully pure, they may accept [the candidate] according to their wish.

Having accepted them, they confer the Three Refuges along with the five precepts (*pañca-śikṣāpada*), thereby establishing the *upāsikā* discipline. This so-called "protection" (*hū*)—the Sanskrit term being *saraṇa*, translated as "protection" (*yǒngù*)—refers to the protection conferred by receiving the refuges and precepts, which prevents one from falling into the three miserable realms.
The older term "lüyí" (律儀) is a literal translation, meaning "the ritual protocols of the vinaya.
If one were to use only the term "hù" (護, "protection"), there is a fear that students might not understand it in detail; therefore, both terms are retained.
In the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, this has already been translated as "guarding" (*ārakṣa*).
It should be conferred in this manner:

First, after instructing the one seeking to go forth to perform prostrations, have them place both knees on the ground before their preceptor, bow their head, join their palms, and teach them to speak these words:
“‘Venerable Ācārya, please attend to me!

I, [name], from this day forth until the end of my life, take refuge in the Buddha, the most honored among two-legged beings; I take refuge in the Dharma, the most honored among those free from desire; I take refuge in the Saṃgha, the most honored among assemblies.’”
Thus he spoke three times.
The Master said:
"Aupika is translated as 'Good'."
He replied: "Sādu is translated as 'good.
Both have already been annotated as previously stated."
Next, the five precepts are conferred, with the instruction:
"Repeat after my words:
'Venerable Ācārya, please attend to me!'"
Just as the noble Arhats, for as long as they live, do not kill living beings, do not take what is not given, do not engage in sexual misconduct, do not speak falsely, and do not drink intoxicants.

I, [Name], from this day forth until the end of my life, shall not kill living beings, shall not steal, shall not engage in sexual misconduct, shall not speak falsely, and likewise shall not drink intoxicants; these are my five precepts of training.
"This is the training ground of all the noble Arhats; I shall train in it, practice it, and uphold it.
Thus he says three times.
"May the Ācārya bear witness that I am an Upāsikā who has taken refuge in the Three Jewels and received the five precepts."
The Master said, "Excellent. He replied:
"Excellent.
Next, he requested that Upādhyāya be translated as "Preceptor" (Kalyāṇamitra).
To speak of him as "Upādhyāya" is merely the colloquial usage of the Western regions; it is not the formal, canonical term.
However, the Sanskrit originals of all the sūtras and vinayas read "upādhyāya.
The instruction states:
"'Ācārya' is translated as 'Preceptor' (軌範師); [O] Upādhyāya, please attend!"
I, [Name], now request the Venerable Ācārya to be my Upādhyāya; may the Venerable Ācārya act as my Upādhyāya, for by having the Venerable Ācārya as my Upādhyāya, I shall go forth into homelessness.

Thus it was said three times; the subsequent words were the same as before, and upon reaching the third repetition, one should say: "It is merely repeated because the Upādhyāya acts as the Upādhyāya and because of his status as the Preceptor."
"Next, one bhikṣuṇī should be requested to act as the proclaimer to the assembly; she should ask her preceptor:
'Have all obstructive dharmas been inquired about?'"
He replied, "I have already asked.
If one asks, it is well; if one makes a report without having asked, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
Next, announce it to the assembly; all members of the *saṃgha* must gather, or you may inform them by visiting their quarters.

Then, having led her into the midst of the assembly and performed the rites of respect, she should kneel with both knees on the ground before the senior elder (*sthavira*), bow her head, join her palms, and speak these words:
"Listen, O Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha!..."

This person, [Name], seeks to go forth from the Bhikṣuṇī [Name]. While still a layperson in white robes and not yet having had their hair shaved, they wish to go forth within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, receive full ordination, and become a Bhikṣuṇī.
This person, [name], having shaved his hair and donned the Dharma robes, has given rise to right faith and left the household life for the homeless state, with [name] acting as his upādhyāya.
"Does the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha grant ordination to so-and-so?

*Juesuluojiā* (厥蘇洛迦) is correctly translated as *chuan* (a grain basket); this name is established based on its shape. It refers to the lower skirt (*nivāsana*) of a nun, which is four cubits long and two cubits wide. The two ends are sewn together; it is inserted through the waistband and pulled up, covering the navel and reaching behind. It is fastened with a waist-cord at a distance of two finger-widths above the ankles; this is the manner in which the community of nuns in the Western Regions wears their skirts.
There is only this single skirt and no other garments; it suffices for the journey because the ground is warm, unlike in cold countries where many layers are required.
The old translations "Jue-xi-luo" or "Qi-xi-luo" are all erroneous.
The *saṃkakṣikā* is what is known here as a "breast-covering cloth" (*fùpǔ*), which is one cubit longer and exactly the appropriate measure for covering the shoulders and armpits.

The Buddha ordained this out of concern that the three robes might become soiled; thus, it is first used to cover both shoulders, after which the formal Dharma robe is worn over it. It is drawn tight around the neck, and its fastening loops are tied at the top of the shoulder; these fastening loops resemble those of a shirt.
The robe completely covered his body, never exposing the chest; both hands emerged from below and were gathered across the breast, identical to the image of King Aśoka.
Even when performing acts such as paying homage to the Triple Gem, receiving full ordination, or partaking of food, he never permitted the chest to be exposed.
When nuns are in the monastery, the rules are all like this; the monks follow the same practice.
However, when eating or performing prostrations, the monks expose their private parts; this is the custom throughout the Five Indias.
One does not see monks or nuns wearing the *saṃkakṣikā*.
If one is in a monastery, there is no rule for fastening it with ties or knots; because the cotton cloth is light and coarse, it does not fall from the shoulder.

In this region, silk is smooth, so a strap is applied across the chest; this is simply a local custom of dress and has nothing to do with the regulations established by the Buddha. It is merely due to the fact that those who previously translated and transmitted the teachings did not grasp its proper form, referring to it as the *saṃkakṣikā* and also calling it the "shoulder-covering robe."
However, the "shoulder-covering robe" (*kaṭhina*) is actually the *saṃkakṣikā*; to call it the *saṃghāṭī* is an incorrect transmission of the term.
These two names refer to one and the same object, yet they have been forcibly assigned two distinct names.
The *saṃkakṣikā* resembles a sash; its original meaning is "covering the shoulders," yet this term does not appear in the Vinaya.

Furthermore, the ancient-style *saṃkakṣikā* used here in this region is not the original model; it should actually be a *guḍaśīrṣaka* (waist-wrap) that is made of a single piece of cloth with one side opened out, serving as an under-skirt.

“The Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha has already granted the formal procedure for pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) to [Name], with [Name] acting as the preceptor (*upādhyāyī*).
The Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha has granted its consent, as indicated by their silence; thus do I now hold it.”

"Next, one should invite the bhikṣu who will perform the *karmavācanā*, as well as the various bhikṣus to enter the maṇḍala site; the two assemblies of the Saṃgha should gather accordingly, with a minimum of ten bhikṣus and twelve bhikṣuṇīs."
The preceptor instructing the candidate for full ordination (upasampadā) must cause them to prostrate three times to the assembly.

There are two kinds of prostrations, as previously explained; one must certainly perform them toward the Saṃgha, and it is also permissible for the nuns to grasp [the candidate’s] calves during the rite.

When the ritual is concluded, one should kneel with both knees on the ground before the senior monk (upādhyāya), join the palms, and stand; then, one should request full ordination (*upasampadā*), saying:
"May the Saṃgha of the two divisions listen!..."
I, [Name], now for the sake of this matter, shall state the name of my upādhyāya; I seek to receive full ordination from my upādhyāya, [Name].
I, [Name], now request full ordination from the Saṃgha of the two assemblies; for the sake of this matter, I shall state the name of my upādhyāya: [Name] shall be my upādhyāya.
May the Saṃgha of both divisions grant me full ordination; may they take me in and rescue me, and instruct me out of compassion for me.
May those who are capable of compassion do so out of pity for me.
Thus he says three times.

Next, he is led to the place of the *karmavācanā* master; with the same dignified demeanor as before, the master performs the single announcement (*jñapti*) and inquires regarding the obstructing factors (*antarāyika-dharma*), which should be stated as follows:
"May the Sangha of the two assemblies listen!

This person, [Name], seeks to receive full ordination from the preceptor, [Name]. This person, [Name], now requests full ordination from the Saṃgha of both divisions, with [Name] acting as the preceptor.

If the two assemblies of the Saṃgha have reached the time and grant their permission, may the two assemblies allow me now to inquire regarding the obstructing dharmas before them; such-and-such a person shall be my upādhyāya.
"Thus it is announced.
Next, the obstructing dharmas are to be inquired about, as should be understood from above.
Next, the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (motion followed by three proclamations) should be performed, as follows:
"Listen, O Saṃgha of the two assemblies!

This person, so-and-so, seeks to receive full ordination from the preceptor, so-and-so. This woman is twenty years of age; she possesses the five robes and the alms bowl, and her parents, husband, and master have all granted their permission."

The Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha has already granted [the probationer] two years of training in the six dharmas and the six secondary dharmas; this so-and-so has already completed two years of training in the six dharmas and the six secondary dharmas, and the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha has already granted her the formal rite for pure conduct.
This woman has already been able to serve the community of nuns, pleasing their minds, and has practiced with purity, committing no transgression among the nuns.
This [Name], now requests full ordination from the dual Saṃgha, with [Name] acting as her preceptor (upādhyāya).

If the two assemblies of the Saṃgha have reached the time and grant their consent, may the two assemblies of the Saṃgha permit that the two assemblies now confer full ordination upon [Name], with [Name] acting as the upādhyāya.
The motion is as follows:
"Listen, O Saṃgha of both divisions! Next, perform the *karmavācanā*: 'Listen, O Saṃgha of both divisions!'"

This [woman], so-and-so, seeks to receive full ordination from her preceptor, so-and-so; she is twenty years of age, possesses the five robes and the alms bowl, and has received the permission of both parents and her husband.

The Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha has already granted [her] two years of training in the six dharmas and the six secondary dharmas; this [person], so-and-so, has already trained for two years in the six dharmas and the six secondary dharmas, and the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha has already granted her the formal rite of pure conduct (*śīlavatī-dharma*).
This woman has already been able to serve the community of nuns, pleasing their minds and practicing with purity, without any transgression among the nuns.
This [Name], now requests full ordination from the Saṃgha of both divisions, with [Name] acting as her preceptor (upādhyāya).
The Saṃgha of both divisions now confers full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon [Name], with [Name] acting as preceptor (*upādhyāya*).
If the Saṃgha of both divisions consents to confer full ordination upon [Name], with [Name] acting as preceptor, remain silent;
if you do not consent, speak.
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
Thus it is said three times.
"The Saṃgha of both divisions has already conferred full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon [Name], with [Name] acting as the preceptor (*upādhyāya*)."
"The Saṃgha of both divisions has granted its consent; by reason of their silence, I now hold it thus.
Next, one should measure the shadow and announce the five periods of the day, performing these according to the rules for Bhikṣus.
Next, you shall be instructed in the three reliances: "Listen, [Name]!

These three reliances are what all the World-Honored Ones—the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas—know and see; they are taught for the sake of those bhikṣuṇīs receiving full ordination as the 'reliances on the Dharma. That is to say, by relying on this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, one goes forth and receives full ordination, thereby accomplishing the nature of a bhikṣuṇī."
What are the three? Listen, [Name]:

First, rag-robe clothing is pure and easy to obtain; by relying on this, a bhikṣuṇī goes forth and receives full ordination within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, thereby accomplishing the nature of a bhikṣuṇī.
"Venerable [Name], from this day forth until the end of your life, will you take delight in supporting yourself with rag-robes?
He replies, "I shall take delight."

"If you obtain long-term benefits such as plain silk, plain cloth, small or large shawls, light gauze, ramie, cotton, or various other items, or if you further obtain pure robes—whether received from the community or from an individual—you may accept them as appropriate; will you know the proper measure in their use?"
He replied, "I accept it. [The preceptor] said: "Listen, you, so-and-so!..."

2. Constantly begging for alms is pure food that is easily obtained; by relying on this, a bhikṣuṇī goes forth and receives full ordination within the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya, thereby accomplishing the nature of a bhikṣuṇī.
"Venerable [Name], from this day forth until the end of your life, will you take delight in supporting yourself by constantly seeking alms?
He replies, "I shall take delight in it."

"If you obtain long-term benefits such as rice, gruel, or drinks; whether it be food invited for the community in turn, or food invited for individuals; whether it be the regular food of the Sangha, or regular individual offerings, or food on the eighth, fourteenth, or fifteenth day; or if you further obtain pure food, whether received from the assembly or from an individual—will you accept these things accordingly and consume them with moderation?"
He replied, "I accept it. [The preceptor] said, "Listen, you, so-and-so!..."

Third, the discarded medicine is a pure substance that is easily obtained; by relying on this, a bhikṣuṇī may go forth and receive full ordination within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, thereby perfecting her status as a bhikṣuṇī.
"O [Name], from this day forth until the end of your life, do you take pleasure in supporting yourself with discarded medicine? He replies, "I do."

"If you obtain long-term benefits such as ghee, oil, molasses, honey, or medicinal substances consisting of roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, and fruits—whether they be *yāvaj-jīvikā* (lifelong), *saptāhika* (seven-day), or *pratimokṣa* (occasional) medicines—and if you further obtain pure medicines, whether received from the Saṃgha or from an individual, will you accept them accordingly and consume them with moderation?"
She replied, “I have accepted it.
Since a nun has no rule for dwelling alone under a tree, there are thus only three types of formal dependence (*niśraya*). Next, the eight *pārājika* rules are explained:

“Listen, [Name]! There are these eight dharmas which the World-Honored Ones—the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas—knowing and seeing, have declared to be the dharmas of defeat for bhikṣuṇīs who have received full ordination.”

O bhikṣuṇīs, if among these eight [rules] one commits even a single offense, at the very moment of such transgression, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, no longer a śramaṇī, and no longer a daughter of the Śākyas; she loses her status as a bhikṣuṇī. She has fallen away, been cut off, and perished from saṃsāra; she is overcome by others and cannot be restored.
For example, just as when the crown of a tāla tree is cut off, it can no longer sprout, grow, or become tall and large, so it is with a bhikṣuṇī.
What are the eight? "Listen, [Name]!..."

These World-Honored Ones, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, according to what they know and see, have by means of immeasurable methods censured all dharmas of sensual desire; they have taught that sensual desire is defilement, sensual desire is moisture, sensual desire is attachment, sensual desire is domesticity, sensual desire is a fetter, sensual desire is indulgence in pleasure—it is something to be severed, something to be vomited out, something to be loathed and extinguished, and it is a matter of darkness.
"You, [Name], from this day forward, you must not casually look upon men with a lustful mind, much less engage in impure acts with them. Listen, you, [Name]!"
As the Blessed One said:

"If a bhikṣuṇī, having received the training rules together with the other bhikṣuṇīs, does not relinquish those training rules, nor confess her weakness in training, and commits an impure act—the practice of sexual intercourse—even with an animal."

Regarding such matters, if a bhikṣuṇī commits [an offense], at the very moment it is committed, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, no longer a śramaṇī, and no longer a daughter of the Śākyas; she loses the nature of a bhikṣuṇī. She has fallen, been cut off, and perished from saṃsāra; she has been overcome by others and cannot be recovered.

"From this day forward, you must not intentionally transgress these rules of desire; you should cultivate a sense of weary detachment, guard them with earnest gravity, give rise to a mind of dread, examine them with discernment, practice diligently, and remain heedful. Are you able to refrain from such actions?"
He replied, "I do not. [The preceptor] said, "Listen, you, [Name]!

These World-Honored Ones, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, according to what they know and see, have in immeasurable ways censured taking what is not given, and have praised and extolled the excellence of abstaining from taking what is not given as a sublime and wondrous matter.

You, [Name], from this day forward, shall not intentionally steal, even with a thieving mind, the belongings of others as small as a grain of sesame or husk, let alone five *māṣakas* or more than five *māṣakas*. (*Māṣaka* is a name for a unit of measure; it consists of eighty cowrie shells and is not originally a coin, as explained in detail in the preceding commentary.)
“Listen, [Name]! As the Blessed One has said:
‘If a bhikṣuṇī, whether in a village or in a secluded place, takes with a thieving mind an object not given by another...’”
When such theft occurs, whether it be the owner, a minister, or others who seize, kill, bind, expel, or rebuke her, saying: "Hey, woman!"
"You are a thief, foolish and ignorant, to commit such theft!

Regarding such a matter, if a bhikṣuṇī commits [an offense], at the very moment it is committed, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, no longer a śramaṇī, and no longer a daughter of the Śākyas; she loses the nature of a bhikṣuṇī. She has fallen, been cut off, and perished from saṃsāra; she is overcome by others and cannot be restored.

"From this day forward, you must not intentionally commit the offense of stealing the Dharma. You should cultivate a sense of weary detachment, guard it with earnest gravity, give rise to a mind of dread, and practice with diligent scrutiny and heedfulness."
"Are you able to refrain from doing this? He replied, "I shall not."

“Listen, [Name]! All these World-Honored Ones, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, through their knowledge and vision, have in immeasurable ways censured the taking of life and have praised and extolled the excellence of abstaining from taking life.”
You, [Name], from this day forth, you must not intentionally take the life of even a mosquito or an ant, much less a human being or a human fetus.
Listen, [Name]! As the Blessed One has said:

"If a bhikṣuṇī, whether it be a human being or a human fetus, intentionally takes its life with her own hand, or provides a knife, or holds a knife herself, or seeks one who holds a knife, or encourages death, or praises death, saying:..."
"Come now, woman!
What use is this sinful, burdensome, and impure evil life to you?
It would be better for you to die now; death is superior to life."

If, following her own intention, she uses other words to exhort and praise [the person] so as to cause them to die, and they die as a result, then regarding such an act, the bhikṣuṇī commits an offense; at the very moment it is committed, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, no longer a śramaṇī, no longer a daughter of the Śākyas, and she loses the nature of a bhikṣuṇī.
"You will thus fall away and perish, lost in saṃsāra; you will be overcome by others and cannot be recovered.

From this day forward, you must not intentionally commit this act of killing. You should cultivate revulsion for it, guard against it with earnestness, examine it with discernment, practice diligently, and remain heedful.
"Are you able to refrain from doing this? He replied, "I will not."

"Listen, [Name]! These World-Honored Ones, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as they know and see, have disparaged false speech through immeasurable means, and have praised and extolled the excellence of abstaining from false speech."
You, [Name], from this day forward, even in jest, you should not intentionally utter a falsehood, much less claim to possess the qualities of a superior person when you do not actually possess them.
Listen, [Name]! As the Blessed One has said:

"If a bhikṣuṇī, being actually without knowledge and without pervasive knowledge, knowing for herself that she has not attained the state of a superior person, the peaceful, noble, and sublime realization, wisdom, vision, and dwelling in bliss, yet says: 'I know; I see.'"
At another time, whether questioned or unasked, desiring to purify himself, he speaks thus:
"I truly did not know and did not see, yet I said that I knew and saw; this was a false, deceptive, and lying speech."
"Excepting those with overweening pride (adhimāna), some may say:
'I have realized the principle of the Four Noble Truths,' or they may say:"
"Devas, nāgas, and spirits come to converse with me;

I have attained the perception of impermanence and other such notions, realized the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations, and have realized the fruits of the four noble stages."

If a bhikṣuṇī commits such an act, at the very moment it is done, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, no longer a śramaṇī, and no longer a daughter of the Śākyas; she loses her status as a bhikṣuṇī. She has fallen, perished, and is cut off from the cycle of saṃsāra; she is defeated by others and cannot be reclaimed.

"From this day forward, you must not intentionally commit the offense of lying; you should cultivate revulsion for it, guard against it with earnestness, examine yourself with care, practice diligently, and remain heedful."
"Are you able to refrain from doing this?
He replied, "I shall not do it."
"Listen, [Name]! As the Blessed One has said:

'If a bhikṣuṇī, with a mind of lust, together with a man who has a mind of lust, with the intent to experience pleasure, engages in physical contact from below the eyes to above the knees, or if she rubs against him excessively;'"
Regarding such matters, if a bhikṣuṇī commits an offense, at the very moment it occurs, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī.
Therefore, one should examine this thoroughly, practice with diligence, and remain heedful.
"Are you able to refrain from doing such things? He replied, "I shall not."
“Listen, [Name]! As the Blessed One has said:

‘If a bhikṣuṇī, being herself possessed of a lustful mind, with a man who is likewise possessed of a lustful mind, engages in flirtatious laughter, makes mutual appointments, exchanges gestures, travels together, stays in improper places where one should not go, or lies down with her body unrestrained—should she consent to these eight matters, then at the moment she commits such an act, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī.’”
"Up to this point, you have examined the matter with discernment and practiced it diligently without negligence.
Are you able to refrain from doing such things in the future? He replied:
"I shall not do it. "Listen, [Name]! As the World-Honored One has said:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having previously known that another bhikṣuṇī had committed a pārājika offense,
failed to speak of it, and only after that person has died, returned to lay life, or departed, should she say:
'Sisters of the community, you should know that I previously knew this bhikṣuṇī had committed a pārājika offense.'"
Regarding such matters, if a bhikṣuṇī commits an offense, at the time it is declared, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī.
