Thus, one should examine this thoroughly, practice diligently, and remain heedful.
"Are you able to refrain from doing such things? He replied, "I shall not."
“Listen, [Name]! As the Blessed One has said:

‘If a bhikṣuṇī knows that a certain bhikṣu has been subjected to the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation) by the harmonious Saṃgha, and that the community of bhikṣuṇīs has likewise subjected him to the *anavaśrāvaṇīya-dharma* (rule of non-prostration), and that bhikṣu manifests an attitude of reverence toward the Saṃgha, seeking deliverance, and personally petitions within the boundary for the lifting of the *pratisāraṇīya-dharma*.’”
That bhikṣuṇī replied to the bhikṣu, saying: "Noble One!

Do not manifest signs of reverence in the midst of the assembly and seek deliverance by requesting the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* of suspension within your own boundary. I shall provide the Noble One with robes, alms-bowls, and all other requisites so that you lack for nothing; you should settle your mind and engage in recitation and mental cultivation."
Then the bhikṣuṇīs said to this bhikṣuṇī:
"Do you not know that the Saṃgha has performed the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* against this person, and that the bhikṣuṇīs have imposed upon him the rule of non-prostration?"
That bhikṣu, having aroused a humble mind, shall himself request within the boundary the formal act of suspension;
you, meanwhile, shall provide him with robes, alms bowls, and other requisites so that he lacks for nothing.
"You should now abandon this practice of compliance.
When the bhikṣuṇīs have thus admonished her, it is well if she abandons it.
If she does not abandon it, they should admonish her earnestly and correctly up to three times; following their instruction, they should reprove her so as to cause her to abandon that matter.
"It is well if she relinquishes it;
if she does not relinquish it, then at the very moment she acts in such a manner, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī.
Thus, one should examine this thoroughly, practice diligently, and remain heedful.
"Are you able not to do this? He replied, "I will not."
The summary verse says:
The nuns have eight *pārājika* offenses; four are the same as those for the bhikṣus.
The remaining are: touching a man with lustful intent, making an appointment, concealing a fault, and being abandoned by the Saṃgha.
"Next, you should explain the Eight Rules of Reverence: 'Listen, [Name]!

These Eight Rules of Reverence are known and seen by all the World-Honored Ones, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas; they have established these Rules of Reverence for the bhikṣuṇīs. They must be practiced and not transgressed, and all bhikṣuṇīs should diligently train in them as long as life lasts.'"
What are the eight? In the Sanskrit language they are called *gurudharma*. *Guru* carries the meanings of "venerable," "weighty," "teacher," and "that which is to be revered.
Since this term contains many such meanings, have previous translators assigned it to one specific sense at a time, all of which are logically consistent with the principle?
Listen, [Name]! As the Blessed One has said:
"First, bhikṣuṇīs must receive full ordination from bhikṣus in order to achieve the status of a bhikṣuṇī."
This is the first rule of respect established by the Blessed One for the bhikṣuṇīs; it should be practiced and not transgressed, and all bhikṣuṇīs should diligently train in it as long as they live.
Second, every half-month, the bhikṣuṇīs should request from the bhikṣus a person to provide instruction for them.
Third, they should not enter the rainy season retreat in a place where no bhikṣus are present.
Fourth, if one sees a bhikṣu commit a transgression, one should not reprimand him.
Fifth, one should not scold a bhikṣu with anger.
Sixth, an elderly bhikṣuṇī should pay homage to a junior bhikṣu.
Seventh, one should perform the *mānatva* penance within the two assemblies every half-month.
Eighth, one should go to the place of the bhikṣus for the purpose of the *pravāraṇā*.
These eight dharmas are to be practiced and must not be transgressed.
“Bhikṣuṇīs, for as long as you live, you should diligently train yourselves.
A summary verse says:
“Full ordination from bhikṣus; every half-month, requesting instruction.”
Relying on the bhikṣus for the summer retreat; not speaking of faults one has seen;
not scolding with anger and bowing to those junior; rejoicing in the minds of both assemblies;
and following one's will in the presence of the bhikṣus—these are called the Eight Rules of Respect.
"Next, the four types of practices to be observed by śramaṇīs are explained: 'Listen, [Name]!

These four types of practices to be observed by śramaṇīs were taught for the full ordination of bhikṣuṇīs by all those World-Honored Ones, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, according to what they know and see.'"
What are the four? "Listen, [Name]!

From this day forward, if others revile you, you should not revile them in return; if others are angry with you, you should not be angry in return; if others mock you, you should not mock them in return; if others strike you, you should not strike them in return. When such disturbances and afflictions arise, are you able to restrain your mind, subdue your anger and pride, and refrain from retaliating?"
He replied, "I do not report it. [The teacher] said, "Listen, you, so-and-so!
Previously, you set your mind upon a specific hope, thinking thus:
"When shall I be able to go forth in the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya of the World-Honored One, receive full ordination, and become a bhikṣuṇī?"

"You have already left the household life and now received full ordination (*upasampadā*). You have obtained a qualified preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and instructor (*ācārya*), and the harmonious Saṃgha has performed the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* without error; you are now perfectly established."
Just as with the other community of bhikṣuṇīs, even those who have completed a hundred years of rain-retreat, that which you ought to study, they also practice and study;
and that which they study, you likewise do the same. You share the same training rules and recite the same Prātimokṣa Sūtra together.

"From this day forward, you should give rise to a heart of reverence toward this place and must not feel weary or detached. You should regard your preceptor as your mother, and the preceptor should likewise regard you as his daughter. As long as life remains, you shall serve, nourish, and attend to him when he is ill, looking after one another with mutual inquiry, giving rise to a heart of compassion until old age and death."

Furthermore, toward fellow practitioners of the holy life—whether seniors, equals, or juniors—one should always give rise to reverence and respect, dwelling with them in accordance with their wishes through diligent service. One should engage in recitation, study, and meditative reflection to cultivate all wholesome deeds; one should seek to understand and realize the teachings on the aggregates, sense bases, elements, the twelve links of dependent origination, the ten powers, and so forth. Without casting off the yoke of virtue, remaining free from all indolence, one should strive to attain what has not been attained, seek to understand what has not been understood, and seek to realize what has not been realized, until finally attaining the fruit of Arhatship and ultimate Nirvana.

I have now provided you with a general outline of the essential points; regarding anything else you may not yet know, you should consult the two teachers, as well as your fellow students, spiritual friends, and associates.
Furthermore, when the *Poṣadha* Sūtra is recited during the half-month, you should personally listen and receive it, and practice diligently according to the teaching.
He spoke in verse, saying:
“In the most excellent teaching, You have fully received the *śīla*;”
One should uphold this with a sincere heart; a body free from obstacles is difficult to obtain.
Those who are upright leave the household life; those who are pure receive full ordination.
These are the words spoken by one who speaks truth, known by the Perfectly Awakened One.
“‘You, [Name], have now completed your full ordination (*upasampadā*); do not be negligent, but you must reverently carry out the precepts.
Then, have him go on ahead.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-ekottara-karmavastu*, Fascicle 2.
The Hundred and One Karmas of the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya,
Volume Three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Command.
Regarding the formal motion for taking on a disciple, as the Blessed One has taught:
"If a bhikṣuṇī who has completed twelve years of seniority wishes to take on a disciple, she should request the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for taking on a disciple from the community of bhikṣuṇīs."
The request should be made as follows:

having spread out the seats and struck the *ghanṭī*, once the formal announcement has been completed and the bhikṣuṇīs have assembled—at least twelve in number—that bhikṣuṇī, having paid respects before the senior bhikṣuṇī, should squat with palms joined and make this formal announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha of Bhikṣuṇīs, please listen!"
I, [Name], having completed twelve years since full ordination, wish to maintain a circle of disciples.

I, [Name], now request from the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha the authorization to maintain disciples. May the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha grant me, [Name], who have completed twelve years since full ordination, the authorization to maintain disciples.
"May those who are compassionate please show us mercy.
This should be said a second and a third time.
Next, one bhikṣuṇī shall perform the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*) as follows:
“‘Venerable Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣuṇī [Name], having completed twelve years since her full ordination, wishes to maintain a female disciple.
This [Name] now requests from the Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha the formal authorization to maintain a female disciple.’”

If it is the proper time for the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha and they grant their permission, may the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha allow that the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha now grant [this] nun, who has completed twelve years since her full ordination, the authorization to maintain a female disciple.
The motion is thus made.
Next, perform the *karmavācanā*:
"Venerable Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣuṇī [Name], having completed twelve years since her full ordination, wishes to maintain female disciples.
This [Name] now requests from the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha the formal authorization to maintain female disciples.
The Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha now grants [the name] So-and-so the full twelve-year period for maintaining a female disciple.
If the venerable ones consent to granting So-and-so the full twelve-year period for maintaining a female disciple, let them remain silent; if they do not consent, let them speak.
"The Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha has already completed the formal procedure for [the nun] so-and-so to keep a female disciple for twelve full years.
The Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha has granted its consent, as indicated by their silence; thus do I now uphold this."
"Once you have attained the Dharma, you should accept disciples and not harbor any doubts.

Regarding the formal motion (jñapti-dvitīya-karman) for a nun to accept an unlimited number of disciples: "If a bhikṣuṇī wishes to accept an unlimited number of disciples, she should request from the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha the procedure for accepting an unlimited number of disciples."
One should beg in this manner:

having completed the formal announcement (*jñapti*), the seats and mats are spread, the *ghanṭī* is struck, and the preliminary preparations are made; then, with palms joined, one makes the following announcement:
"May the Noble Community of Nuns listen!..."
I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], wish to maintain an unlimited number of disciples.

I, [Name], now request from the saṃgha of bhikṣuṇīs the rule for maintaining an unlimited number of disciples; may the saṃgha of bhikṣuṇīs grant me, [Name], the rule for maintaining an unlimited number of disciples.
"May those who are capable of compassion please show us mercy.
A second and third time, it was spoken in this same manner.
Next, one bhikṣuṇī performed the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*):
"Venerable Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣuṇī [Name] wishes to maintain an unlimited number of female disciples; this [Name] now requests from the Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha the formal procedure for maintaining an unlimited number of female disciples."

If it is the proper time for the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha and they grant their consent, may the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha permit that the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha now grant [the nun] so-and-so the rule of maintaining an unlimited number of disciples.
"I state this as follows.
Next, perform the *karmavācanā*:
"Venerable Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣuṇī, so-and-so, wishes to maintain an unlimited number of female disciples; she now requests from the saṃgha of bhikṣuṇīs the formal authorization to maintain an unlimited number of female disciples.
The Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha now grants so-and-so the rule of maintaining an unlimited number of disciples.
If those venerable ones approve of granting so-and-so the rule of maintaining an unlimited number of disciples, they should remain silent; if they do not approve, they should speak.
“The Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha has already completed the formal act of granting [the status of] ‘one who keeps unlimited disciples’ to so-and-so.
The Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha has granted its consent, as is evident by their silence; thus do I now uphold this.”
"Once a bhikṣuṇī has received this rule, she may keep as many as she wishes according to her inclination; do not harbor any doubt.

The *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (formal motion with one proclamation) regarding not being separated from the *saṃghāṭī*: "If a bhikṣu is aged and infirm, or if he is afflicted by illness and lacks physical capability, and his *saṃghāṭī* robe is so heavy that he cannot carry it while walking, that bhikṣu should request from the Saṃgha the rule of not being separated from the *saṃghāṭī* robe."
One should beg in this manner:

having performed the preliminary rites, with at least four persons within the precincts of the maṇḍala, that bhikṣu should bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, and squat before the elder with palms joined, paying respect as appropriate. He should then make the following formal announcement:

"It should be known that in the Western tradition, one does not wear shoes when entering the assembly; the instruction here to 'remove them' is intended for profound prevention. If anyone comes wearing them, they must all be removed. In cases of illness, one should act according to the circumstances. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
I, the bhikṣu [Name], am aged and infirm, or perhaps afflicted by illness and lacking physical capacity; the saṃghāṭī robe is heavy and I am unable to carry it while traveling.

I, the bhikṣu [Name], now request from the Saṃgha the practice of not being separated from the saṃghāṭī robe. May the virtuous Saṃgha grant me, [Name], the practice of not being separated from the saṃghāṭī robe.
"May those who are capable of compassion please show mercy.
A second and a third time, he should speak thus.
Next, one bhikṣu shall perform the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*) as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu [name], being aged and infirm, or suffering from illness and lacking physical capability, is unable to carry and travel with his saṃghāṭī robe due to its weight."
This [person], so-and-so, now requests from the Saṃgha the practice of not being separated from the saṃghāṭī robe.

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha grant its permission; the Saṃgha shall now bestow upon this person, so-and-so, the practice of not being separated from the saṃghāṭī robe.
"Thus it is announced.

"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This bhikṣu [Name] is aged and infirm, or perhaps afflicted by illness and lacks physical capacity; he is unable to carry and travel with his saṃghāṭī robe because it is heavy."
The bhikṣu [Name] now requests from the Saṃgha the practice of not being separated from his saṃghāṭī robe; the Saṃgha now grants the practice of not being separated from the saṃghāṭī robe to [Name].
"If the Venerable Ones approve of granting the procedure for not being separated from the saṃghāṭī robe to [Name], let them remain silent; if they do not approve, let them speak.
The Saṃgha has finished granting the procedure for not being separated from the saṃghāṭī robe to [Name]."
"The Saṃgha has granted its consent; by reason of their silence, I now hold it to be so.
Once a bhikṣu has received this authorization, he may wear his upper and lower robes and travel as he pleases; let him not harbor any doubt.
"Just as it is for the bhikṣus, so should it be granted to the bhikṣuṇīs accordingly.
Next, the method for establishing the boundary (sīmābandha) is explained as taught by the Blessed One:
"O bhikṣus, you should establish a boundary within your dwelling place."
At that time, the bhikṣus did not know how many kinds of boundaries there were,
nor how they should be demarcated.
The Buddha said:
"There are two kinds of boundaries:

first, the small boundary (kṣudrasīma), and second, the great boundary (mahāsīma). Within the marked limits of the great boundary, one may establish a small boundary precinct in a location free from obstacles or difficulties."
The resident bhikṣus should together examine the four sides of the small boundary (*kṣudrasīman*) for long-established landmarks.

For example, in the east, these may be the appearance of a wall, or a tree, or a fence, or an earthen mound, or an upright stone, or a driven stake; the landmarks for the south, west, and north should be understood accordingly according to the specific circumstances.

Having already identified the boundary markers and completed the formal announcement (*jñapti*), one should perform the preliminary rites until the entire assembly has gathered. Once the resident bhikṣus have collectively designated the long-standing boundary markers for the four sides of the small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*), they should instruct one bhikṣu to perform the formal act of motion (*jñapti-karman*) in this manner:
"Listen, venerable Saṃgha!..."

Now, here at this place, the resident bhikṣus together proclaim the long-standing boundary markers for the four sides of the small boundary: such-and-such a marker in the east, and so on, up to such-and-such a marker in the north.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha grant permission that the Saṃgha now establishes a small boundary (kṣudrasīmā) within this marked area.
This is the formal motion (jñapti).

"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! Now, all the resident bhikṣus here together declare the long-standing boundary markers for the four sides of this small boundary: such-and-such a marker in the east, up to such-and-such a marker in the north."
The Saṃgha now intends to establish a small boundary (sīmā) within these marked limits.
If the venerable ones consent to the establishment of this small boundary within these marked limits, let them remain silent; if they do not consent, let them speak.
"The Saṃgha has finished establishing this small boundary within these marked limits.
Since the Saṃgha has granted its consent by remaining silent, I now hold it to be so."

Next, the method for binding the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) is explained: "The resident bhikṣus shall first collectively observe the long-standing boundary markers at the four cardinal directions of the great boundary. For example, in the east, these may be the appearance of a wall, or a tree, or a fence, or an earthen mound, or an upright stone, or a driven stake; the same should be understood for the south, west, and north accordingly."
Having thus declared the boundary markers, they spread out the seats, struck the *ghanṭī*, and performed the preliminary rites until the entire assembly had gathered.
The resident bhikṣus then collectively recited the four directional markers of the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*).
Once the assembly has recognized these boundary markers, they should have one bhikṣu perform the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*) as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

Now, all the resident bhikṣus here together proclaim the long-established boundary markers for the four sides of the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*): such-and-such a marker in the east, up to such-and-such a marker in the north."

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha permit that the Saṃgha now establish within these boundary marks a Great Boundary (mahā-sīmā) for the purpose of the *poṣadha* and the practice of dwelling together, extending from the forest hermitage to this residence, excluding the village and its surrounding precincts.
The motion is thus made.
Next, perform the *karmavācanā*: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

Now, all the resident bhikṣus here together proclaim the long-established boundary markers for the four sides of the great boundary: such-and-such a marker in the east, and so on, up to such-and-such a marker in the north.

The Saṃgha now establishes within these boundary markers a great boundary for the Saṃgha—a single *poṣadha* residence—extending from the forest hermitage to this dwelling place, excluding the village and its surrounding precincts.

Venerable sirs, if you approve of establishing this great boundary for the Saṃgha—a single *poṣadha* residence within this marked domain, extending from the forest hermitage to this dwelling site, with the exception of the village and its precincts—then remain silent;
if you do not approve, please speak.
“The Saṃgha has completed the formal delimitation of this great boundary for the Saṃgha’s shared residence and the *poṣadha* ceremony within these marked limits.
Since the Saṃgha has granted its consent by remaining silent, I now hold it to be so.”

“If, in this dwelling place, the Saṃgha has already completed the formal demarcation of the Great Boundary (mahā-sīmā), all the bhikṣus residing therein should assemble in one place to perform the Poṣadha and the Pravāraṇā ceremonies, as well as all types of formal acts (karmans), such as the single motion (jñapti), the motion with one proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya), and the motion with three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha).”
If the assembly does not gather, the ritual procedure will not be accomplished, and one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
Furthermore, within the boundaries of the great perimeter (mahā-sīmā), one may establish a "robe-not-left-behind" boundary (cīvara-asthāpana-sīmā) for bhikṣus.
It should be bound in this manner:
having performed the preliminary rites, one bhikṣu shall first make the formal announcement (*jñapti*), and then the *karmavācanā* shall be performed.
The formal announcement for binding the boundary where robes need not be kept within (*acīvarāpattika-sīmā*) is as follows: "Listen, venerable Saṃgha!
In this dwelling place, the harmonious Saṃgha has previously together established a single *poṣadha* boundary for co-residence and a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) for the Saṃgha.

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and they grant permission, may the Saṃgha allow that the Saṃgha now establish upon this great boundary a *bhiḳṣu-acīvara-asthāpana-sīmā* (the boundary within which monks do not lose their robes).
"Thus it is announced. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

In this dwelling place, the harmonious Saṃgha has previously together established a great boundary (mahā-sīmā) for the community, according to the rule of a common residence for the single Poṣadha ceremony."
The Saṃgha now intends to establish, upon this great boundary (mahā-sīmā), a zone where monks do not lose their robes (acīvara-nāśana-sīmā).
If the venerable ones consent to establishing this zone where monks do not lose their robes upon this great boundary, let them remain silent; if they do not consent, let them speak.
“The Saṃgha has completed the formal establishment of the ‘Boundary for Not Losing Robes’ for Bhikṣus upon this Great Boundary.
Since the Saṃgha has granted its consent by remaining silent, I now hold it to be so.”

If the Saṃgha has already established the *acīvarāpatti-sīmā* (the boundary where one is not guilty of being separated from robes), then even if one travels outside that boundary with only the upper and lower robes, there is no fault of being separated from one's robes.
If it is necessary to dissolve the *mahāsīmā* (the great boundary), it should be dissolved by means of a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).
Upon the great boundary (mahā-sīmā), one should spread out the seats and strike the *ghanṭī* bell; if the assembly does not gather, there must be at least four.
The bhikṣu should first perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*), and only then carry out the ritual act (*karman*).
The formal motion for dissolving the large and small boundaries (*sīmā*) by means of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
At this residence, the harmonious Saṃgha has previously together established a single great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) for the community of monks who dwell together according to the *poṣadha* rules."
"If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha grant permission; the Saṃgha shall now dissolve the great boundary (mahā-sīmā).
This is the formal motion (jñapti). "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"

In this dwelling place, the harmonious Saṃgha has previously together established a great boundary (mahā-sīmā) for the practice of the Uposatha and communal residence; the Saṃgha now dissolves this great boundary.
"If the Venerable Ones approve of the dissolution of this great boundary (mahā-sīmā), let them remain silent; if they do not approve, let them speak.
This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third [proclamations] are to be spoken in the same manner."
"The Saṃgha has finished dissolving the great boundary (mahā-sīmā).
Since the Saṃgha has granted its consent by remaining silent, I now hold it thus.
When it is desired to dissolve a small boundary (kṣudra-sīmā), it should be dissolved by means of a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman).

Within the small boundary of the ritual arena, one should arrange seats and strike the *ghanṭī*; with at least four *bhikṣus* present, one should first perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*) before proceeding to the ritual action (*karman*).
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
At this dwelling place, the harmonious Saṃgha has previously together established a small boundary (sīmā).
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and you grant permission, may the Saṃgha allow that the Saṃgha now together dissolve this small boundary."
"Thus it is announced. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
At this dwelling place, the harmonious Saṃgha has previously together established a small boundary enclosure (*kṣudrasīmā*). The Saṃgha now together dissolves this small boundary enclosure."
"If the Venerable Ones approve of this small boundary field, let them remain silent; if they do not approve, let them speak.
This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third [proclamations] are likewise spoken."
"The Saṃgha has finished dissolving the small boundary enclosure.
Since the Saṃgha has given its consent by remaining silent, I now hold it to be so.

If one wishes to simultaneously establish both the small and great boundaries, as well as simultaneously dissolve them both, the resident bhikṣus must first establish the four directional markers for the small boundary; they must first determine the eastern wall-mark, whether it be a tree, a fence, a hedge, an earthen mound, a standing stone, or a driven stake, and the same applies to the south, west, and north.

Next, one should determine the boundary markers for the four directions of the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), following the same procedure as previously explained for the small boundary (*khuḍḍaka-sīmā*).

Upon both boundaries, the two saṃghas shall assemble; each shall arrange their seats and strike the *gaṇḍī*. After the formal announcement has been made and the assembly has gathered, a single bhikṣu should proclaim the boundary markers for the four directions of the small boundary, beginning from a certain marker in the east and proceeding up to a certain marker in the north.

Having thus recited the boundary markers, one next recites the markers for the four sides of the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), beginning from a certain marker in the east and proceeding up to a certain marker in the north.

Once the markers of the great boundary have been recited, the monk presiding over the rite should place either a bed, a stool, or a mat upon the two boundaries; he must first perform the formal motion (*jñapti*) before proceeding with the ritual act (*karmavācanā*).
“‘Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

Now, at this location, all the resident bhikṣus together proclaim the long-standing boundary markers for the four sides of the small boundary: such-and-such a marker in the east, up to such-and-such a marker in the north;
they together proclaim the long-standing boundary markers for the four sides of the great boundary: such-and-such a marker in the east, up to such-and-such a marker in the north.’”
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and they grant their permission, let the Saṃgha authorize that the Saṃgha now establishes a small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*) within these marked limits.

Let the Saṃgha now establish a great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) for the *poṣadha* and the rule of communal residence within these marked limits, extending from the forest hermitage to this dwelling place, excluding the village and its surrounding area.
The motion is thus made.
Next, the *karmavācanā* is performed: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

Now, at this location, all the resident bhikṣus together proclaim the long-standing boundary markers for the four sides of the small boundary: such-and-such a marker in the east, up to such-and-such a marker in the north;
they also together proclaim the long-standing boundary markers for the four sides of the great boundary: such-and-such a marker in the east, up to such-and-such a marker in the north.

The Saṃgha now establishes a small boundary field within these marked limits, and within these same marked limits, it establishes a great boundary for the Saṃgha—a single *poṣadha* residence governed by the rules of communal living.
From the forest hermitage to this dwelling place— excluding here the village and its precincts—

if the Venerable Ones consent to demarcate a small boundary (kṣudrasīmā) within these marks, and to demarcate within these marks a great boundary (mahāsīmā) for the Saṃgha’s shared residence for the purpose of the Poṣadha ceremony, from the forest hermitage to this dwelling place— excluding here the village and its precincts—
let those who consent remain silent; if you do not consent, speak.

"The Saṃgha has already established a small boundary (sīmā) within this marked area, and has completed the establishment of the great boundary (mahāsīmā) for the Saṃgha’s shared residence and the performance of the Poṣadha ceremony within this marked area."
"The Saṃgha has granted its consent, as indicated by their silence; thus do I now uphold it.

Thereafter, the assembly of bhikṣus rose from their seats, gathered together in one place within the great boundary (mahā-sīmā), and established a "bhikṣu’s non-separation-from-robes boundary" (acīvara-vippavāsa-sīmā) inside the limits of the great boundary, performing the formal act of motion and resolution (jñapti-dvitīya-karman) as previously described.
If one wishes to achieve simultaneous dual-release in both realms, one should assemble the two saṃghas within the two boundaries, arrange the seats, and perform the preliminary formalities.
The presiding officer, having pressed down upon both boundaries with beds, mats, stools, and the like, should first make the announcement (*jñapti*), and then perform the *karmavācanā*:
"Listen, venerable Saṃgha!..."

In this dwelling place, the harmonious Saṃgha has previously together established a great boundary (mahā-sīmā) for the practice of the Poṣadha and communal residence, as well as a small boundary enclosure (kṣudra-sīmā).

"If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha grant permission that the Saṃgha now dissolve the great boundary (mahā-sīmā) and dissolve the small boundary field (kṣudra-sīmā).
This is the formal motion (jñapti). "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"

In this dwelling place, the harmonious Saṃgha has previously together established a single Great Boundary (mahā-sīmā) for the practice of the Poṣadha and communal residence, along with the Small Boundary Enclosures (khuḍḍaka-sīmā). The Saṃgha now dissolves this Great Boundary and dissolves the Small Boundary Enclosures.
If the Venerable Ones approve of the dissolution of this great boundary and the dissolution of the small boundary enclosure, let them remain silent; if they do not approve, let them speak.
This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third times were spoken in the same manner:
"The Saṃgha has completed the dissolution of the great boundary (mahā-sīmā) and the dissolution of the small boundary enclosure (kṣudra-sīmā).
Since the Saṃgha has granted its consent by remaining silent, I now hold it to be so."
The Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One, saying: "Bhadanta,
since there is no such thing as a 'non-dharma-realm' (adharma-dhātu), to what extent can something be called a 'realm' (dhātu)?"
The Buddha said:

"If there are bhikṣus residing in a village, within the area enclosed by walls or fences, as well as the surrounding territory, they should assemble in one place to perform the *poṣadha* ceremony and the *pravāraṇā*. They should perform all formal procedures, from the single motion (*jñapti*), the motion with one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*), up to the motion with three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*)."
"If they do not assemble, the ritual act will not be accomplished, and one incurs the offense of separate residence.
"Venerable Sir! In a place where there is no village:"
"To what extent are an araṇya (forest hermitage) and an empty field defined as a boundary?
The Buddha said:

"Each is defined by a circumference of one krośa. All bhikṣus should assemble in one place; within this boundary, they may perform the poṣadha ceremony, as well as all matters up to the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*."

If they do not assemble, the ritual procedure will not be accomplished, and one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma (*vyatikrama-dharma*). "Not performing the dharma-boundary" means not performing the formal act of establishing the boundary (*sīmā-bandha*).
The old translation "spontaneous" (*svayambhū*) is incorrect.
The Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One, saying:
"Bhadanta, as the Blessed One has said:..."
“Monks, you should establish a great boundary (mahā-sīmā).
The community of monks did not know up to what extent the establishment of a boundary was called a “great boundary.
The Buddha said:

Regarding the establishment of the Great Boundary (mahā-sīmā), it may extend up to two and a half *yojana*s. As for the term *yojana*, since there is no direct equivalent in meaning, it corresponds to one *li* in the Eastern Land (China), which is approximately thirty li or more.
The old term "yojana" is a corruption and abbreviation.
According to the secular conventions of the Western Regions (India), four krosas constitute one yojana; one krosa is calculated to be eight *li*, which corresponds to thirty-two *li* here.
According to the internal teachings, eight *krośas* constitute one *yojana*; one *krośa* consists of five hundred *dhanus*, and each *dhanu* is measured by the number of steps.
Calculating by these paces, it amounts to just over one and a half *li*; multiplying this by eight yields twelve *li*, which does not even suffice for a single postal station (*yì*).

Having personally verified that a *yojana* in the Western Regions today corresponds to approximately one postal station, I have now translated [the term] as "one postal station" throughout, so that there may be no excessive distance or delay.
"In that case, Nālandā Monastery is five krośas south of Rājagṛha; by calculation, its distance is only slightly more than one postal station. "Venerable Sir!"
"If it exceeds two and a half *yojanas*, can it still constitute a boundary?
The Buddha said, "It may, provided it does not exceed two and a half *yojanas*; that is the limit of its boundary."
“Venerable One! Downward, to what extent is it called the 'Great Boundary' (mahā-sīmā)?
The Buddha said:
"The point where one reaches water is called the boundary. "Venerable Sir!
If one goes two and a half *yojanas* further downward until reaching water, would that also be called a boundary?"
The Buddha said:
“It is only two and a half yojanas; that is its boundary.
“Venerable Sir! [he asked.]
"Upward, to what limit is it called the Great Boundary?
The Buddha said:
"If there is a tree within the boundary, the boundary extends to the treetop."
"If there is a wall within the boundary, and the boundary extends to the top of that wall, this is called a boundary.
"Venerable Sir! If it is two and a half *yojanas* outside, reaching as far as the treetops or the top of a wall, is this also a boundary?"
The Buddha said, "It extends for exactly two and a half yojanas; that is its boundary.
"Venerable Sir! [he asked.]
"If there is a mountain within the boundary, to what extent is it considered part of that boundary?
The Buddha said,
"It extends upward as far as the water."
“Venerable Sir! Is that which lies beyond two and a half *yojanas* on the outer side, reaching as far as the water, also called a boundary (*sīmā*)?
The Buddha said:
"Because two and a half *yojanas* is the fixed measure.
The Venerable Upāli then requested of the Blessed One, "Bhadanta!..."
"Is it possible that, having failed to dissolve a previous boundary, one may subsequently re-establish it again, and thereby succeed in forming a valid boundary?
The Buddha said,
"It is not possible."
“Venerable Sir! Is it possible to enter another realm by means of one realm?
The Buddha said:
"No. "Venerable sir! How many kinds of boundaries are there that do not overlap?"
The Buddha said:
"There are four kinds of boundaries. What are the four?"
That is to say: a small boundary enclosure, a place where water currently remains, the boundary of bhikṣus, and the boundary of bhikṣuṇīs.
None of these may be entered, nor may they be re-established. "Venerable Sir!"
"Is it possible to enclose one boundary with another boundary?
The Buddha said:
"It is not possible, except for places where water is currently present, small boundary areas, and the boundary of bhikṣuṇīs."
“Venerable Sir! How many factors cause the loss of the great boundary (mahā-sīmā)?
The Buddha said:
"There are five. What are the five?
First, the entire Saṃgha has all undergone a transformation of their sexual organs."
Second, the entire Saṃgha collectively abandons [the site] and departs;
third, the entire Saṃgha all return to lay life;
fourth, the entire Saṃgha passes away simultaneously.
"Fifth, all the Saṃgha performs the ritual to dissolve it. "Venerable Sir,
is it possible to use a single tree as the boundary marker for two, three, or four dwelling places?"
The Buddha said, "It may be done;
you should take the trees and each occupy one side.
"Venerable Sir! [they replied.]
"Is it permissible to perform a *karmavācanā* by taking the number of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, as part of the *saṃgha*?
The Buddha said:
"It is not permissible."
"Because of the distinction in the nature of the Buddha-jewel. "Venerable Sir!
As the Blessed One has said:"
"There is pure ground and impure ground.
I do not yet know what is called pure ground,
and what is called impure ground?
The Buddha said:
"As long as the True Dharma remains in the world, there are pure grounds and impure grounds.
However, after the True Dharma has disappeared, all shall become pure."
“If that is so, what is meant by the ‘abiding of the True Dharma,’ and what is meant by the ‘disappearance of the True Dharma?
The Buddha said:

"There are those who preside over the *karmavācanā* and those who practice in accordance with the teachings; since there are both those capable of performing the legal rites and those who follow the practice, this is called the True Dharma abiding in the world."
"If the *karmavācanā* is not performed and there are no practitioners who follow the teachings, this is called the disappearance of the True Dharma.
"Venerable Sir, is it possible to cross from one boundary to another?"
The Buddha said, “It is not permitted. [He asked:
“If that is so, how many places are there that one must not transgress?”
The Buddha said:
"There are five places. What are the five?"
First, a small boundary field;
second, a place where water currently remains;
third, the boundary of the bhikṣus.
"Fourth, the boundary of the bhikṣuṇīs;
fifth, the space between two boundaries. "Venerable Sir!"
"If that is so, may one establish a boundary (sīmā) across places where there is water?
The Buddha said:
"If there are bridges between rivers, one may establish a boundary across them; otherwise, it is not permitted."
“Venerable One! If a bridge is broken, for how long may one remain within the boundary without it being lost?
The Buddha said:
"I shall maintain this bridge for up to seven days without forming the intention to abandon it;
if I do not do so, its boundary will be lost. "Venerable Sir!"
"When the boundary is being formally established, if the officiant suddenly dies, is the establishment of the boundary accomplished?
The Buddha said:

"It is not accomplished. However, if the ritual for the boundary's dimensions has been performed and the *karmavācanā* has already been recited for the majority of its parts, the establishment of the boundary is accomplished even if he passes away."
If, after the boundary markers have been designated, a portion of the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) is deficient, the establishment of the boundary is not accomplished and must be performed again.
The same should be understood for the boundary of bhikṣuṇīs.
"Venerable Sir! Is it possible for one person who has received one motion (*jñapti*), one formal act (*karmavācanā*), and one presiding officer to perform a formal act in four locations?
The Buddha said:
"One may establish four boundaries, each accommodating three people.
The one who presides over the legal procedure may place a bed, a mat, a stool, a board, or similar object upon the four boundaries, and only then perform the legal act."
This one person may fulfill the requirement for the four boundaries (*sīmā*) to constitute the quorum.
If there are five persons, four persons shall be stationed at each of the four boundaries for the Dharma-affairs;
if there are ten persons, nine persons shall be stationed at each of the four boundaries for the affairs of the Saṃgha.
Regarding the matter of twenty persons, each of the four boundaries requires nineteen people.
However, for such a *karmavācanā*, one person who presides over the ritual may serve all four boundaries; thus, he should preside over them all.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of saṃghas that perform *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical acts). What are the five?
The first is a saṃgha of four persons;...
Second, the saṃgha of five persons;
third, the saṃgha of ten persons;
fourth, the saṃgha of twenty persons.
Fifth, beyond this:

if there are four persons residing in a dwelling place, they may perform all *karmas*, with the sole exception of the *pravāraṇā*, the full ordination (*upasampadā*), and the removal of offenses before a group of twenty; all other [acts] may be performed.

If there are five persons in a residence, all [formal acts] may be performed except for the full ordination in the Central Kingdom and the removal of offenses within a group of twenty; all others may be carried out.
If there are ten members of the Saṃgha in a residence, all [formal acts] may be performed except for the removal of offenses; all others may be carried out.
"If there are twenty members of the Saṃgha or more at a residence, all *karmas* should be performed; do not harbor any doubts.

Regarding the small boundary (*sīmā*), the great boundary, and the boundary for not losing one's robes (*acīvarāpatti-sīmā*) for bhikṣuṇīs—whether they are being dissolved or established, whether the ritual procedure is valid or invalid, and the spatial dimensions and limits—their rules are the same as those for the great bhikṣus; since they follow that precedent, they are not set forth again here.
The Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One: "Bhadanta,
how many types of Prātimokṣa Sūtra are there in total?"
The Buddha said:
"There are five kinds. What are the five?

First is the recitation of the introduction; the remainder is informed by what is commonly heard. That which is called *poṣadha* in the Indic language—where *poṣa* means "nourishing" and *dha* means "purifying and washing"—intends that every half-month one should recall the transgressions committed, confess those sins before those who have not erred, and hope to reform past faults.

First, it prevents further transgressions in the present; second, it serves as a warning against arrogance regarding the Dharma in the future. For these reasons, everyone must assemble together to hear the *Prātimokṣa Sūtra*, thereby causing wholesome dharmas to flourish. Is this not the supreme foundation for upholding the teachings? How could it be merely a matter of performing prostrations and repentance in the hall?
This is merely a general inclusion of lay associates, wherein one restrains coarse appearances while setting the mind [on purity].
According to the standards of the monastic community, it is insufficient to clear away one's culpability for transgressions.
The traditional rendering as "uposatha" (布薩) is erroneous.
Second, having finished reciting the introduction and the four *pārājika* dharmas, the remainder is announced as being "always heard.
Third, having finished reciting the introduction up to the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas, the remainder is announced as being "always heard."
"Fourth, recite the introduction up to the two *aniyata* dharmas; the remainder may be announced as having been heard regularly.
Fifth, recite the introduction through to the end.
At that time, on the fifteenth day during the *poṣadha*, the World-Honored One took his seat among the assembly of bhikṣus and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“The night has passed; it is time for the Poṣadha ceremony.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms in reverence, and spoke these words:
“Venerable Sirs!...”
"In a certain room there is a bhikṣu who is suffering from illness; what should be done about this?
The Buddha said, "You should receive his *chanda* and *śuddhi*."
At that time, the bhikṣus did not know who was entitled to take [the portions].
The Buddha said:
"One person may take one, another two, and another many; even if one can merely call out their names within the great assembly, they may take as much as they wish."
The Buddha said:
"I shall now explain the rules of conduct for a *śuddhaka-dharmakāma* (a person who has given his consent).
All bhikṣus who have given their consent should first bare their right shoulders, remove their leather sandals, pay their respects, and then squat with palms joined, speaking as follows:"
"Venerable one, please bear this in mind!
Today is the fourteenth day for the *poṣadha* ceremony of the Saṃgha; I, the bhikṣu [Name], shall also perform the *poṣadha* ceremony on the fourteenth day."

I, [Name], declare that I am entirely pure and free from all obstructing dharmas; for the sake of the cause and condition of illness, regarding that legal matter of the Saṃgha, I now grant my consent and purity.
"Please explain this matter to me.
He spoke thus a second and a third time. "Venerable Sir!"
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu who has granted his consent and purity is ill and unable to rise or sit up, may he still grant his consent and purity through a physical gesture?
The Buddha said:
"This constitutes a valid granting of consent and purity."
If one expresses [consent] through vocal karma for the sake of those who desire purity, it is considered a valid expression of consent for the sake of purity.

If a sick person is unable to perform either bodily or vocal expressions, all the bhikṣus should go together to the sick person's location, or they should carry the sick person into the midst of the assembly.
"If it is not done thus, the ritual act will not be accomplished, and one will incur the offense of separate residence (*pārivāsika*).
As the Blessed One said:
"I shall now explain the proper conduct for all bhikṣus who have received the consent for purification."

Once this bhikṣu has received the *kāyabhiniḥsarga* (the formal transfer of the *poṣadha*), he must not run, leap, or jump; he must not cross over ditches, nor stand upon railings or dangerous precipices. Within the monastery, on the upper galleries, he should not step across two stair-rungs with a single stride, nor tread upon two ladders at once; he must not go outside the boundary, nor fly through the air, nor fall asleep, nor enter into meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Furthermore, there are two kinds of base matters:
first, lack of shame (*ahrīkya*); second, indolence (*kausīdya*).
As it is said when reciting the *Prātimokṣa*, one speaks these words:
"Those bhikṣus who have not arrived should announce their *chanda* (consent) and *pāriśuddhi* (purification).
One who holds the *chanda* and *pāriśuddhi* should address either a sitting neighbor or another person, speaking as follows:
"Venerable sir, please attend!..."

In such-and-such a room, the bhikṣu named so-and-so is afflicted by the suffering of illness. Today, on the fourteenth day, the Saṃgha performs the poṣadha; that bhikṣu named so-and-so shall also perform the poṣadha on the fourteenth day. That bhikṣu named so-and-so has personally declared himself pure and free from all obstructing dharmas; for the sake of this cause of illness, he grants his consent and purity regarding the legal business of the Saṃgha.
"The matters he has related, I shall now state in full.

If there are further circumstances, they should be stated accordingly at that time; otherwise, the ritual act will not be accomplished, and one will incur the offense of separate residence (nānāsaṃvāsa).
The Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One, saying: "Venerable Sir,
if a bhikṣu who holds the *chanda* and *pāriśuddhi* should pass away immediately after having received the *chanda* and *pāriśuddhi*, does he remain one who holds the *chanda* and *pāriśuddhi*?"
The Buddha said, "It is not accomplished; you should take the consent again.
[He replied,] "Venerable Sir!"
If a bhikṣu who maintains the desire for purity says of himself:
"I am a śrāmaṇera," or says:
"I am a layperson," or he says,
"I am one who is undergoing parivāsa (probation)."
"In these cases, would the formal act of entrusting the purity (śuddhivāraṇa) be valid?
The Buddha said, "It would not be valid."
“If one who holds a *kṣānti* (consent) dies suddenly while on the road or in the midst of the assembly, does that constitute holding the *kṣānti*?
The Buddha said, “It does not;
one must take the *kṣānti* again.”
The procedure for the transmission of the *chanda* (consent) and *pāriśuddhi* (purity) by a bhikṣu who has granted his consent should be understood as follows.
Regarding the specific distinctions therein: if it concerns the performance of the *poṣadha*, one should say, "I grant my consent and my purity";

if it is not the *poṣadha*, but other *karmans* and so forth, one need only grant the consent (*chanda*) without needing to state one's purity. If both are being performed together, one grants both the consent and the purity.
The Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One: "Bhadanta,
if there is a residence where only a single bhikṣu dwells alone, and the day for the Poṣadha ceremony arrives, what should he do?"
The Buddha said:

"When the time for the Poṣadha arrives, go to a secluded place, smear it with fresh cow dung, sweep and sprinkle it, arrange seats and mats, strike the ghaṇṭā, and having completed these preliminary preparations, recite a small or large portion of the sūtras yourself."
Next, go to a high and open place and look around in all directions.
If you see a bhikṣu coming, after having greeted him with inquiries of well-being, say to him:
"Venerable one!"
"Today the Saṃgha is performing the Poṣadha; you should come together with us to one place for the Poṣadha ceremony.
If no one comes, that bhikṣu should remain at his own seat and, with mental reflection and verbal recitation, speak as follows:
"Today is the fourteenth day, and the Saṃgha is performing the Poṣadha; I, the bhikṣu [Name], shall also perform the Poṣadha on this fourteenth day."

I, the bhikṣu [Name], declare that I am completely pure regarding all obstructing dharmas. For now, I shall observe the poṣadha; should I later encounter a harmonious assembly for the poṣadha, it shall be so that the aggregate of precepts may be fulfilled.
The second and third times were also spoken in this manner.

If there are two bhikṣus in a single residence, when the time for the Poṣadha arrives, they shall perform the procedures together in the same sequence as described above; however, they must then perform the rite face-to-face with one another.
If there are three bhikṣus in a single residence, they should again perform the ritual for one another as previously described.
If there are four bhikṣus in a single residence, they should perform the *poṣadha* ceremony according to the Dharma; it is not permissible for them to take formal consent (*chanda*) for purification.
If there are five bhikṣus or more in a single residence, they should perform the poṣadha extensively according to the Dharma.
If there is a valid reason, it is permitted for one person to grant their consent (chanda) for the purification.

For example, at the time of the *poṣadha* on the fifteenth day, if a bhikṣu recalls an offense he has committed, he should, together with other pure bhikṣus, repent and eliminate the offense according to the Dharma; only then should he perform the *poṣadha*.

Furthermore, on the fifteenth day during the *poṣadha*, if a bhikṣu has doubts regarding an offense, that bhikṣu should go before a bhikṣu who is proficient in the Tripiṭaka and inquire about it, requesting that his doubtful offense be cleared; only after confessing and repenting according to the Dharma may the *poṣadha* be performed.

Furthermore, on the fifteenth day at the time of the *poṣadha*, if a bhikṣu should recall an offense committed within the community, that bhikṣu should temporarily maintain mindfulness of that offense in his mind, saying:
"Today the Saṃgha performs the *poṣadha* on the fifteenth day; I, the bhikṣu [Name], also perform the *poṣadha* on the fifteenth day."

I, the bhikṣu [Name], now recall within this assembly a transgression I have committed. I, [Name], maintain awareness of this transgression in my own mind; once the Saṃgha has performed the Poṣadha ceremony, I shall confess it according to the Dharma before a pure bhikṣu so that the offense may be removed.

Furthermore, on the fifteenth day during the time of the *poṣadha*, if a bhikṣu is within the assembly and harbors doubt regarding a transgression he has committed, that bhikṣu should temporarily maintain mindfulness of that offense, saying:

"Today the Saṃgha performs the *poṣadha* on the fifteenth day; I, the bhikṣu [Name], also perform the *poṣadha* on the fifteenth day. I, [Name], recall having committed a transgression, yet my mind harbors doubt."

I, [Name], regarding this doubtful offense, shall maintain it within my own mind; after the Saṃgha has performed the Poṣadha ceremony, I will approach a Bhikṣu who has mastered the Tripiṭaka to inquire about and resolve this doubtful offense, and I shall repent and eliminate it according to the Dharma.

If, while the Prātimokṣa Sūtra is being recited, a bhikṣu remembers an offense he has committed or suspects he may have committed one, he should, as before, maintain mindfulness of it within his own mind according to the proper sequence; subsequently, he must confess the offense according to the Dharma before a pure bhikṣu.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-ekottara-karman*, Fascicle Three;
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-ekottara-karman*,
Fascicle Four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.

The Single-Announcement (Ekajñapti) for All the Saṃgha Having Faults during the Poṣadha: "If on the fifteenth day at the time of the poṣadha, the entire saṃgha has all committed offenses, yet not a single person is able to go to another residence to confess their transgression according to the Dharma before a pure bhikṣu, such that we might, in the presence of that bhikṣu, lawfully repent and eliminate our offenses."
The entire Saṃgha shall perform the Poṣadha by means of a *jñapti-karman* alone; afterwards, they must confess their offenses at another residence.
Next, the *jñapti* should be performed as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

Today, on the fifteenth day, the Saṃgha performs the poṣadha ceremony; however, all members of the Saṃgha residing here have committed offenses. Since not a single person has been able to go to another residence to confess their transgressions before pure bhikṣus, let the Saṃgha now perform the formal confession according to the Dharma before those bhikṣus.

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha grant permission; let the Saṃgha now perform a *jñapti-karman* for the Poṣadha ceremony, so that later, upon going to another residence, the offenses may be expiated according to the Dharma.
"Recite the *Poṣadha* formula thus.
Having performed these actions, one should then conduct the *Poṣadha*; it must not be omitted or neglected.
If one does otherwise, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.

"If, on the fifteenth day during the *poṣadha*, the entire *saṃgha* has doubts regarding an offense, yet not a single person among them can go to another residence to seek a decision from a *bhikṣu* who has mastered the Tripiṭaka so that we may have our doubtful offenses resolved and removed in his presence—"

The entire Saṃgha shall perform only a *jñapti-karman* for the *poṣadha*; thereafter, having requested the removal of doubts from another residence, they shall eliminate their offenses according to the Dharma.
It should be performed in this manner: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

Today, on the fifteenth day, the Saṃgha performs the poṣadha. All members of the Saṃgha residing here have doubts regarding their offenses; yet, not a single person is able to go to another residence to seek a resolution for these doubtful offenses from a bhikṣu who has mastered the Tripiṭaka. Therefore, let the Saṃgha resolve and eliminate these offenses in the presence of that bhikṣu."

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and they grant permission, the Saṃgha should allow that the Saṃgha now perform a *jñapti-karman* (formal motion) for the *poṣadha*. Thereafter, having sought a resolution for doubts at another residence, one shall eliminate the offense in accordance with the Dharma.
"Thus it is announced.
Having performed this single announcement (*jñapti*), one may then perform the *poṣadha*.
If one does not do so, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma (*dharmātikrama*)."
The Venerable Upāli requested the Blessed One, saying: "Bhadanta,
if there is a bhikṣu who has committed an offense, is it permissible for him to confess that offense in the presence of another person who has also committed an offense?"
The Buddha said,
"It is not permitted.
[He asked,] "If that is so, before whom should one confess?"
The Buddha said:
“If one speaks to someone who is not of the same class [of practitioners], one’s offense is cleared.
“Venerable Sir! [he asked.]
"What is a concordant offense?
What is a non-concordant offense?
The Buddha said:
"Pārājika is a 'concordant' (sabhāga) category with respect to pārājika, but it is 'non-concordant' (visabhāga) with respect to the others;
saṃghāvaśeṣa is a concordant category with respect to saṃghāvaśeṣa, but it is non-concordant with respect to the others;
this should be understood to apply accordingly for the pāyattika down to the duṣkṛta."
The *Poṣadha-jñapti*: "If there are bhikṣus who have committed offenses, once they have performed the aforementioned procedure at the time of the *poṣadha*, the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* should be recited."
Having finished reciting the introduction, one should perform a *jñapti-karman* (formal motion) as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Today, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, the Saṃgha shall perform the *poṣadha*."
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha permit that the Saṃgha now perform the poṣadha and recite the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
"Next, the precepts should be recited; the above constitutes the formal procedure for the Great Saṃgha.
If there are bhikṣuṇīs performing the rite, it should be conducted according to the same principles.

Regarding the time of the *poṣadha*, if one does not come for the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal motion with one proclamation), or if during the *pravāraṇā* (the invitation to point out faults) it is not within a designated boundary (*sīmā*), and there is a bhikṣu who is insane, unable to give his consent (*chanda*), and incapable of being assisted or carried [to the assembly], the Buddha said:
"A formal act (karmavācanā) should be performed so that the assembly incurs no offense; it should be carried out in this manner.
If there are other matters that prevent [certain members] from assembling, it should be done according to these same principles."
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! That bhikṣu, so-and-so, has been afflicted by the onset of insanity;

he is unable to give his consent (*chanda*) nor can he be supported or carried. The Saṃgha now performs the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for him as one suffering from illness, so that the assembly may remain free from offense."
"If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha permit that the Saṃgha now grant the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of illness to the bhikṣu so-and-so.
This is the motion (*jñapti*).
The formal act is established according to the motion.
Regarding the formal procedure for assigning bedding and seats, as spoken by the Blessed One:
"O Bhikṣus, when the sixteenth day of the fifth month arrives, it is the time for you to enter the summer retreat."
The bhikṣus did not know how to observe the summer retreat (varṣā).
The Buddha said:

"When the day of the retreat approaches, one must pre-arrange the lodgings and all the bedding and seating items belonging to the Saṃgha, down to the basins for washing the feet; these must all be gathered together and distributed equally."
The bhikṣus did not know who should be appointed to distribute [the goods].
The Buddha said:
"There are twelve kinds of persons for distributing bedding and other items; one who possesses five qualities should be appointed."
If these five qualities are absent, one who has not been appointed should not be appointed, and one who has already been appointed should be dismissed. What are the five? They are:
being possessed by attachment, aversion, fear, or delusion; and being unable to determine whether bedding and furniture have been distributed or not.

Regarding these twelve kinds of persons: if they are the opposite of the five previously mentioned, those who have not yet been appointed should be appointed, and those already appointed should not be dismissed.
Having performed the preliminary procedures (*pūrvakalpa*), one should appoint them in this manner.
Next, one should ask:
"O [Name], are you able to serve as the bhikṣu who distributes bedding for the Saṃgha during the summer retreat?
He should reply:
“Yes. He then instructed one bhikṣu to perform the formal motion and second proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya-karman) to appoint him, saying: “Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, is capable of acting as the distributor of bedding for the Saṃgha during the summer retreat.

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, may the Saṃgha authorize this: the Saṃgha now appoints so-and-so to act as the distributor of bedding for the Saṃgha during the summer retreat.
"Thus it is announced. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu [Name] is capable of acting as the distributor of bedding for the Saṃgha during the summer retreat. The Saṃgha now appoints this bhikṣu [Name] to act as the distributor of bedding for the Saṃgha during the summer retreat."
Venerable sirs, if you approve of appointing this bhikṣu, so-and-so, as the distributor of bedding for the saṃgha during the summer retreat, remain silent; if you do not approve, speak.
"The Saṃgha has already authorized this bhikṣu, so-and-so, to act as the distributor of bedding for the Saṃgha during the summer retreat.
The Saṃgha has granted its consent, as indicated by their silence; thus do I now uphold this decision."
The formal motion with a second announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) for appointing a person to store the robes: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, is capable of serving as the custodian of the Saṃgha’s clothing."
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha permit that this bhikṣu, so-and-so, be appointed as the custodian of robes and utensils.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
"The formal act (*karmavācanā*) is established accordingly.
To appoint the person who distributes the robes, one performs the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the motion followed by one proclamation):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This bhikṣu, so-and-so, is capable of acting as the distributor of robes for the Saṃgha."
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha grant permission that the Saṃgha now appoint this bhikṣu, [Name], as the distributor of robes.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
"The *karmavācanā* shall be established according to the motion (*jñapti*).
[The formal motion for] appointing a person to store the utensils: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "There must be a specific cause and condition; I now authorize the bhikṣus to observe the seven-day rule and go outside the boundary.

The Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One: "Bhadanta,

"The Saṃgha has already granted this bhikṣu, [Name], the maintenance of a forty-night period to go outside the boundary for the sake of the Saṃgha's business; this person has completed his rains retreat here this summer."

one bhikṣu should first perform the formal motion (jñapti) before proceeding with the ritual act (karman):
