If there are five or more persons, one should then make a formal announcement (*jñapti*) for the purpose of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony.
One who performs the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism) should be appointed with the consent [of the assembly].

If there are sick persons, they should be brought into the assembly; if there are six or more people present, everyone shall perform the *jñapti* (formal motion) alone for the matter of the *pravāraṇā*.

When performing the *pravāraṇā*, if there is a sick person, one should receive their formal consent (*chanda*) and purification; this must not be done in the presence of laypeople, novices, or *paṇḍakas*. Furthermore, all participants must be pure, share the same views, and be in the same location to perform it; however, I do not permit the *pravāraṇā* to be omitted.

At that time, some bhikṣus, having previously engaged in quarreling and mutual dispute, harbored resentment toward one another while performing the *pravāraṇā* ceremony together in one place. The Buddha said:

"One should not perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony together while resentment and ill-will have not yet subsided; first you must offer mutual confession (*kṣamāpanā*), and only afterwards should the ritual be performed."
At that time, the bhikṣu sought forgiveness within the great assembly, but the bhikṣu with whom he had quarreled was unwilling to grant it. The Buddha said:
"There are still seven or eight days remaining before the time for the *pravāraṇā*; you must mutually seek forgiveness from one another before performing the *pravāraṇā*."
At that time, the Saṃgha all felt mutual shame and apologized; however, the assembly of brahmins and the various lay travelers then gave rise to criticism, saying:
"All these bhikṣus harbor enmity toward one another."
The Buddha said:
"If there are those who harbor resentment, one should request their forgiveness and offer an apology.

Once they have granted you their pardon, you should pay respects according to seniority and cultivate mutual joy; only then may you act according to your own preference. As for those with whom you have no enmity, there is no need to offer an apology."
When the bhikṣus had finished the *pravāraṇā*, they performed the *poṣadha* on that very same day. The Buddha said:
"The *pravāraṇā* itself constitutes purification; there is no need for the recitation of the precepts."

When the robes had been assigned for the purpose of making the *kaṭhina* cloth through the formal procedure of a motion and a second (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*), a great number of bhikṣus, having completed their summer retreat and finished the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, went to the Jeta Grove and prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One.
On the road he encountered rain, and his three robes were all soaked; it was extremely difficult for him to carry them.
Upon arriving at the Jetavana, he set aside his robes and bowl, washed his feet, and prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One. The Buddha asked:
"Are you dwelling in peace and comfort? Is alms-seeking easy for you?"
He said, "Venerable Sir! We have arrived here exhausted and weary."
The Buddha thought to himself:

"How may I now cause the bhikṣus to dwell in peace and happiness, while also increasing the merit and benefit of the donors? I should permit the bhikṣus to complete the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, and on the sixteenth day, spread the *kaṭhina* robe."
When spreading this robe, ten benefits are obtained during the five months; whatever material goods are acquired at that place, one should select the finest item to make the *kaṭhina* robe.
On the fourteenth day of the eighth month, he informs the assembly so that they may know; he spreads out the seats and performs the preliminary rites as prescribed above.
He then instructs one bhikṣu to perform the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*): "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This robe is the distribution of goods obtained by the Saṃgha during the summer retreat at this location; the Saṃgha now intends together to make this robe into a kaṭhina.
This robe shall be spread out as the kaṭhina for the Saṃgha.
If the kaṭhina has already been spread, even if one goes outside the boundary, there is still no offense of being separated from the three robes; how much more so for other robes!
If the Saṃgha deems it the right time and grants permission, the Saṃgha should allow that the Saṃgha shall now take this robe and formally spread it as the kaṭhina for the Saṃgha.
"If the robe has already been spread out, even if one goes outside the boundary, there is still no offense of being separated from one's three robes, let alone other garments!
The motion is as follows.
The formal ritual act (*karmavācanā*) is accomplished according to this motion.

After the monks had performed the formal ritual (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) for appointing the person to oversee the *kaṭhina* robe, they finished making the *kaṭhina* robe from that cloth material and informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Appoint a bhikṣu endowed with the five virtues to serve as the *cīvaradhara* (distributor of robes).
Ring the *ghanṭā*, perform the preliminary rites, and once the assembly has gathered, one should first ask:..."
"Are you, [Name], able to serve as the person who prepares the kaṭhina robe for the Saṃgha? He replies,
"I am able."
He should instruct one bhikṣu to perform the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*): "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu [Name], who desires to act as the kaṭhina-spreader, shall now spread the kaṭhina robe for the Saṃgha."

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha permit that the Saṃgha now appoint the bhikṣu so-and-so as the person who shall spread the kaṭhina robe; this so-and-so shall spread the kaṭhina robe for the Saṃgha.
"Thus it is announced. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, wishes to perform the kaṭhina-spread; he now spreads the kaṭhina-cloth for the Saṃgha."
Now the Saṃgha appoints this bhikṣu, so-and-so, as the kaṭhina-spreader; this so-and-so shall spread the kaṭhina for the Saṃgha.
If the venerable ones consent to appoint so-and-so as the kaṭhina-spreader, such that this so-and-so shall spread the kaṭhina for the Saṃgha, let them remain silent;
if you do not consent, please speak.

"The Sangha has already granted its consent that this person, so-and-so, shall act as the *kaṭhina*-spreader; this person, so-and-so, has now completed his service as the *kaṭhina*-spreader for the Sangha."
“The Saṃgha has granted its consent, as indicated by their silence; I now hold it accordingly.

[Then] perform the formal motion and one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) for the entrustment of the *kaṭhina* robe: “Next, perform the formal motion and one proclamation, and subsequently entrust the robe to the person designated to handle the robe.”
It should be performed in this manner: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This robe shall be made into the kaṭhina for the Saṃgha; this bhikṣu, so-and-so, has been appointed by the Saṃgha as the kaṭhina-spreader."
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha grant permission that the Saṃgha now makes this robe into kaṭhina and entrusts it to the bhikṣu [Name].
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This robe shall be made into a kaṭhina for the Saṃgha;
this bhikṣu, so-and-so, has already been appointed by the Saṃgha as the kaṭhina-spreader. The Saṃgha now bestows this robe as the kaṭhina upon this bhikṣu, so-and-so."
Venerable sirs, if you approve that this robe be made into the *kaṭhina* for the Saṃgha, and that the Saṃgha now make this robe into the *kaṭhina* and entrust it to the bhikṣu [Name], remain silent;
if you do not approve, speak.
"The Saṃgha has already permitted this robe to be made into kaṭhina for the Saṃgha, and it has been entrusted to the bhikṣu [Name].
Since the Saṃgha has granted its consent by remaining silent, I now hold it as such."

The Single-Announcement (Ekakarmavācanā) for the Suspension of the Kaṭhina Robe: "Once this bhikṣu has received the robe, he should, together with other bhikṣus, perform the washing, dyeing, sewing, and stitching; all other formal procedures are detailed in the section on the matter of the Kaṭhina robe."
At that time, when the bhikṣus had collectively received the kaṭhina robe and the five months had reached their completion, they did not know what to do.
They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"On the fifteenth day of the first month, the person who spreads the robe shall address the Saṃgha, saying:"
"Venerable sirs! Tomorrow the kaṭhina robe shall be taken out; may each of you maintain possession of your own robes.
When the next day arrives and the Saṃgha has assembled, having performed the preliminary formalities, one bhikṣu should perform a *jñapti-karman* (a motion) as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
In this residence, the harmonious Saṃgha has together spread the kaṭhina robe.
If the Saṃgha deems it the proper time and grants its consent, may the Saṃgha permit that the Saṃgha now together take up the kaṭhina robe."
"Thus it is declared.
At that time, once the bhikṣus had brought forth their robes, they did not know what to do and informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"O bhikṣus, when you are spreading out the robes, ten benefits are obtained; once the robes have been finished, this practice must be prohibited. Whoever violates this incurs an offense."
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-ekottara-karmavastu*, Fascicle Four;
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-ekottara-karmavastu*,
Fascicle Five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.

In the fifth year [of the reign], regarding the separate recitation of the Prātimokṣa for those sharing the same offerings, a formal motion (jñapti-dvitīya-karman) was made. The Venerable Upāli requested of the World-Honored One, saying: "O Bhadanta!..."
In a certain village there was an elder who constructed a dwelling, fully equipped with all necessities, and offered it to the Saṃgha of the four directions.

At that time, the elder was arrested by the king; having heard this, the bhikṣus abandoned the monastery and departed elsewhere, whereupon the property belonging to the Three Jewels and various requisites were stolen by bandits.
The elder was released and, realizing the monastery had been plundered by thieves, said:
"Noble One! For what reason have you abandoned the monastery and gone elsewhere?"
The bhikṣu replied, “I heard that the householder was seized by the authorities; filled with fear and alarm, I have gone elsewhere.
The householder said:
"I have kinsmen there who can provide for me; why should I be in such a hurry?
The bhikṣus did not know what to do, so they reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"Ask his kinsmen; if they are able to provide for him, that is well.

If they are not able, the bhikṣus shall perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* and should collectively follow him to a nearby monastery, sharing the same *lābha* (alms-offerings) for five years, while performing the *poṣadha* separately."

Having first informed that monastery and prepared the seats and preliminary arrangements, he should have one bhikṣu perform the formal motion (jñapti) and the second part of the ritual (dvitīya-karman):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
The donor who built this monastery at this residence is currently being held in custody by the king.

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, may the Saṃgha permit that this residence and that residence shall, for five years, share the same distribution of offerings (lābha) while performing the Poṣadha separately.
The motion is thus made.
Next, the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is performed: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The donor who built this monastery at this residence has now been imprisoned by the king.
The Saṃgha shall, for five years, share the same distribution of offerings (*lābha*) and perform the separate *poṣadha* ceremony between this residence and that [other] residence.
Venerable sirs, if you approve that these two residences shall share the same distribution of offerings but perform separate *poṣadha* ceremonies for five years, remain silent;
if you do not approve, speak.
“The Saṃgha has already granted permission for these two residences to share the same distribution of offerings and perform separate *poṣadha* ceremonies for five years.
Since the Saṃgha has consented by remaining silent, I now hold it to be so.”

"If there are other circumstances, one should know that the ritual must be performed according to the specific situation and inform the lay households. Then, with a formal motion (*jñapti*) and a second [announcement] (*karmavācanā*), the Venerable Upāli requested the Blessed One, saying:
"O Bhadanta!..."
If bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs commit improper acts in the homes of laypeople, causing the lay community to lose faith and respect and giving rise to widespread criticism and suspicion, what should be done?
The Buddha said:
"O bhikṣus, you should appoint a bhikṣu endowed with five virtues to go to the households of the laity and proclaim the unlawful conduct of those two men."
The appointment should be made as follows:
after the seats have been spread and the preliminary rites performed, one must first ask the candidate:
"Are you, [Name], able to go to the homes of the laity and speak of the unlawful conduct of the bhikṣu Pṛthukūṭa and the bhikṣuṇī Śākhā?"
He replied, "I can.
Then he instructed a bhikṣu to perform the formal motion (jñapti-karman), which should be done as follows:
“‘Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu [Name] is able to go to the homes of laypeople and speak of the improper conduct of the bhikṣu Pṛthukola and the bhikṣuṇī Śākhā.’”

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha grant permission that this bhikṣu, so-and-so, be dispatched now to the households of the laity to proclaim the improper conduct of the bhikṣu Pṛthupūṭa and the bhikṣuṇī Śākhā.
The motion is thus made.
Next, the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is performed: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, is capable of going to the homes of laypeople to proclaim the unrighteous conduct of the bhikṣu Pṛthukola and the bhikṣuṇī Śākhā.
The Saṃgha now appoints this bhikṣu, so-and-so, to go to the homes of laypeople to proclaim the unrighteous conduct of the bhikṣu Pṛthukola and the bhikṣuṇī Śākhā.

If the venerable ones consent to dispatch this bhikṣu, so-and-so, to the households of the laity to proclaim the unlawful conduct of the bhikṣu Pṛthukola and the bhikṣuṇī Śākhā, let them remain silent; if they do not consent, let them speak.

"The Saṃgha has already granted its consent for this bhikṣu, so-and-so, to go to the households of the laity and announce that the bhikṣu Pṛthukola and the bhikṣuṇī Śākhā have committed unrighteous acts."
"The Saṃgha has granted its consent, as indicated by their silence; thus do I now uphold it.

When the formal motion (*jñapti*) regarding the grave offense of another was being recited, the bhikṣus, having received the Buddha’s instruction, performed the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation) and dispatched a bhikṣu to various lay households to proclaim the unlawful conduct of those two individuals.
When the bhikṣu Viśāṇa heard this matter, he went to where the other bhikṣus were and spoke these words:
"Did you, sirs, speak of my faults while in the homes of the laity?"
He replied, "I have obtained the means to go to laypeople's homes and speak of your faults.
Pṛthukapola answered:
"I am capable of doing you harm; I shall split open your belly, take out your intestines and coil them around the Jetavana Grove, and sever your head and hang it upon the gate of the monastery."
When the bhikṣus heard these words, they immediately informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"He may be able to deceive an individual, but he cannot deceive the assembly."
A single *jñapti* (motion) should be made, and the entire assembly should go together to the householders' home to explain his transgressions.
Having prepared the seating and performed the preliminary rites, one bhikṣu should perform the *jñapti-karman*: "Listen, Venerable Saṃgha!
Those bhikṣu Viśālamukha and bhikṣuṇī Śākhā committed various unrighteous acts within the households of laypeople, causing the lay followers to lose their faith and respect.
At present, there is no other individual capable of going to the households of the laity to speak of their faults.
The Saṃgha shall now go together to the households of the laity to declare that the conduct of those two individuals is contrary to the Dharma. You should speak as follows:

"Venerable sirs, you should know that the bhikṣu Pṛthukūṭa and the bhikṣuṇī Śākhā have brought ruin upon the Noble Teaching and have destroyed themselves. They are like scorched seeds that can no longer produce sprouts; they are unable to grow within the True Law and Discipline."
Virtuous ones, you should contemplate the traces of conduct of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, as well as those of Ājñātakauṇḍinya and the other great bhikṣus.

"If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha grant permission: let the Saṃgha now go together to the households of laypeople to proclaim the improper conduct of the bhikṣu Pṛthukola and the bhikṣuṇī Śākhā."
"Thus it is announced.
Having made this announcement, one should speak accordingly in each case.
The Venerable Upāli then requested of the Blessed One:
“Venerable Sir!
After the community of bhikṣus has performed the *jñapti-dharma* for those two individuals and finished notifying all the lay households, we do not know what should be done.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not provide lay followers with clothing, food, bathing water, or medicine; nothing whatsoever that they require should be given to them.

Having thus advised those who would cause a schism in the Saṃgha through a formal motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*), the Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One, saying: "O Bhadanta!..."
For the sake of fame and profit, Devadatta went to Kāśyapa and said:
"Venerable One! Teach me the matters of supernatural powers."
At that time, Kāśyapa did not examine his mind and taught him the Dharma of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).

Having heard the Dharma, Devadatta practiced with diligence during both the first and last watches of the night; in the final part of the night, by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), he realized the first dhyāna and thereby manifested supernormal powers.
Having attained this supernatural power, he gave rise to an evil thought and said to his four companions:
"You four, together with me, shall break the harmonious Saṃgha of that śramaṇa Gautama and destroy the Wheel of Dharma."
"After my passing, I shall attain a good reputation that will spread throughout the ten directions.
Having said this, he immediately joined his four companions, intending to break up the harmonious Saṃgha and destroy the Wheel of Dharma.
When the community of bhikṣus learned of this matter, they immediately informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"Bhikṣus, you must carry out a formal admonition against him."
When he was being admonished separately, he stubbornly clung to his position and refused to relinquish it, saying:
"This alone is true; all else is false.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“O monks, you should perform the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* to admonish Devadatta.
If there are others of a similar sort, they should be admonished in this manner:
having prepared the seating and performed the preliminary rites, one monk should perform the *jñapti-karman* as follows:”
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This Devadatta desires to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha, engaging in contentious matters and remaining in unrighteousness.
The bhikṣus have offered him separate admonitions."
When being admonished individually, he stubbornly clung to his position and refused to relinquish it, saying:
"This alone is the truth; all else is false.
The Saṃgha now admonishes that Devadatta by means of the formal procedure of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*:
“Devadatta, do not cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha by engaging in strife and dwelling in what is contrary to the Dharma.

Devadatta, you should live in harmony with the Saṃgha, joyful and without dispute; being of one mind and one voice, like water mixed with milk, you should cause the Teacher’s dispensation to shine forth and abide in peace and happiness.”

"If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and they grant permission, may the Saṃgha allow that the Saṃgha now perform a formal motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) to admonish Devadatta regarding his act of schism."
The motion is thus made.
Next, perform the *karmavācanā*:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This Devadatta, wishing to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha, engaged in acts of contention and remained in unrighteousness; the bhikṣus then offered him a formal individual admonition.
During this individual admonition, he stubbornly clung to his position and refused to relinquish it, saying:
"This alone is the truth; all else is false."
The Saṃgha now exhorts Devadatta with the formal procedure of one motion and three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman):
"Devadatta, do not cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha by engaging in strife and dwelling in what is contrary to the Dharma."

Devadatta, you should live in harmony with the Saṅgha, joyful and without dispute, with a single mind and a single voice, like water mixed with milk, so that the Great Teacher’s teaching may be made radiant and you may dwell in peace and happiness.
"Venerable sirs, if you consent to granting this Devadatta the formal act of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* as a censure for his schism of the Saṃgha, remain silent; if you do not consent, speak."
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third are also spoken in this manner.
"The Saṃgha has now finished admonishing Devadatta regarding his act of schism by means of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*."
"The Saṃgha has granted its consent, as indicated by their silence; I shall now hold it thus.

Having received the Buddha’s instruction regarding the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for admonishing those who assist in schism, the bhikṣus then performed the formal ritual (*karman*) and admonished Devadatta.
At that time, having received the formal act (*karmavācanā*), Devadatta stubbornly clung to it and would not relinquish it.
Furthermore, he had four companions who assisted him:
first, Kokālika; second, Khaṇḍadravya; third, Kaṭamorakatiṣya; and fourth, Samudradatta. They followed Devadatta and engaged in the matter of schisming the Saṅgha.
The bhikṣus then informed the Buddha, who said:
"Bhikṣus, you should offer a formal admonition to those four men.
When they were being admonished, they spoke as follows:
"Venerable sirs! Do not engage in any discussion with Devadatta, whether it be favorable or unfavorable. Why is that?
"That Devadatta speaks in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya.
When he heard this admonition, he remained stubbornly attached to his position and would not relinquish it.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“O bhikṣus, perform the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) to admonish those four men.
You should admonish them in this manner:
having prepared the seats and performed the preliminary rites, next have one bhikṣu perform the *jñapti-karman*.”
It should be performed in this manner: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

These individuals—Kokālika, Khaṇḍadravya, Kaṭamorakatiṣya, Samudradatta, and others—know that Devadatta intends to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha and persists in engaging in unlawful acts of contention."
At that time, these four individuals followed Devadatta in his act of schism against the Saṃgha, and the bhikṣus gave them a formal individual admonition.
During this individual admonition, these four—Koṭikarṇa and the others—spoke as follows:
"Venerable sirs!..."
Do not engage in discussion with Devadatta regarding what is good or bad. Why is this?
Devadatta speaks in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, relying upon the Dharma and the Vinaya; he speaks with knowledge and does not speak out of ignorance.
"Whatever they delight in, I too shall delight in.
Thus, these four individuals, including Kokālika and the others, remained stubbornly attached and refused to relinquish their position, saying:
"This alone is the truth; all else is false."
"The Saṃgha now proceeds with the formal act of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* to admonish these four individuals, Kokālika and his companions, who assist Devadatta in the matter of schism:

'You four, Kokālika and the others, must not assist that Devadatta in causing a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha, nor engage in acts of strife and discord, remaining in what is contrary to the Dharma.'"

"You four, Kokālika and the others, should live in harmony and joyful concord with the Saṃgha, free from dispute; being of one mind and one voice, like water mixed with milk, you should cause the Teacher’s dispensation to shine forth and abide in peace and happiness."

"If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and they grant their consent, let the Saṃgha permit that the Saṃgha now, by means of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, should admonish these four individuals, Kokālika and his companions, who assisted Devadatta in the matter of schism."
"Thus it is announced.
Next, the formal ritual (karmavācanā) is performed according to the announcement.
Having performed the single-announcement rite for the *śikṣādattaka* (the one given the rules of training), the Venerable Upāli requested of the World-Honored One, saying:
"Venerable Sir!

That householder Siṃha formerly served non-Buddhist teachers; however, because he went to the Buddha’s presence to listen to and receive the Dharma, he severed all afflictions and delusions beneath his seat and realized the fruit of Stream-entry (*srotāpatti*). Toward the Triple Gem, his aspiration became purely virtuous and he gave rise to deep faith; he constantly delighted in giving away all his wealth and possessions until he became impoverished, which led his worldly companions to criticize and disdain him."
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
The Buddha said, "Bhikṣus,
you should perform the *śikṣādattaka-karman* (the formal act of declaring a family as one under training) for the householder Siṃha, thereby prohibiting the bhikṣus from going to his home."
Having arranged the seats and performed the preliminary rites, a single bhikṣu should perform the *jñapti* (formal motion) as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

That householder Siṃha possesses profound faith and pure, virtuous intentions; he bestows all his existing wealth and resources upon the Three Jewels and shows no stinginess toward those who seek them. Due to these causes and conditions, his food and clothing have been completely exhausted."

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha grant its permission; the Saṃgha shall now perform the *śikṣādattaka-karman* for the householder Siṃha. This is the motion (*jñapti*).
"Once the ritual has been performed, those who go there shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.

When the community of bhikṣus had performed the formal rite of declaring a family as "one whose learning is restricted" (śikṣā-dattaka) by means of a single motion (jñapti), they immediately ceased going to that house to receive food and drink.
At that time, this householder diligently applied himself to farming, and before long his granaries and treasuries were overflowing, more than double what they had been previously.
Seeing that his family estate had flourished, he thought of visiting a field of merit to make offerings as he had done before; he went to the Buddha’s dwelling and made a fervent request.
The Buddha then granted his permission and instructed the elder:
"Report the matter in full to the Elder so that he may have the *khaṇḍi* struck.
Once the Saṃgha has been assembled, squat before the Elder with palms joined and make this formal announcement (*jñapti*):"
“‘Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

My teacher Siṃha possesses deep faith, a resolute intention, and pure virtue; regarding the Three Jewels, he always delights in bestowing whatever wealth he currently possesses, and he is likewise without stinginess toward those who seek it.’”
Due to these causes and conditions, our food and clothing have been exhausted until we reached poverty.

When the Saṃgha saw this, they gave rise to a heart of compassion and established the *śikṣādattaka* (learner’s) discipline for my teacher Siṃha, so that the noble assembly would no longer enter our home.

"O my Teacher, at this time my storehouses have once again become full; I now request from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *śikṣādattaka* (learner's) status. I only pray that the virtuous Saṃgha will grant me the lifting of the *śikṣādattaka* status."
"May those who are capable of compassion take pity on me.
Thus he spoke three times.
Having made this formal announcement, he prostrated to the assembly and departed.
At that time, the Saṃgha had one person perform a *jñapti-karman* (formal motion): "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

That householder Siṃha possesses profound faith and pure, wholesome intentions. He bestows all his existing wealth and property upon the Three Jewels, and he is likewise without stinginess toward those who seek it."

Due to these circumstances, their food and clothing were completely exhausted; consequently, the Saṃgha performed the *śikṣādattaka-karman* (the formal act of declaring one a householder under training) for that elder, ordering the bhikṣus not to go to his home to receive food and drink.
The householder’s food and clothing have now returned to their former state; he now requests from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *kula-śikṣāpada-karma*.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and they grant permission, the Saṃgha should authorize this: let the Saṃgha now grant that householder the lifting of the *kula-śikṣāpada-karma*.
"Thus it is announced.
At that time, after the bhikṣus had performed the *karmavācanā* for the householder to lift the restriction on his household, they did not know what to do.
They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“O Bhikṣus! You may go to those households to receive food and drink; there is no offense whatsoever.
Having observed the perilous forest, the Venerable Upāli, who had received the formal act of two persons (jñapti-dvitīya-karman), requested the World-Honored One, saying:
“Venerable Sir!

The summer retreat has concluded, and today various brahmins and householders brought excellent food and drink to offer to the noble assembly. They sent female servants to accompany them on the journey, but when they reached the midpoint of the road, they were all plundered by bandits.”
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, wishing to go for alms in an araṇya, saw various foods along the way and had a naked maidservant hand them to him; the women were filled with shame.
Then the brahmin said to the bhikṣu,
"Why do you not station someone to guard the place in the perilous forest?
This would allow me to deliver the food without it being plundered by bandits."
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
The Buddha said:

"By means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, one should appoint a bhikṣu endowed with five qualities to act as a guardian in the dangerous forest. The preliminary procedures should be understood according to the aforementioned rules."
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu [Name] is capable of proceeding toward dangerous forests and places of fear, and is well-versed in observing the path."

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha grant permission for this bhikṣu, so-and-so, to be appointed by the Saṃgha as an observer in that dangerous forest and place of fear.
"Thus it is announced.
"The formal act (karmavācanā) shall be performed according to this announcement.
Having been granted the training rules, the Venerable Upāli, having completed the fourfold formal procedure (jñapti-caturtha), requested the World-Honored One, saying:
"Venerable Sir!

There is currently a bhikṣu named Nanda who, without renouncing the precepts, has violated the holy life by engaging in sexual misconduct. Not for a single moment has he harbored a mind of concealment; rather, like a poisoned arrow piercing his chest, he dwells in grief and distress, not knowing what to do."
The Buddha said:
"O bhikṣus, you shall grant the lifelong training rules to the bhikṣu Nandika; if there are others of a similar kind, they shall all be dealt with according to this same precedent."
Having struck the *gaṇḍī*, he should instruct the monk Prahlāda to kneel before the elder monks with palms joined and make this request:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!"
I, the bhikṣu Ānanda, did not abandon the precepts, yet I violated the holy life by engaging in sexual intercourse.
I, the bhikṣu Ānanda, have not entertained a single thought of concealment; I now beg the Saṃgha for the lifelong precepts.
"May the virtuous Saṃgha grant me the lifelong training rules with joy.
May those who are compassionate do so out of compassion.
Thus one should say three times.
He should have the monk Prahlāda stay in a place where he can be seen but not heard, and have one monk perform the *karmavācanā* for him as follows:
"Listen, venerable Saṃgha!

That bhikṣu, Pāṇḍulohitaka, did not relinquish the training rules; having violated the holy life by committing an act of sexual misconduct, he did not harbor a single thought of concealment. He now requests from the Saṃgha the lifelong training rules.
"If the Saṃgha deems the time has come and grants its permission, may the Saṃgha allow that the Saṃgha now bestow upon the bhikṣu Nandika the lifelong training rules.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"

That bhikṣu Nandika did not relinquish the precepts; having violated the holy life by engaging in sexual misconduct, he did not harbor a single thought of concealment. He now requests from the Saṃgha the lifelong precepts, and the Saṃgha now grants the lifelong precepts to the bhikṣu Nandika.
"If the Venerable Ones consent to granting the lifelong training rules to the bhikṣu Nandika, they should remain silent;
if they do not consent, they should speak. This is said a second and a third time.
"The Saṃgha has already granted the lifelong training rules to the bhikṣu Nandika.
Since there is silence, the Saṃgha has consented; thus do I now understand it."
Having given his robe to Śrīgupta, the Venerable Upāli addressed the Blessed One with this formal motion (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Sir,
the bhikṣu Śrīgupta has been appointed by the harmonious Saṃgha to distribute the bedding and utensils for the assembly and to oversee the sequence of meals."

He possesses faith and a purely virtuous intention; he oversees the affairs of the community without declining any labor or hardship, and he bestows all his livelihood and possessions as offerings upon the Triple Gem.
"Having given these gifts in this manner, my own three robes have all been worn out; I do not know what to do.
The Buddha said, "You assembly of bhikṣus should gather together and perform the *jñapti-dharma* (the formal motion) to bestow a robe upon Śrīgupta."
It should be performed in this manner: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

That Śāriputra possesses respectful faith and a virtuous disposition; he manages affairs for the community without declining its hardships, and having bestowed all his requisites upon the Triple Gem, his own three robes have now become worn out."
At this time, the Saṃgha has obtained some fine white cotton cloth; let us take this cloth together to make a robe for Śrīgupta.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and they grant permission, may the Saṃgha consent that the Saṃgha now take this white cotton cloth to make a robe for Śrīgupta.
“Thus it is announced.
The Buddha said, “O bhikṣus, since you have already performed the formal announcement (jñapti), you should give the white woolen cloth to Śrīgupta; do not harbor any doubt regarding this.”
Facing him, they slighted and disparaged him with a formal motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*). Then the Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One:

"Bhadanta, the bhikṣu Sthiramati has been appointed by the community to distribute bedding and to oversee the sequence of meals. However, because the karmic conditions of long-standing enmity between the two bhikṣus Mitra and Bhūmi have not yet been exhausted, these two bhikṣus have expressed their resentment and disparagement in the presence of Sthiramati."
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
The Buddha said:
"You bhikṣus should perform a formal act (karmavācanā) to reprimand the two bhikṣus, Mitra and Bhūmi, for their face-to-face disparagement of Sthiramati."
If there are others of a similar class, they should be granted [the robe] in this same manner.
Having struck the *gandi* as a preliminary preparation, one bhikṣu should perform the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*) as follows:
"Listen, venerable Saṃgha!..."

These two bhikṣus, Māṭhara and Gokhali, knowing that the Saṃgha had appointed Sthavira Śrīgupta to distribute bedding and determine the order of meals, spoke words of disparagement and reproach in the presence of Sthavira Śrīgupta.

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha permit that the Saṃgha now reprove the two bhikṣus, Yu and Di, for their face-to-face disparagement and reviling of Śrīgupta.
"Thus it is announced. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

These two bhikṣus, Yu (Yǒu) and Dì, knowing that the harmonious Saṃgha has appointed Śrīgupta to distribute bedding for the assembly and to oversee the sequence of meals, have disparaged Śrīgupta to his face. The Saṃgha now censures the two bhikṣus, Yu and Dì, for their face-to-face disparagement of Śrīgupta."
"Venerable sirs, if you approve of the censure of the two bhikṣus, Sunakṣatra and Upasena, for their face-to-face disparagement of Sthiramati, remain silent;
if you do not approve, speak. This was said a second and a third time.
"The Saṃgha has already granted its consent for the formal censure of the two bhikṣus, Mittra and Bhūmija, who openly reviled and disparaged Sthiramati.
Since the Saṃgha has granted its consent by remaining silent, I now hold it to be so."

Having thus feigned contempt during the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal procedure consisting of one motion and three proclamations), and having performed the *tāḍana-karman* (act of censure) against the two monks, Mitra and Bhūmi, in accordance with the Buddha’s instructions, they later, at another time, spoke words of reproach and disparagement in the presence of Sthiramati, without mentioning his name.
When the bhikṣus had heard these words, they immediately informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"Bhikṣus, you should perform a *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) against the two, Mitraka and Pṛthivībandhu, in the presence of Sthiramati, for having slandered him under false pretenses by mentioning other matters without naming him."
The procedure should be performed as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

These two bhikṣus, Yau and Di, knowing that the Saṃgha has appointed Śrīgupta to distribute bedding and furniture and to oversee the sequence of meals, have, in the presence of Śrīgupta, falsely pretexts other matters and, without mentioning his name, have disparaged him."

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and they grant their permission, may the Saṃgha allow that the Saṃgha now reprimand the two bhikṣus, Yau and Di, who, under false pretenses and by not mentioning his name, have slandered and disparaged another.
The motion is thus made.
Next, perform the *karmavācanā*: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

These two bhikṣus, Mettiya and Bhummaja, knowing that the Saṃgha had appointed the bhikṣu Sāḷha to distribute bedding and assign the order of meals, conspired before Sāḷha to disparage him under false pretexts, avoiding the mention of his name.
The Saṃgha now censures the two bhikṣus, Yu and Di, for falsely using other matters to disparage them without mentioning their names.

If the venerable ones consent to the censure of the two bhikṣus, Yu and Di, for falsely using other matters to disparage them without mentioning their names, let them remain silent; if you do not consent, speak.
For a second and third time, he spoke in this same manner:
"The Saṃgha has already censured the two bhikṣus, Yu and Di, yet they continue to slander and disparage them under false pretexts, failing to mention their names."
"The Saṃgha has granted its consent; because of their silence, I now hold it thus.

At that time, after the monks had performed the *karmavācanā* against the two, Upāli and Maudgalyāyana, these two bhikṣus still confronted Sthūlanandika face-to-face and used pretexts to disparage him.
The assembly of bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If, after having received the formal authorization (karmavācanā), one does not relinquish [the offense], one incurs a pāyattika.
One incurs an offense by showing contempt or disparaging those among the twelve types of persons who have been appointed by the assembly."

"You should know that just as those twelve kinds of people who, having been appointed by the community to perform a task, incur the offense of *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) for disparaging it once the task has been suspended.
At that time, the Venerable Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa rose from his seat, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable Sir!"
"In a borderland country there is one named Kātyāyana, who is my upādhyāya; he bids me pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One and inquire after his well-being and ease."
...and so on, until the Buddha asked:
"O bhikṣus, are you living in peace and comfort?
They replied: "Venerable Sir!"
My preceptor respectfully transmits these five matters for inquiry to the World-Honored One; I pray that you will, out of compassion, provide a definitive resolution regarding them.
Venerable Sir!
In frontier lands there are few bhikṣus; if one were to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), it would be difficult to complete the quorum of ten members.
"Venerable Sir!
If there are regions where the ground is so hard and firm that it forms hoofprints for oxen, is it permissible to wear leather shoes?
And if one frequently visits bathing places, may one bathe many times?"
Furthermore, there are border regions where people use the hides of oxen, sheep, or deer as bedding; may these be used?
If a bhikṣu sends clothing to another bhikṣu, but the recipient dies before it arrives and the clothing does not reach him, and ten days have passed, who incurs the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense?
The Buddha said:
"I permit those in border regions who understand the Vinaya to serve as the fifth person for the conferral of full ordination (*upasampadā*).
In places where the ground is hard and firm, I permit the wearing of single-layered leather shoes, but not those of two or three layers."
If the bottom is worn through, it should be mended or replaced.
At bathing places, one may bathe as one pleases.
Regarding the use of leather bedding, one may use them as one pleases.
Furthermore, if this bhikṣu entrusts his robe to another, but dies before it reaches him, there is no offense for which he must undergo expiation.
The Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One, saying:
“As the Blessed One has said:”
"In border countries, one may receive full ordination (*upasampadā*) with a fifth person who is proficient in the Vinaya.
"Venerable Sir,
what constitutes a 'border country'?"
The Buddha said:

"In the east there is a country named Puṇḍravardhana. Not far to the east of the city is a śāla tree named Puṇḍrakhā; this is called the eastern boundary, and from here onwards it is known as a borderland."

To the south there is a city named Śrāvastī; to the south of that is a river named Śrāvastī, which is called the southern boundary. From this point onward, the lands are known as the border countries.
To the west there are two villages named Sthūṇa and Upasthūṇa; both villages are inhabited by brahmins. This is called the western region, and from here onwards, they are known as the borderlands.

To the north there is a mountain named Uśīragiri; this is called the northern frontier. From here onwards, the lands are known as the border regions. As for the general estimate of the distances between them, the two boundaries from east to west extend for more than three hundred stations (*yōji*), and the two sides from south to north extend for more than four hundred stations. Although I have not witnessed these myself, I have learned of them through detailed inquiry.

However, about forty stations to the south of the eastern border, one reaches the country of Dhanalipta; there are five or six monasteries there, and the local people are prosperous and wealthy, being subject to Eastern India.
From here to Mahābodhi and Śrī-Nālandā Monastery, there are approximately sixty stations; this is the place where one boards a ship to enter the sea and return to Tang.

From here, after two months at sea sailing southeast, one arrives at the kingdom of Kāṭha, which belongs to Fo-shih (Śrīvijaya). When the ship arrives, it is usually during the first or second month of the year. If one intends to set sail for Siṃhala Island toward the southwest, it is said to be seven hundred stations away; one should remain here until winter.
Sailing southward on a merchant vessel for about one month, they arrived at the island of Malayu, which is now the kingdom of Fo-shi-t'o (Śrīvijaya).
They also arrived during the first or second lunar month and remained there until midsummer.
Sailing northward on a merchant vessel, one reaches Guangzhou in a little over a month; the journey there has already taken nearly half a year.
If one is supported by the power of merit wherever one goes, it is as pleasant as walking through a marketplace;
yet if one’s past causes and karma are meager, one will find oneself in actual peril at every stop, like a nest on the verge of collapsing.

Prefacing this with an account of the four directions, I shall briefly describe the route of my return, hoping that those of discerning knowledge will gradually broaden their understanding and hearing.

Furthermore, throughout the various islands of the South Sea, there is widespread reverence and faith; the kings and rulers of these lands cherish the cultivation of merit. In this kingdom of Fo-shih-kia (Suvarṇabhūmi), the monastic community numbers over a thousand, who are devoted to learning and mostly practice the alms-bowl. Their scriptural studies are no different from those of the Middle Kingdom, and the monastic discipline of the śramaṇas is entirely without distinction.

If the monk from Tang intends to go to the West as a listener-lecturer, it would also be excellent for him to stay here for one or two years to practice the ritual methods before proceeding to Central India.
The Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One:
"Bhadanta, as the Blessed One has said:..."
"Regarding the statement, 'If a bhikṣu obtains leather shoes previously worn by a layperson,
he should use them,' Venerable Sir,
I do not yet know what constitutes leather shoes previously worn by a layperson."
The Buddha said,
"If one merely allows a layperson to walk seven or eight paces while wearing them, these are then termed 'previously used items.
But what should be done with new leather shoes, sandals, or boots that have never been used before?"
The Buddha said:
"This should be entrusted to a trustworthy layperson.
Inform them, saying:"
"This is your property.
Thinking it was his own, he put on leather shoes and walked seven or eight paces. One should then pick up the shoes and go to the bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable One!..."
"This is my property; I pray that you will show me compassion and accept it for your own use as you please.
The Venerable Upāli then requested of the Blessed One: "Bhadanta!..."
As the Blessed One has said:
"In the various countries of cold snow, the wearing of fur boots (pura) is permitted.
We do not yet know which regions constitute these countries of cold snow.
The Buddha said:
"It is that which becomes ice in water-vessels where there is frost and snow.
[The interlocutor asked: "As the World-Honored One has said:"
"There are four kinds of medicines that should be used. What are the four?
First, medicine for the proper time; second, medicine for the subsequent period; third, seven-day medicine; and fourth, lifetime medicine."
At that time, the bhikṣus did not yet know their nature.
The Buddha said:

"The 'timely medicines' (kālabhojana) refer to the five kinds of *khādaniya*—translated as the 'five chewed foods,' namely roots, stalks, flowers, leaves, and fruits; the meaning is that they are to be bitten and chewed. The five kinds of *bhojaniya*—translated as the 'five masticated foods,' namely parched grain flour, cooked rice, wheat, beans, and cakes; as for meat and cakes, here the intention is to name them after the act of taking them into the mouth and chewing."
Regarding what was formerly called *śyānī*, this name does not appear at all in the complete Sanskrit manuscript.
As for what is termed "subsequent medicine," it refers to the eight kinds of fermented liquors (*parisrut*):
first, *takra*, a fermented liquid that resembles plum vinegar in appearance and is like soapberry in consistency; [and so forth].
2. The *mora* juice is that of the ripe plantain fruit;
3. The *kolaka* juice is from a fruit shaped like the jujube;
4. The *aśvattha* seed juice is that of the Bodhi tree seed.
5. Udumbara juice: its fruit is as large as a plum;
6. Parūṣaka juice: its fruit is shaped like a blackberry;
7. Mṛdvīkā juice: this is the grape fruit.
The *kharjūra* fruit is shaped like a small jujube, astringent yet sweet.

It originates from the central region of Persia; although its flavor there is slightly different, its tree grows in isolation and resembles a *tāla* palm. These fruits are frequently brought to the border regions, where the local people call them "Persian dates"; their taste is somewhat similar to that of dried persimmons.
Regarding "seven-day medicines," these refer to clarified butter, oil, sugar, and honey.

Regarding "lifetime medicines," these refer to roots, stalks, flowers, leaves, and fruits; that is to say, all medicinal substances derived from plants and trees do not exceed these categories, and thus the classification of all medicinal types is hereby concluded. This also includes the five kinds of salt, as detailed elsewhere.

Among these, regarding the medicines for the proper time (*kālabhaiṣajya*), the medicines for the subsequent period (*yāmika-bhaiṣajya*), the seven-day medicines (*saptāhika-bhaiṣajya*), and the lifelong medicines (*yāvajjīvika-bhaiṣajya*)—the latter three types of medicine, if mixed with a medicine for the proper time, should be consumed within that [specific] time; if the time has passed, they must not be eaten.
Regarding the two lower types of medicine mixed with *yāmika* (medicines for a watch of the night): they should be consumed until the end of that watch.

Regarding the one lower type of medicine mixed with *saptāhika* (medicines for seven days): it should be used until the end of those seven days. As for the old explanation that when four types of medicine are mixed, one should consume them according to the stronger, this means that among the *kālika* (timely) and *akālika* (non-timely), there is inherent strength or weakness regardless of their quantity.
Some claim that if yeast and ginger are mixed together, it is permissible to consume when the yeast is predominant even at improper times, whereas if the ginger is predominant, it is not;
these are all mere conjectures. Regarding medicinal substances for the duration of one's life (*yāvajjīvika*), if one wishes to maintain them for long-term use, one should proceed as follows:
first, wash the hands thoroughly and receive the medicine; then, squatting before a single *bhikṣu* with palms joined, speak as follows:
"Venerable sir, please bear this in mind:
I, the bhikṣu [Name], have this ailment; I now formally accept these pure medicines to be kept for as long as life lasts, for my own use and that of my fellow practitioners of the holy life."
The second and third times were also spoken thus. Regarding the seven-day medicinal substances and the subsequent medicines (*yāmika-bhaiṣajya*), they should be maintained as prescribed above.

As for these subsequent medicines, they should be consumed throughout the day; however, if it reaches the night, they may only be taken until the first watch. According to the Vinaya teachings, one night is divided into three sections:
The first portion is called the "first watch"; one should not consume [liquids] once this has passed.
If measured according to the five watches, it corresponds to slightly more than one watch.
The traditional term "non-time" (asīta) is not a literal translation.
"Whenever one wishes to formally take possession of any of the three medicines, it must be done before midday; this is the established rule.
He asked: "Regarding the three lower medicines, once they have been formally taken possession of, their respective portions are clearly demarcated."
"If one must not maintain [the medicine] by formal observance, for how long may it be used? He replied:
"Regarding these three medicines, if they have been received before midday, it is improper to consume them once noon has passed."
If one receives them after midday, or obtains food during the first watch of the night, they are treated the same as medicines for that watch.

Furthermore, once these four types of medicine have been formally accepted, if they have not yet passed their allotted time and have been touched by one who is not fully ordained (*asaṃvṛta*), they may be re-accepted and consumed accordingly;
however, if they have exceeded their own limit, whether they were touched or not, they must be discarded.
He asked again:
“If one has already consecrated the three medicines and then touches them before being fully ordained, may they still be used?
He replied:

"The original intention of maintaining [the robe] was to prevent taking it for oneself; once another has touched it, the legal status of the object is extinguished. By principle, it should be discarded and is not fit for reuse.

However, if the owner is poor, an exchange with another person is permitted: having resolved to give it away, the recipient takes it back as a gift; in meaning, this is equivalent to obtaining it anew!"
Regarding the formal procedure (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) for constructing small rooms, the Venerable Kāśyapa requested of the Blessed One: "Bhadanta!

There are certain bhikṣus who trouble their donors by repeatedly begging for materials to extensively construct dwellings; once they have completed them, they may find them too long or too short, or too wide or too narrow. What should be done about this?"
He reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The bhikṣu who builds the dwelling should request from the Saṃgha permission to inspect the site of the dwelling; if it is pure in three respects, he is permitted to build."
What are the three?
First, a pure place that accords with the Dharma;
second, a place free from dispute and contention.
“There are three places where beings proceed.
“What are their lengths, widths, and extents?
The Buddha said:
"It shall be twelve spans long and seven spans wide; this is its measurement.
The bhikṣu constructing the dwelling shall strike the *gandī*, perform the preliminary rites as prescribed above, and finally, squatting with palms joined, make the following announcement:
'Venerable Saṃgha, listen!'"

I, the bhikṣu [Name], who am engaged in construction, have inspected a certain plot of land and found it to be pure and free from all obstacles; I wish to construct a small dwelling. I pray that the venerable Saṃgha will grant me permission, as the bhikṣu [Name] engaged in construction, to build a small dwelling on this pure site.
"May those who are compassionate take pity on us.
Thus he says three times.
Next, two or three trustworthy bhikṣus, or the Saṃgha together, shall go to inspect the site; if there are no obstacles and the three locations are pure, they may authorize its construction.
Having completed the inspection, he returns to the assembly and, employing the same formal procedure as before, makes this announcement: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
