Furthermore, after the six-night *mānāpya* (probation), one must likewise complete the *śubhacarita*.
"What shall I do? Then the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"You bhikṣus, because you intentionally discharged semen with the bhikṣu Udāyin, you have committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense. Having concealed it for half a month, you must undergo the parivāsa probation for as many days as it was concealed."
If one commits the second offense and likewise conceals it, one must undergo the *parivāsa* (probation) again from the beginning and perform the *caryā* (proper conduct).

If one commits the third offense, which is of the same category as the preceding offenses and is likewise concealed, one must again undergo the fundamental *parivāsa* and once more perform the *caryā*.
The six-night *mānatva* penance is likewise completed when the proper conduct has been fulfilled.
If there are others of a similar category, it should be granted in the same manner.
One should arrange the seats, strike the *ghanṭī*, announce the assembly, and ensure that there are at least twenty persons present.

Then the bhikṣu Udāyin bared his right shoulder, removed his leather sandals, and having paid homage according to their seniority, he squatted before the elder monks with palms joined and spoke these words:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

I, the bhikṣu Udāyin, intentionally emitted semen and committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, which I concealed for half a month. I, the bhikṣu Udāyin, have requested the practice of *parivāsa* (probation) for as many days as I concealed it; the Saṃgha has already granted me, the bhikṣu Udāyin, the *parivāsa* dharma for as many days as I concealed the intentional emission of semen that constituted the saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.

While I, the bhikṣu Udāyin, was practicing the *parivāsa* (probation) within a half-month period, I committed a second offense of the same category as the previous one, which I also concealed. I have already requested from the Saṃgha the reinstatement of the original *parivāsa*, and the Saṃgha has already granted me, the bhikṣu Udāyin, the reinstatement of the original *parivāsa* for this offense of the same category.

I have performed the *parivāsa* (probation) for the original offense; the Saṃgha has now granted me, the bhikṣu Udāyin, the re-imposition of the *mūla-parivāsa* (probation from the beginning) for this subsequent offense of a similar class.
I, the bhikṣu Udāyin, having concealed the aforementioned category of offense for half a month, have properly practiced the *parivāsa* (probation) according to the number of days it was concealed.
Having committed this second grave offense of the same category, I shall undergo the original *parivāsa* once again, and likewise practice it properly.
The third offense is of the same category as the previous ones; I have again undergone the *mūla-parivāsa* and the six-night *mānāpya*, and have also completed the *su-carita*.
Now I beg the Saṃgha for the rite of exculpation from this offense. May the virtuous Saṃgha grant me, the bhikṣu Udāyin, the rite of exculpation.
"May those who are capable of compassion show pity out of their compassionate nature.
A second and third time, he should speak in this same manner.
Next, one bhikṣu shall first perform the formal motion (jñapti), and then carry out the censure, followed by the formal ritual act (karman).
“Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu Udāyin intentionally emitted semen, thereby committing a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, which he concealed for half a month.”

This bhikṣu Udāyin has already requested from the Saṃgha the *parivāsa* discipline for as many days as he concealed [the offense]; the Saṃgha has now granted Udāyin bhikṣu the *parivāsa* for as many days as he concealed the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense of intentional emission of semen.

While he was practicing the *parivāsa* (probation), he committed a second offense of the same category as the previous one and again concealed it. Having already requested from the Saṃgha to undergo the restoration of the original *parivāsa* in accordance with the days of concealment, the Saṃgha has now granted the bhikṣu Udāyin the restoration of the original *parivāsa* in accordance with the days of concealment for this second offense of the same category.

While he was practicing the *parivāsa* (probation) for his original offense, he committed a third offense of the same category as the former, which he also concealed. Having requested from the Saṃgha the re-imposition of the fundamental *parivāsa* for the duration of that concealment, the Saṃgha has now granted the bhikṣu Udāyin the re-imposition of the fundamental *parivāsa* for the duration of the concealment of the previous offense of the same category.
This bhikṣu Udāyin intentionally discharged semen and committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense; for as many days as he concealed it, he must undergo the *parivāsa* probation.
Having committed a second offense of the same category, he must again undergo the original *parivāsa* and likewise perform the *caryā* penance.
The third offense is of the same category as the preceding one; he has again undergone the *mūlaparivāsa* and the *sucarita*.

Having already requested from the Saṃgha the performance of the six-night *mānāpya*, and having completed the six-night *mānāpya* granted by the Saṃgha to the Bhikṣu Udāyin, he now requests absolution from the Saṃgha.
"If the Saṃgha deems the time has come and grants its permission, may the Saṃgha allow that the Saṃgha now absolve the bhikṣu Udāyin of his offense.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). Thereafter, one should issue this reprimand:

“Oḍāyī, you bhikṣu, you should know that there are two kinds of persons who can extinguish the torch of the Dharma, obscure the radiance of the Dharma, and destroy the flame of the lamp of the Dharma. What are these two?

This refers to having committed an offense and failing to repent and eliminate it according to the Dharma; this is precisely what is called the two minor [faults], the two forms of delusion, the two types of lack of clarity, and the two kinds of unwholesomeness.

Furthermore, there are two kinds of fundamental heavy offenses: being unwilling to excavate them, not diligently applying effort toward the task of going against the current, not desiring to dry up the various torrents, not engaging in battle with Māra, not breaking the banners of Māra, lacking the intention to establish the victory banner of the sublime Dharma, not severing evil views, and not turning the wheel of Dharma in accordance with the unsurpassed true teaching of the Great Master.

Furthermore, there are two kinds of affliction by bitter poison, and there are two kinds of increase in the fluxes of existence (*āsrava*): namely, having committed an offense, one does not repent according to the Dharma. You, Udāyin!
As the World-Honored One has said:
"One should always contemplate remaining far removed from desire, hatred, and delusion.
Why do you now commit such a loathsome act?
"You foolish person!
How can you take these two hands, which have received the offerings of others given with pure hearts, and then use those very hands to commit such loathsome deeds?"
Furthermore, you fool!

It would be better for you to take two hands and seize a terrifying, venomous snake to bite it than to intentionally grasp the *aṅga-śīrṣa*—translated as "vital organ" (*shengzhi*), which refers to the root—for such a loathsome act.
"O Udāyin! Because you did not confess and eliminate the offense you committed, you have fallen away from the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in impermanence,
the perception of non-self in suffering, the perception of revulsion toward food, and the perception of disenchantment with all worldly realms."
The perception of affliction, the perception of what can be severed, the perception of the unlovely, the perception of death, the perception of impurity,
the perception of a livid corpse, the perception of a festering corpse, the perception of a dismembered corpse, the perception of a bloated corpse,

the perception of a blood-stained corpse, the perception of a mangled corpse, the perception of a skeleton, and the perception of the contemplation of emptiness— all such perceptions of phenomena no longer appear.
Previously, he also could not attain the first dhyāna, the second, third, or fourth dhyānas; loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, or equanimity;
the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, or the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
nor could he attain the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arhatship—none of these he could attain at all.
He did not realize or attain the supernormal power of the divine realm, nor the supernormal powers of the divine eye, the divine ear, the discernment of others' minds, the recollection of past lives,
or the knowledge of death and rebirth that exhausts all taints of existence.
"You, Udāyin! Because you did not confess your transgression, after the end of your life, you shall be reborn in one of two states, which are places of fear: namely, the hells or the animal realm."
As the Blessed One said:
"Karma shrouded by the two obscurations leads toward the realms of hell-beings and animals; it is because they do not believe my words that they conceal their transgressions."
Having thus earnestly issued this reprimand, he hoped that [the offender] would repent and reform.
Next, he performed the *karmavācanā*:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
This bhikṣu Udāyin intentionally emitted semen and committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, which he concealed for half a month.

This bhikṣu Udāyin has already requested from the Saṃgha the practice of *parivāsa* (probation) for as many days as the offense was concealed; the Saṃgha has already granted this bhikṣu Udāyin the *parivāsa* for as many days as the intentional emission of semen constituting the saṃghāvaśeṣa offense was concealed.
While practicing the *parivāsa* (probation), he committed a second offense of the same category as the previous one and likewise concealed it.

He has already requested from the Saṃgha the restoration of the original *parivāsa* according to the number of days he concealed that subsequent offense; the Saṃgha has now granted the bhikṣu Udāyin the restoration of the original *parivāsa* according to the number of days he concealed that subsequent offense of the same category.

While he was performing the *parivāsa* (probation) for his original offense, he committed a third offense of the same category as the previous one and likewise concealed it; having already requested from the Saṃgha the performance of a renewed *mūla-parivāsa* corresponding to the days of that concealment, the Saṃgha has now granted the bhikṣu Udāyin a renewed *mūla-parivāsa* corresponding to the days of concealment for the previous category of offense.
This Udāyin, having committed the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense of intentional emission of semen, underwent the *parivāsa* probation for as many days as he had concealed it.
Having committed a second offense of the same category, he returned to the original *parivāsa* and likewise underwent the *caryā* (probationary conduct).
The third offense is of the same category as the previous one; it involves again undertaking the *mūlaparivāsa* and the *sucarita*.

Having already requested from the Saṃgha the performance of the six-night *mānāpya*, the Saṃgha has already granted the six-night *mānāpya* to the bhikṣu Udāyin, and he has also completed the *sucarita*.

I now request from the Saṃgha absolution from my offense; may the Saṃgha now grant the *parivāsa* of good conduct to the bhikṣu Udāyin for the intentional emission of semen, which constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, in accordance with the number of days it was concealed.

A second commission of the same offense is of the same category as the previous offense; one must again undergo the *parivāsa* (probation) from the beginning and likewise perform the *caryā* (proper conduct).
A third commission of the same offense is also of the same category as the previous offense; one must again undergo the *parivāsa* from the very beginning and likewise perform the *caryā*.
Having completed the six-night *mānatva* penance and having also successfully performed the proper conduct, I now request the Saṃgha for absolution from the offense.
Venerable sirs, if you grant absolution to the bhikṣu Udāyin, remain silent; if you do not consent, please speak.
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third are also spoken in this manner.
'The Saṃgha has already completed the removal of the offense for the bhikṣu Udāyin.'"
"The Saṃgha has granted its consent, as indicated by their silence; I now hold it to be so.
Next, one should offer this praise: "Excellent, Udāyin!"
Excellent, Udāyin!
There are two kinds of wise people, two kinds of discerning people, and two kinds of virtuous people.
What are these two?
First, not committing offenses;
second, being able to repent and eliminate them according to the Dharma after having committed one.
There are two kinds of people who can thus kindle the torch of the Dharma and establish the banner of the Dharma.
What are these two? First, not committing offenses; second, being able to repent and eliminate them according to the Dharma once they have been committed.

Furthermore, there are two kinds of heavy offenses that can fundamentally uproot [the mind]: one who exerts diligent effort in the work of going against the current, who can cause the various torrents to dry up, who can wage war against Māra, who can break the banner of Māra, who can firmly establish the sublime banner of the Dharma, who can sever evil views, and who can turn the wheel of Dharma in accordance with the unsurpassed true teaching of the Great Master.
What are these two? First, not committing offenses; second, having committed an offense, repenting and eliminating it in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of not being afflicted by suffering, and two kinds of not increasing the fluxes of existence (*āsrava*).
What are the two? First, not committing an offense;
second, being able to repent after having committed one.

"You, Udāyin! Since you have already confessed and repented for your many transgressions, you ought to attain the perception of impermanence and the perception of suffering in impermanence, and so on, up to being able to exhaust the outflows of existence."
"You will certainly attain rebirth in the two realms of humans and devas without any doubt.
As the World-Honored One has said:
'There are two kinds of unobstructed karma that enable one to proceed toward the two realms of humans and devas; those who can believe my words do not conceal their transgressions.'"
"You should understand this: Udayin, you have now been cleared of your offense. Do not be negligent; constantly cultivate all that is wholesome.
If there should be another who commits an offense, the formal procedure should be carried out for them in the same sequence as was done for the bhikṣu Udayin.
Next, after having been cleared of the offense, one should request the Saṃgha for the confession of a sthūlātyaya offense. The request should be made as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!..."
I, the bhikṣu [Name], have committed a sthūlātyaya offense involving the preliminary preparation for intentional emission of semen.
I, [Name], now request from the Saṃgha the rite of confession. May the venerable Saṃgha grant me, [Name], permission to confess this sthūlātyaya offense.
"May those who are capable of compassion please show us mercy.
A second and third time he spoke thus.
Then, one bhikṣu first made the formal motion (*jñapti*), after which the *karmavācanā* was performed:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has committed a sthūlātyaya offense through the preliminary preparation of intentionally emitting semen.
This so-and-so now requests the Saṃgha to grant him the confession of this sthūlātyaya offense."

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and they grant their permission, may the Saṃgha allow that the Saṃgha now grant [the formal act of] confession for the sthūlātyaya offense involving the preliminary preparation of intentional emission of semen to so-and-so.
The motion is thus made.
Next, the *karmavācanā* is performed: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, committed the preparatory offense of a sthūlātyaya regarding intentional emission of semen.

This so-and-so now requests from the Saṃgha the confession of this sthūlātyaya offense; the Saṃgha now grants this so-and-so the confession for the preparatory offense of a sthūlātyaya regarding intentional emission of semen.
Venerable sirs, if you agree that I may confess the sthūlātyaya offense involving the preliminary effort of intentional emission of semen, please remain silent; if you do not agree, please speak.
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third are also spoken in this manner:

'The Saṃgha has already granted [the formal act] to so-and-so regarding the preliminary effort (*pūrvaprayoga*) for the offense of *sthūlātyaya* arising from intentional emission of semen; it is heard that the confession is concluded.'"
"The Saṃgha has granted its consent; because of their silence, I now hold it thus.

Subsequently, in the same manner and sequence, one should, in the presence of a single bhikṣu, duly confess and expiate all previously incurred numerous *duṣkṛta* offenses as well as numerous *pāyattika* offenses for disrespecting the teachings.
There are two kinds of *sthūlātyaya* offenses:
first, those that have the *pārājika* as their cause; second, those that have the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* as their cause.
Regarding those with the *pārājika* as their cause, there are further two kinds:
First, grave; second, light.
Among these, regarding the grave offenses, one should confess the transgression before the great assembly. "The great assembly" refers to the gathering of all members within the boundary.
Regarding "light offenses," this refers to cases involving four or fewer individuals; within the ritual enclosure (*maṇḍala*), one should confess the offense.
Regarding the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, there are likewise two types:
first, the heavy, and second, the light.

Among these, for those offenses that are grave, one should confess them before an assembly of four or more persons in a ritual enclosure; for those that are light, one should remove the offense according to the Dharma by facing a single person.

Regarding the offenses of *pāyattika* and *dukkaṭa* mentioned previously, one should act in accordance with the preceding rules; all numerous offenses of concealment, whether major or minor, must be confessed and repented.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-ekottara-karmavastu*, Fascicle Six;
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-ekottara-karmavastu*,
Fascicle Seven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.

Regarding the remainder of the expiation for communal offenses: the Venerable Upāli requested of the World-Honored One, "If one who is undergoing the parivāsa penance sees an incoming bhikṣu and does not announce his presence to him, what is the nature of that offense?"
The Buddha said,
"If a guest arrives, you must announce it. At that time,
seeing a guest arrive, the bhikṣu, without yet having set aside his robes and bowl, went forward and made this announcement:
"Venerable sir!

I, the bhikṣu [Name], have intentionally emitted semen and committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense—as previously described in detail—with such-and-such days remaining. May the Venerable sir please take note of this."
At that time, the visiting bhikṣu manifested an expression of anger and replied, "Stop!
You foolish man!"
"Do not speak of practicing the *paryuṣaṇā* in my presence.
He then felt ashamed, lowered his head, and departed in silence.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, if a guest bhikṣu newly arrives, you need not announce him before he has laid aside his robes and bowl.
At another time, when each one was announced individually, he was again met with anger as before. The Buddha said:
"One should not announce them one by one; rather, they must be announced only when the assembly has gathered."

Alternatively, one may strike the *gandī* to cause the laypeople and the novices (*śrāmaṇera*) to come out; once they have emerged, they should go to where the bhikṣus are and announce [the matter], but they should not do so in a place where no bhikṣus reside.

Even if one must depart, one should not stay overnight; at the time of dusk, one should ensure the temperature is neither too cold nor too hot, and should prepare warm water for the bhikṣus to wash their feet and provide them with oil for anointing; if they do not wish for it, the oil should be set aside.
Next, one should mindfully form the intention of rising before finally lying down to rest.
If any bhikṣus, when practicing the *parivāsa* penance or the *mānatva* discipline, do not act in accordance with what I have taught, they commit an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who was correctly practicing the *parivāsa* penance; they did not give him a room, nor did they give him a share of the profits. The Buddha said:
"One should give him a lower-quality room, but he should receive the profits later."
The Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One: "Bhadanta,

when one is performing the *parivāsa* or the *mānatva*, if it is heard that a bhikṣu who is quarrelsome, a detractor, or of a shameless and indolent nature intends to come to this place, what should that person do toward him?"
The Buddha said:
"If one knows that those wicked people intend to come here, the person practicing the *parivāsa* (probation) should relinquish that practice before the bhikṣus.
It should be relinquished in this manner."
Squatting with palms joined, he spoke thus:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me!
I, [name], intentionally emitted semen and thereby committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, which I concealed for half a month."
I, [Name], have requested from the Saṃgha the practice of *parivāsa*. The Saṃgha has already granted me, [Name], *parivāsa* for as many days as were concealed.
While I was practicing *parivāsa*, I heard that a bhikṣu intended to come here—one who is quarrelsome and contentious—who intends to do me harm.
I, [Name], now before the venerable one, relinquish the practice of *parivāsa*. I have completed this much of the practice; this much remains.

May the venerable one know me as a pure bhikṣu. Once that wicked person has departed and ceased his interference, I shall return to those virtuous and pure bhikṣus and receive the rules for the practice from them.
One should accept it in this manner.
Having paid homage, one should squat with palms joined and speak as follows:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me!

I, the bhikṣu [name], previously intentionally emitted semen and committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, which I concealed for half a month; the Saṃgha has granted me the parivāsa discipline for as many days as I concealed it.
While I was dwelling in my travels, I heard that there were bhikṣus intending to come here—those who are quarrelsome and contentious—who intended to do me harm.
For this reason, I relinquish that preparatory practice.
I, [Name], now before the Venerable One, receive the preparatory practice; I have already completed [so many] days of the practice, and [so many] days remain.
"May the Venerable One bear this in mind.

Just as it is with the *parivāsa* (probation) regarding equanimity and sensation, so too should it be for the *mūlaparivāsa* (renewed probation), the *mānāpya* (trial period), and the *mānāpyacāra* (observance of the trial period).
Having thus concluded the explanation of the procedures for performing the communal legal acts, the Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One:

"Bhadanta, is it possible for one person who performs the formal motion (*jñapti*), the single proclamation (*karmavācanā*), and the presiding over the rite (*karmakāraka*) to confer full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon two individuals?"
The Buddha said, “They have attained it.
[The interlocutor asked: “Between these two persons, who is the greater?”
The Buddha said,
"There is no distinction between great and small.
[He asked,] "Venerable Sir!"
"Is it permissible for one person who performs the formal motion and the single *karmavācanā* to confer full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon three people?
The Buddha said, "It is permissible."
“Among these three persons, which one is the greatest?
“There is neither great nor small. “Venerable Sir!”
“Is it permissible for one person who performs the ritual action— using one motion (*jñapti*) and one proclamation (*karmavācanā*)— to confer full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon four people?
The Buddha said,
“It is not permissible.”
“What fault is there in this?
The Buddha said,
“There is none, because it is a matter for the community to manage.”
"Venerable Sir! In future ages, there will be monks whose power of mindfulness is meager and whose physical faculties are frail; they will not know where the World-Honored One expounded this Dharma."

"How should this be done? The Buddha said, "Recall any one of the six great cities and speak of it; or else, recall any other place where you have stayed for a long time and speak of that. There is no fault in either case."
“Venerable One! If you should forget the names of any of the kings, whom would you wish to speak of?
The Buddha said:
“The King should be called Prasenajit;
the elder should be called Anāthapiṇḍada;
and the upāsikā’s name should be Viśākhā.”
“Venerable Sir! I have forgotten the name of the city where the Buddha was born; which city do you wish to speak of?
The Buddha said:
"One should go to the city of Vārāṇasī. There,
the king is named Brahmadatta,
and the householder is named Sandhāna."
"The upāsikā named Upoṣadha may speak as she pleases.
"As the Blessed One has said:"

"There are five things that should not be written down: first, the Prātimokṣa; second, its extensive commentary; third, the various other Vinayas; fourth, their extensive commentaries; and fifth, all items donated by donors, as well as the personal property of individuals—provided it is not communal property—which is what is meant by 'individual property.'"
"O Venerable One!

In future ages, the bhikṣus will be dull and inferior in both body and mind; they will not even be able to remember the proper sequence of formal procedures. How can one expect such people to act otherwise?"
The Buddha said:
"You should write it on paper or leaves and read and uphold it according to your inclination.
Regarding the keeping of a staff, the Venerable Upāli requested of the World-Honored One with a formal motion (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*):
"If there is a bhikṣu who is aged and infirm, lacking strength and incapable of exertion, and who cannot survive without a staff, how should this be handled?
The Buddha said,
"He should request from the Saṃgha the formal act (karmavācanā) for the possession of a staff."
One should request in this manner:
having spread out the seats and mats, and so forth, one should address the assembly, saying:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!"

"I, the bhikṣu [Name], am old, sick, and decrepit, lacking all capability; without a staff, I am unable to sustain myself. I, the bhikṣu [Name], now request from the Saṃgha the authorization to carry a staff. May the Saṃgha grant me, the bhikṣu [Name], who am old, sick, and decrepit, lacking all capability, the authorization to carry a staff."
"May those who are compassionate show us mercy.
A second and third time, he should speak thus.
Then, one bhikṣu shall first make the formal motion (*jñapti*), after which the *karman* (formal ritual act) is performed:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so by name, is aged and infirm, or perhaps afflicted by illness and lacks physical capability; if he is separated from his staff, he will be unable to sustain himself."
This [person], so-and-so, because of old age and illness, now requests from the Saṃgha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for the carrying of a staff.

If the Saṃgha deems the time appropriate and grants permission, the Saṃgha should consent; the Saṃgha now grants to this person, so-and-so, who is aged, ill, and lacking strength, the formal act for the carrying of a staff.
"Thus it is announced. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, is aged and infirm, or perhaps afflicted by illness; if he is separated from his staff, he will be unable to sustain himself."

This person, so-and-so, because of old age and illness, now requests from the Saṃgha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for the carrying of a staff; the Saṃgha now grants to this person, so-and-so, because of old age and illness, the formal act for the carrying of a staff.
"Venerable sirs, if you consent to granting the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for so-and-so to carry a staff for the sake of old age and illness, remain silent; if you do not consent, speak.
"The Sangha has completed the formal act for so-and-so to carry a staff for the sake of old age and illness."
"The Saṃgha has granted its permission; because of their silence, I now hold it thus.
Just as it is with the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for keeping a staff, so it is with a bowl-bag; at times, both the staff and the bag may be permitted together.

Furthermore, just as the distribution of bedding is performed by a formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*), so too are the distribution of rooms and the distribution of alms-food; this applies to each and every one of the twelve types of persons.
Regarding the four-month period of co-residence with non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), the Venerable Upāli addressed the World-Honored One:
"If members of non-Buddhist sects should develop a pure mind and come to seek refuge in the True Dharma, requesting to go forth, what should be done?"
The Buddha said:
"Request one bhikṣu to act as your upādhyāya; for four months, wear the robes of an upādhyāya, eat the regular food of the Saṃgha, and dwell together with him."
The community of bhikṣus did not know how they should proceed regarding communal residence.
The Buddha said:
"If there is an outsider who comes seeking to go forth, his upādhyāya should inquire about the obstructing dharmas."

If one is completely pure, they should be accepted; having been granted the three refuges and the five precepts, they become a *upāsaka* protected by the vows that guard body, speech, and mind, ensuring that these are not violated or lost.
The term "vinaya" (律儀) used in older translations is merely a semantic rendering.
All members of the present *saṃgha* should assemble; having instructed that outsider to pay homage, he should squat before the elder, join his palms, and speak as follows:
"Venerable *saṃgha*, listen!"

I, [Name], a follower of other paths, seek to go forth under the preceptor [Name]. I, [Name], a follower of other paths, now request from the Saṃgha that for a period of four months I may wear the robes of the preceptor, eat the regular food of the Saṃgha, and dwell together with them.

I pray that the virtuous Saṃgha will grant me, the outsider [named] So-and-so, the privilege of wearing the robes of an upādhyāya and eating the regular food of the Saṃgha for the duration of four months, so that we may dwell together.
"May those who are capable of compassion please have pity on us.
A second and third time he should speak in this manner.

Next, he should have the non-Buddhists move away from the place where they can hear and stand where they can only see. Then, one bhikṣu should first perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*), after which the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) should be carried out.

"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This outsider named So-and-so seeks to go forth under the preceptor named So-and-so. This outsider named So-and-so now requests from the Saṃgha that, for the duration of four months, he shall wear the robes of his preceptor and partake of the regular food of the Saṃgha while living in common with them."

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and they grant permission, may the Saṃgha allow that this certain outsider now be granted the *upādhyāya-vastra* by the Saṃgha for a period of four months, eating the regular food of the Saṃgha, and dwelling together with them.
"Thus it is announced.

"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This outsider named So-and-so seeks to go forth under the preceptor named So-and-so. This outsider So-and-so now requests from the Saṃgha that, for a period of four months, he wear the robes of his preceptor and consume the regular food of the Saṃgha while living in common with them."
The Saṃgha now grants this outsider [name] the right to wear the robes of an *upādhyāya* and partake of the community’s regular food for four months, while living in common with us.

If the venerable ones consent to this outsider [name] wearing the robes of an *upādhyāya* and partaking of the community’s regular food for four months while living in common, let them remain silent; if they do not consent, let them speak.
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third are also spoken in this manner.

"The Saṃgha has already granted the outsider [named] So-and-so the right to wear the preceptor’s robe and consume the regular food of the Saṃgha for the duration of four months, and has completed the formal co-residence with him."
"The Saṃgha has granted its consent; by reason of their silence, I now hold it thus.

If such a non-Buddhist has been granted by the Saṃgha, within the four-month period, the wearing of the upādhyāya’s robes and the eating of the Saṃgha’s regular food while living together with them, they shall be employed according to the precedent set for śrāmaṇeras.
The Venerable Upāli requested the Blessed One, saying: "Bhadanta,
if one grants the going forth only when those of other sects have their minds tamed, what is meant by 'the mind being tamed'?"
The Buddha said:
"One should respond before those non-Buddhists by praising all the magnificent virtues of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, and also discuss the various activities of those non-Buddhists."

If those non-Buddhists, upon hearing praise for the true virtues of the Triple Gem or hearing of the activities of the non-Buddhists themselves, harbor feelings of attachment or resentment within their hearts, and manifest anger with no sign of joy on their faces, this is called the untamed mind of a non-Buddhist.
If one does not give rise to even the slightest malice toward outsiders who differ from this, it is said that one’s mind is already tamed.
As the Blessed One said:
“When one has accomplished the five dharmas and completed five years of residence (pañca-varṣa), one may leave the formal dependence [on a preceptor] and wander among the people.”

What are the five? First, knowing what constitutes an offense; second, knowing what does not constitute an offense; third, knowing what is light; fourth, knowing what is heavy; and fifth, being well-versed in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* regarding its prohibitions and allowances, as well as being able to recite and uphold it.
"Venerable Sir!
If one has accomplished five dharmas and completed five years of summer retreat, one may leave one's formal reliance and travel among the people.
Venerable Sir!"
"If there is one who has completed four years of summer retreat and is well-versed in the five dharmas, may this person also be exempt from dependence?
The Buddha said, "No."
"Because five years is established as the fixed duration.
"Venerable Sir! Is there one who has completed five years of residence but is not yet proficient in the five dharmas; may such a person be released from the requirement of dependence?"
The Buddha said:
"It is not permitted,
because the accomplishment of five factors is established as the definitive standard."
“Venerable Sir! If a bhikṣu is well-versed in the Tripiṭaka, has realized the three vidyās, and has already eliminated the three impurities, yet has only just completed his third summer retreat—
must such a person still rely upon a teacher?”
The Buddha said:
"It is not by this means.
One attains freedom from dependence only when what was not yet attained is attained, what was not yet realized is realized, and what was not yet awakened to is awakened to."
"However, in accordance with the matters that must be observed, one must necessarily have completed five years of residence.
Once these five qualities are accomplished, one may depart from one's teacher.
If one arrives at another dwelling place, for how long may one remain without needing to rely upon a preceptor?"
The Buddha said:
"If one does not cease [the search] and instead seeks another support, one may stay for five nights.
[As the World-Honored One has said:]

"Regarding the statement: 'If one has completed ten years of seniority and has accomplished the five aforementioned dharmas, one may become independent of formal reliance (niśraya), and even be permitted to keep a novice (śrāmaṇera),' Venerable Sir!

Suppose there is a bhikṣu who, since his full ordination (upasampadā), has reached eighty years of age and completed sixty years of seniority, yet has never recited the Prātimokṣa Sūtra nor understood its meaning—how should this case be handled?"
The Buddha said:
"Even if one has completed sixty years of the rains retreat, one must still rely upon a teacher.
[The monk asked: "Venerable Sir!"
"On whom should one rely?
The Buddha said, "One should rely on an elder; if there is no elder, one may rely on a junior."
“Venerable One! If one should pay homage to the Teacher, how should this be done?
The Buddha said:
"Except for performing prostrations, all other duties should be performed; such a person is called a 'young' or 'old' bhikṣu.
As the Blessed One said:
"If one is seven years of age and capable of scaring away crows, they may be granted the going-forth (pravrajyā)."
"Venerable Sir!
Suppose there is one who has reached six years of age and is capable of driving away crows from the monastery kitchen; would he also be fit for ordination?
The Buddha said:
"It is not appropriate; one must be at least seven years old, as this is the fixed standard. "Venerable Sir!
If there is one who is seven years old, yet is unable to drive away crows from the monastic kitchen, would it be appropriate to grant him ordination?"
The Buddha said:
"It is not permitted.
It must be able to drive away crows, as that constitutes the proper measure."

“Venerable Sir! If there is a bhikṣu who has accomplished the seven qualities, he should instruct the bhikṣuṇīs; if one has not yet been appointed, he should be appointed, and if one has already been appointed, he should not be dismissed.”
"What are the seven?
First, upholding the precepts;
second, extensive learning."
Third, being of senior standing;
fourth, being skilled in the dialect of the capital city;
fifth, never having defiled a bhikṣuṇī with one’s body.
Sixth, they are able to extensively proclaim all that is permitted and prohibited regarding the eight rules of defeat (*pārājika*);
seventh, they are well able to expound upon the eight rules of respect (*gurudharma*).
What is meant by "upholding the precepts"?
Among the four defeats (*pārājika*), one has not committed even a single transgression.
What is meant by "having heard much" (*bahuśruta*)?
It means that one has already read and recited the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* in its entirety.
What is meant by "senior in standing"?
One who has completed twenty rainy-season retreats (*varṣa*), or more than that.
What is meant by "being skilled in the language of the capital city"?
This refers to the discourse concerning the great city of Āpānaka.
What is meant by "never having defiled a bhikṣuṇī with one's body"?
It means not having made physical contact with a bhikṣuṇī.
The remaining two points may be understood from the text as they appear.

Having fulfilled these seven qualities, one should be appointed in this manner: having spread out the seats and struck the *ghanṭī*, and made the formal announcement (*jñapti*), one first asks whether he is capable.
"Venerable [Name], Bhikṣu, are you able to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs in the higher training of morality, the higher training of mind,
and the higher training of wisdom? He replies, "I am able."

Next, one bhikṣu should first make the formal announcement (jñapti), and only then perform the ritual action (karman). The procedure for the nuns who have come to request instruction is as follows and should be understood: the Elder, having gauged the time, shall respond to their matter.
The formal motion (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) for the instruction of bhikṣuṇīs: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu [Name] is capable of going to instruct the community of bhikṣuṇīs in higher morality (*adhiśīla*), higher concentration (*adhicitta*), and higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*)."

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha grant permission: the Saṃgha shall now appoint this bhikṣu, so-and-so, to go and instruct the community of bhikṣuṇīs in higher morality, higher concentration, and higher wisdom.
The motion is thus made.
Next, perform the *karmavācanā*:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, is capable of going to instruct the community of bhikṣuṇīs in higher morality, higher concentration, and higher wisdom; the Saṃgha now appoints this bhikṣu, so-and-so, as the instructor of the community of bhikṣuṇīs in higher morality, higher concentration, and higher wisdom.

If the venerable ones consent to appoint this bhikṣu, so-and-so, as the instructor of the community of bhikṣuṇīs for higher morality, higher concentration, and higher wisdom, let them remain silent; if they do not consent, let them speak.
"The Saṃgha has already appointed this bhikṣu, [Name], to go and instruct the community of bhikṣuṇīs in higher ethics, higher concentration, and higher wisdom."
"The Saṃgha has granted its consent, as indicated by their silence; thus do I now uphold it.
Once this bhikṣu has received the Dharma, he should go to instruct the community of nuns; let there be no doubt.
The Buddha said:
"If there is no one to provide extensive instruction, one should provide a brief instruction.
All the ritual procedures for this, I shall now explain."
Every half-month, the community of bhikṣuṇīs should go to the residence of the bhikṣus, pay homage to the assembly, and speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!"

The community of bhikṣuṇīs from [Name] Monastery, being in harmony, prostrate at the feet of the Venerable Saṃgha of [Name] Monastery and respectfully inquire: Are you free from illness and affliction? Is your daily life light and easy? Are your physical strength and vitality at peace?
"My community of bhikṣuṇīs has come here for the fortnightly invitation to request instruction from a bhikṣu.
The Elder replied, "Sisters!"
"Is the community of bhikṣuṇīs at such-and-such monastery in harmony?
The bhikṣuṇī should reply,
"The community is in harmony."
He asked again,
"During this half-month, have you committed no transgressions?
The nun replied:
"No. "Sisters, you must know! Within this assembly, there is no bhikṣu who is able to go and provide instruction to the community of bhikṣuṇīs during the half-month."
"Sisters! You should practice diligently for yourselves; do not be negligent.
The nuns should respond with palms joined, saying:
“Sādhu. “Whenever a bhikṣuṇī enters a bhikṣu monastery, once she has reached the gate, she must announce her presence to a bhikṣu before proceeding further;
if she fails to do so, she incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.”
The announcement should be made as follows: having paid respects to a bhikṣu, one should say:
"Venerable sir!
I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], now wish to enter the monastery."
The bhikṣu replied,
"One who has not committed an offense should enter.
The bhikṣuṇī answered:
"If you say, 'There are none,' it is well; if you do not speak thus, you shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
This is the formal motion with three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) for admonishing a bhikṣuṇī regarding living in mixed residence.
At that time, there were two bhikṣuṇīs in Śrāvastī:
one named Priyā and the other named Anupriyā, who lived together in a disorderly manner.
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha addressed the bhikṣuṇīs:
"You should admonish them in private, and even proceed up to the formal act of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* to admonish those two nuns.
If there are others of this same sort, assemble the community as before and have one nun perform the *jñapti-karman*."
"Listen, Venerable Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha!
These two bhikṣuṇīs, Kāntā and Anukāntā, dwell in disorder, being restless and frivolous, and striking one another."
The nuns admonished them in private:
"Do not live in a confused mixture; when living in such confusion, it causes the wholesome Dharma to decline and prevents it from increasing; you ought to live separately."
"While living apart, wholesome qualities will increase and no longer decline.
When those two were thus admonished, they stubbornly clung to their position and refused to relinquish it, saying:
"This teaching alone is true; all others are false."

"If it is the proper time for the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha and they grant permission, may the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha authorize that the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha now perform the formal act of *ajñapti-karman*—neither relinquishing mixed residence nor accepting admonition—against the two bhikṣuṇīs, Kāminī and Anukāminī."
"Thus it is announced.
The formal procedure (*karmavācanā*) is completed according to this announcement.

Having received these instructions, the bhikṣuṇīs performed the white-four-fold formal procedure (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) to admonish those two nuns regarding the prohibition against separate residence.
Stubbornly refusing to relinquish their position, they did not associate with one another but remained apart.
At that time, the nun Thullanandā went to those two nuns and spoke to them as follows:
"Venerable ladies!..."
"Why do you not dwell together in a mixed and disordered manner?
If you dwell in such a mixed and disordered way, it will cause wholesome dharmas to increase rather than decline.
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they informed the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Up to the point of the fourth formal motion (jñapti-caturtha-karman), one should admonish the bhikṣuṇī Tullā-nandā for not relinquishing her evil view of living in a mixed community.
If there are others of a similar kind who ought to be admonished, they should be dealt with according to the above procedure."
“‘Venerable Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, listen!

The two bhikṣuṇīs, Kāntā and Anukāntā, were living in disorderly association. When the Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha performed the formal act of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* to prohibit their disordered cohabitation, those two nuns immediately ceased associating with one another and lived separately.’”
The nun Thullanandā went to two other nuns and said to them: "Venerable ladies!
You should dwell together with me in a communal and informal manner; in this way, the wholesome dharmas will increase."
"If one lives separately, wholesome qualities will decline.
The Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha has already admonished her in private, yet she persists firmly and refuses to relinquish her position, saying, "This is the truth; all else is false."

"If the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha deems it timely and grants its permission, may the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha authorize that this formal procedure of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* be performed against the Bhikṣuṇī Toraṇandā for her refusal to relinquish the evil view of living in association."
"Thus it is announced.
Next, the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) shall be performed according to this announcement.

Regarding the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation) for "not paying homage": "If a bhikṣu lives in association with bhikṣuṇīs, and the harmonious Saṃgha has performed the *utkṣepaṇīya-karman* (act of suspension) against him, the community of bhikṣuṇīs shall perform the rite of 'not paying homage' toward that bhikṣu."
It should be performed in this manner:

having spread out the seats and struck the *ghanṭī*, once the community of *bhikṣuṇīs* has assembled, one *bhikṣuṇī* should first make the formal motion (*jñapti*), and only then perform the ritual act (*karman*).
“‘Venerable Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, listen!

That bhikṣu so-and-so has been subjected by the harmonious Saṃgha to the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation), and the Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha has subjected him to the *anavaśrāvaṇīya-karman* (act of non-prostration).’”

If it is the proper time for the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha and they grant their consent, may the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha permit that the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha now perform the formal act (*karma*) of non-prostration toward the Bhikṣu so-and-so.
[The motion] is thus stated.
"Venerable Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, listen!

That bhikṣu so-and-so has been subjected by the harmonious Saṃgha to the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation), and the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha has subjected him to the *anavaśrāvaṇīya-karman* (act of not being saluted)."
The Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha now performs the formal act of "not to be saluted" against the bhikṣu [Name].
If the venerable ones consent to performing the formal act of "not to be saluted" against the bhikṣu [Name], they should remain silent; if they do not consent, they should speak.
"The Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha has completed the formal act of *akartavyavandanā-karman* against the bhikṣu so-and-so.
The Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha has granted its consent, as indicated by their silence; thus do I now uphold this."

"If a bhikṣu has already been subjected by the Saṃgha to the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation), and the community of bhikṣuṇīs has likewise completed the *anavaśrāvaṇīya-karman* (act of non-prostration) against him, the bhikṣuṇīs shall not converse with him nor offer him prostrations;
yet, as soon as they see him, they must immediately rise from their seats, because he belongs to the higher order."

Regarding the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for admonishing a nun who follows [a suspended monk]: "Once the formal procedure has been performed, even if she does not offer salutations, if she continues to follow him, one must further perform the *utksepanīya-karman* (act of suspension) against her."
It should be performed in this manner:
"Venerable Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has acted contrary to the Dharma; the Saṃgha has performed the *sthāpanīya-karman* (act of suspension) against him."

This bhikṣuṇī [Name], knowing that the conduct of that person is contrary to the Dharma and knowing that he has incurred the *pratikṣepaṇīya-karman* (the act of suspension), nevertheless follows, associates with, and serves him, thereby causing that person not to comply with the instructions of the Saṃgha.

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha grant permission: the Saṃgha now prohibits this bhikṣuṇī from approaching and attending upon that bhikṣu, so-and-so.
"Thus it is announced.
"The formal ritual (karmavācanā) shall be concluded according to this announcement.
While she was living in the same room with her child, after the nun Guptā had given birth to the boy Kāśyapa, she no longer slept with him; the child then began to cry.
The bhikṣuṇīs reported the matter to the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"That bhikṣuṇī Guptā should request from the community of bhikṣuṇīs the formal ritual (karmavācanā) for staying in the same room as her child."

Having spread out the seats and struck the *gandī*, and having completed the formal announcement (*jñapti*), once the community of *bhikṣuṇīs* has assembled, they join their palms and speak these words:
"Listen, O Saṃgha of *bhikṣuṇīs*!"
I, the Bhikṣuṇī Gupta, have given birth to a son; I now request from the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha the formal ritual (karmavācanā) for sleeping in the same room as my child.
May the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha grant me, Gupta, the permission to sleep in the same room as my child.
"May those who are capable of compassion please show us mercy.
A second and third time, it should be said in this same manner.
Next, one bhikṣuṇī should first perform the formal announcement (jñapti), and then carry out the ritual procedure (karman):
"Venerable Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣuṇī Guptā has given birth to a son, Kāśyapa.
This Guptā now requests from the Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha permission to sleep in the same room as her child."

If it is the proper time for the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha and they grant their consent, may the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha permit that the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of allowing the Bhikṣuṇī Guptā to sleep together with her child now be performed.
The motion is thus made.
Next, perform the *karmavācanā*:
"Venerable Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣuṇī Guptā has given birth to a son, Kāśyapa.
This Guptā now requests from the saṃgha of bhikṣuṇīs permission to sleep in the same room as her child; the saṃgha of bhikṣuṇīs now grants Guptā permission to sleep in the same room as her child.
"Venerable sirs, if you approve of Guptā sleeping in the same room with her son, remain silent; if you do not approve, speak.
"The Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha has already granted permission for Guptā to sleep in the same room with her son."
"The Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha has granted its consent, as indicated by their silence; I now hold it to be so.
Once the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha has bestowed the *gup-tā* rule upon her, she should sleep in the same room with the child; do not harbor any doubt regarding this.
This means that while it is permitted for a child to stay overnight with her, once she has grown up, she must be barred according to the rule.

Regarding the formal motion (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) concerning a nun’s correspondence with secular relatives: "If a nun encounters a time of famine and scarcity, when people are filled with distress and alms-food is difficult to obtain, even to the point that her kinsmen say:
'I cannot provide food for many; if you come alone, I shall provide for you.'"
"In this case, she should request from the community of bhikṣuṇīs the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for visiting her lay relatives.
She should request it in this manner:
having prepared the seats and struck the *gaṇḍī*, once the announcement has been completed and the community of bhikṣuṇīs has assembled, she should join her palms and speak as follows:"
"Venerable Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, listen!
I, so-and-so, have encountered a time of famine, and people are filled with suffering and distress such that alms-food is difficult to obtain.

I, so-and-so, now request from the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of visiting and returning to my lay relatives. May the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha grant me, so-and-so, the formal act of visiting and returning to my lay relatives."
"May those who are capable of compassion show us mercy.
A second and third time, it should be spoken in this same manner.
Next, one bhikṣuṇī should first perform the formal announcement (jñapti), and then carry out the ritual act (karman):
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣuṇī, so-and-so, has encountered a time of famine; people harbor distress, and it is difficult to obtain almsfood.
This so-and-so now requests from the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of being permitted to visit her lay relatives."

If it is the proper time for the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha and they grant their consent, may the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha permit that the Bhikṣuṇī [Name] now perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of social interaction with her lay relatives.
The motion is thus made.

Regarding the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) for subduing [an offender]: at that time, there were several eminent and noble bhikṣus who repeatedly committed offenses against the various rules of training (*śaikṣa-dharma*). The other bhikṣus granted them the *parivāsa* (probation), the *mūla-parivāsa* (probation from the beginning), and even the re-imposition of the *mūla* and the *mānāpya* (penance); yet they committed the offenses once again.

The preliminary procedures (*pūrvaprayoga*) should be understood as described above. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This eminent and excellent bhikṣu repeatedly committed offenses against the various rules of training (*śaikṣadharma*). Although the bhikṣus performed for him the *parivāsa* penance and even the *mānatva* probation, he committed them again.

Just as one performs the *paryuṣaṇā* (observance), if one does not act in accordance with it, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma (*dharmātikrama*).

Having thus performed the rite of subjugation (*nigraha*), one should manifest extreme reverence and diligence, never again giving rise to contempt toward the Saṃgha, and even go before the assembly to request the rite of withdrawal (*saṃvaraṇa*), declaring:
"I, [Name], have committed numerous offenses; I shall cease them forever."

Having explained the causes and conditions at length, up until the point where the *saṃvaraṇa-karman* (act of reconciliation) should be performed, one should understand that it follows the procedure for the *bhaya-karman* (act of intimidation). However, regarding the differences, one should say:
"I, [Name], shall forever cease from committing these various offenses."
"The rest may be understood by analogy.

At the time of the formal motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) for their expulsion, the Venerable Aśvajit and Punarvasu were residing at the monastery on Mount Kiṭā, where they committed acts that defiled the householders and were evil deeds, contrary to the Dharma of a śramaṇa. Or...
He instructs others to act as follows: to sit on the same bed with various women; to eat from the same dish; to drink wine from the same cup;
to personally gather flowers or instruct others to gather them; to personally tie flowers together or instruct others to do so;
to place flowers in their topknots or fashion them into pearl crowns; to apply yellow pigment above the eyebrows as decorative dots; and to dance personally or instruct others to do so.
They dance, sing themselves, and teach others to sing; they beat drums themselves and teach others to beat drums;
they hurriedly fasten their robes and leap or stamp about; they whirl on wooden poles, catch them in mid-air, and cause them to remain steady;
at times they rotate their arms, or perform the leaping of fish; or they halt mid-stride in steep mud or flowing torrents; or they imitate the neighing of horses.
Some bellowed like oxen, some trumpeted like elephants, some cried out like peacocks;
some beat water-drums, some tossed water as if it were spears, some drummed on their mouths, and some blew mouth-conches with the sound of peacocks or the warbling of yellow orioles.
They engaged extensively in such conduct unbecoming of śramaṇas, and consequently, beneath Mount Kiṭa...

The assembly of brahmins all felt a sense of disdain and lost their faith; they began to criticize and disparage the bhikṣus, even to the point that they would no longer give alms to them when they went begging for food.
Ānanda reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"O Bhikṣus! If you wish to go to that mountain, you should stop at one place along the way and appoint a bhikṣu endowed with the five virtues to assemble the community as is customary."
One should first ask:
"You, Bhikṣu [Name], are you able to interrogate Aśvajit and others on Mount Kiṭāgiri regarding their conduct in household affairs?"
He replied, "I can. Then,
as is customary,

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, is capable of going to Mount Kiṭā to interrogate the bhikṣus Aśvajit and Punarvasu regarding their conduct in defiling household affairs.

Drinking wine from the same goblet as women, eating from the same platter, gathering flowers to weave garlands, and engaging in restless dancing and singing—they thus perform such unbecoming conduct for a śramaṇa, causing all their lay associates to lose their faith.

The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

Having struck the *ghanṭī* as a preliminary rite, one bhikṣu should perform the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*) in this manner:

This bhikṣu, being devoid of the [proper] signs, has conceived a wrong view and speaks thus:

The Blessed One does not speak thus; rather, through immeasurable skillful means, the Blessed One has declared that sexual misconduct is an obstructive dharma.

"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha permit that the Saṃgha now perform the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of suspension) against Aniruddha for not relinquishing his evil view.

"The formal act (karmavācanā) shall be completed according to the motion.
At that time, after the bhikṣus had performed the formal act of "not relinquishing evil views" against that Vimala, Vimala remained stubbornly attached to his views and would not relinquish them.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"When the third [motion] is completed, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
Having been thus expelled for holding wrong views, the novice (śrāmaṇera) requested the World-Honored One through the full formal procedure (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) with the venerable Upāli:
"Venerable Sir!..."

At that time, these bhikṣus felt remorse; they fully confessed and purified the offenses they had committed, gave rise to a courageous mind to sever all afflictions and delusions, and realized the sublime fruit.
Those two novices then gave rise to a wrong view and said to the bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs!
Those bhikṣus previously engaged in unrighteous acts with us; how is it that they have now obtained such superior fruits?"
"I have heard the Buddha say that practicing sexual desire is an obstructive dharma, yet when one practices it, it is not an obstruction.
The bhikṣus did not know what to think.

Having performed the preliminary rites, place those two persons in a location where they can see but cannot hear, and have one bhikṣu perform the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*) as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Those two novices, Kṣudrapāla and Dīrgha, having grown up, gave rise to evil views and spoke as follows:
"I have heard the Buddha say that sexual desire is an obstructive dharma, yet when one practices it, it is not an obstruction."

The bhikṣus had already performed the formal admonition through the individual counsel and even up to the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) regarding those two śrāmaṇeras.
Yet, those two remained obstinate in their evil views and refused to relinquish them, saying:

The bhikṣus said to those two śrāmaṇeras:
"From this day forward, you must not say, 'The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is my teacher';
nor should you follow other venerable elders or fellow practitioners of the holy life."
"Unlike other śrāmaṇeras, who are permitted to stay overnight with a mahābhikṣu for two nights, you have no such privilege.
You foolish man! Depart at once!"

"If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and if the Saṃgha consents, let the Saṃgha authorize that the Saṃgha now perform the formal act of *pravāsanīya-karman*—expulsion for not relinquishing evil views—against those two śrāmaṇeras."
"Thus it is announced.
"The formal ritual (karmavācanā) shall be completed according to this announcement.
At that time, after the bhikṣus had performed the ritual of banishment against those two novices, they did not know what to do.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Once those two śrāmaṇeras have received the formal act (karmavācanā), the bhikṣus should not dwell or sleep together with them; whoever violates this incurs an offense."
"As prescribed by the Vinaya, you should understand this.

When the bhikṣus of Vaiśālī and the group of bhikṣus from Koṭi-vambaka had regained their original state of mind following the *jñapti-caturtha* (fourth-motion) formal act, they went to the place where the World-Honored One was and spoke these words:
"Venerable Sir!..."
"I now wish to be reconciled. The Buddha said, "Sādhu."
Translated as "well-accomplished," this means being able to successfully accomplish that task.
The old version says: "Excellent, O bhikṣus!

It would be difficult indeed to take a hair-tip, divide it into a hundred parts, or even into ten billion parts, and then cause them to recombine exactly as they were; yet to cause what has already been broken to be joined together again is even more difficult than that.
Therefore, I now authorize the bhikṣus that those who have been subject to the act of suspension (pravāsanīya-karman) should request to be readmitted.
They should request in this manner, as previously described, up until they speak these words:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

Because I, [Name], and others acted as the instigators of disputes, we have caused the Saṃgha to dwell in disharmony; we have caused disputes that had not yet arisen to arise, and we have caused those already arisen to increase. When others offered righteous admonition, we instead rejected and concealed it, or said: "I am guilty."
Some said, "There is no offense," while others said:
"Whether one should confess or not. Or he says: "I am an offender."

May the virtuous Saṃgha grant me this favor!
"Have compassion and accept me;
you who are capable of compassion, I pray that you will have pity on me.
He spoke thus a second and a third time.

This bhikṣu [Name] was the primary instigator of a dispute, thereby causing the Saṃgha to dwell in disharmony; he caused disputes that had not yet arisen to arise, and caused those already arisen to increase."
While he was offering sincere admonition, the other immediately rejected and concealed it,
sometimes saying, "I have committed an offense," or else saying:

"If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha permit that the Saṃgha now grant [this person] the lifting of the *sthāpanīyakarman*.

Next, the *karman* should be performed according to the motion, up until: 'I now maintain it thus.'"

The request should be made as follows:
the preliminary procedure should be understood according to what was stated above, up until he joins his palms and speaks thus:
“‘Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

I, [Name], having been subjected to the act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*), have repented my former transgressions and have already requested from the Saṃgha the lifting of that act of suspension; the Saṃgha has now granted me the lifting of the act of suspension.
I, [Name], now request from the Saṃgha to act as a reconciler; may the Saṃgha grant me, [Name], the resolution of suspension, and further, may we together perform the reconciliation.
"May those who are capable of compassion show us mercy.
This is said three times.
Next, one bhikṣu performs the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*).
“‘Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
