This [person], so-and-so, having been subjected to the act of suspension, has repented his former transgressions and requested from the Saṃgha the lifting of that act of suspension; the Saṃgha has now granted him the lifting of the act of suspension.
This [person], so-and-so, now requests from the Saṃgha that they act in harmony together.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and they grant permission, may the Saṃgha consent; the Saṃgha shall now perform the act of reconciliation with so-and-so. This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
The *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is performed according to the preliminary announcement (*jñapti*), up to the words: "I now maintain it thus.
When the Saṃgha has reached concord and performed the *poṣadha*, the Blessed One said:
"Now that the Saṃgha has reached concord with that bhikṣu, I shall now declare all the rules of conduct (*caryā-dharma*) that must be observed."
That bhikṣu should request a *poṣadha* of reconciliation from the Saṃgha; he should request it in this manner, speaking as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
With myself as the leader, the details are as previously explained.

I, [Name], having previously been subject to the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation), have already requested from the Saṃgha the lifting of that *pratisāraṇīya-karman*; the Saṃgha has now granted me, [Name], the lifting of the *pratisāraṇīya-karman*.
I, [Name], have already requested from the Saṃgha that we dwell together in harmony; the Saṃgha has already granted me [Name] the state of dwelling together in harmony.
I, [Name], now request from the Saṃgha that we perform the *poṣadha* in harmony; may the Saṃgha grant me the *poṣadha* in harmony.
"May those who are capable of compassion please show us mercy.
This was said a second and a third time.
Then, one bhikṣu first made the formal announcement (jñapti), after which the ritual action (karman) was performed:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This person, so-and-so, was previously subject to the act of suspension; he has now requested from the Saṃgha the lifting of that act of suspension.
This person, so-and-so, now requests from the Saṃgha the *poṣadha* of communal harmony."
"If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha permit that the Saṃgha now perform the *poṣadha* in harmony with [the name of] so-and-so.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Next, the *karman* (formal ritual act) is performed according to the motion, up until: "I now maintain it thus."
"If the Saṃgha has already performed the *poṣadha* together with [the absent monk], then even though it is not his own *poṣadha* day, he should perform the *poṣadha* together with the Saṃgha.

However, the community of bhikṣus should not perform the *poṣadha* on a day that is not their *poṣadha* day, except for the auspicious *poṣadha*—namely, the *poṣadha* during times of difficulty and the *poṣadha* performed in assembly, which is termed 'auspicious.'"
"One who performs the *poṣadha* for another who should not perform it incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu afflicted by the suffering of illness, yet no one attended to him; the community of bhikṣus did not know whom to send to look after his medical needs.
The Buddha said:
"If there is one who is ill, [the community] shall go from the senior monk of the saṃgha down to the junior ones.
At that time, the entire assembly went; the Buddha said:
"You should not go there all at once; you should take turns in attending to him.
Once you have reached the sick person's quarters, you should inquire after their strength and condition.
If the patient is too weak to speak, you should ask the caregiver about their condition."
"If anyone violates this, the attendant shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
If both the patient and the attendant are poor and lack medicine, the Buddha said:
"If the patient has a close disciple, a dependent disciple, or a preceptor, an instructor, or the like, one should seek the cost of the medicine from them and provide it together."
If there is absolutely nothing [to provide], one may take medicine and the funds for medicine from the communal storehouse to attend to the patient.
If one does not comply with this, both incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma; there is further extensive text on this matter as explained elsewhere.
The Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One: "Bhadanta,
as the Blessed One has said:"
"One should provide medical supplies for the sick. [The monks asked:
"We do not yet know what things are suitable for sustaining the sick?
The Buddha said:
"Except for those actions that constitute natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), all other things may be provided for use so as to relieve them from suffering.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu afflicted with dysentery. A young monk served as his attendant; when he arrived at the patient's side, he prostrated in salutation.
Next, an elder came, and the patient rose to pay his respects. Because of this exertion, the patient became utterly exhausted.
The Buddha said:
"One should not pay homage to a bhikṣu who is possessed by defilement, nor should a bhikṣu possessed by defilement pay homage to another.
When seeing such a person paying homage, one must not accept it; whoever violates this incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma."
“Venerable Sir! What is meant by ‘with defilement’ and ‘without defilement’?
The Buddha said:

"There are two kinds of defilement: first, the defilement of impurity; second, the defilement of food and drink. This refers to when the body is stained by excrement, filth, saliva, or spittle; when one has not yet washed after passing stool or urine; when the body is covered in grime and grease, or when the person is smeared with mud and dirt; or when, at the time of dawn, one has not yet chewed a tooth-stick, is currently chewing a tooth-stick, or is clearing away refuse—these are all termed the defilement of impurity."

Whether one is in the process of eating, has not yet rinsed the mouth, or even if one has rinsed and brushed but still has residual saliva remaining—down to the point of drinking water before having washed the mouth—all such instances are termed "contamination by food."

If one carries these two types of defilement without having purified one's person, and they come into contact with one another, both parties become impure. Considering this, how could one fail to understand that causing a vessel to prostrate [on one's behalf] incurs transgression?
"The details are as explained elsewhere.
At that time, when the six bhikṣus were eating, they relied on their own status and greatness to cause others to rise and make way for them. The Buddha said:
"One should not cause others to rise; even when receiving medicine or being invited to take salt, one should not rise."
If one causes another to do so, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma (*dharmātikrama*).

Furthermore, all bhikṣus must properly know the sequence of seniority by years since ordination as well as the order of seating; if one eats without following this sequence, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
"It is exactly as set forth in the Mahā-vinaya.
As the Blessed One said:
"There are three kinds of ultimate purification (*paramārtha-pariśuddhi*):"
First is the washing of the body;
second is the washing of speech;
third is the washing of the mind.
"Why, in this case, is it taught that one should wash away only the impurities that defile the body?
The Buddha said,
"It is because I wish to have the foul odors removed so that they may dwell in peace and comfort."

Furthermore, seeing those among the non-Buddhist sects who harbored pride regarding their ritual purity, [the Buddha] caused them to develop faith; desiring to lead them to give rise to a heart of profound reverence so that they might enter this Dharma, abandon error, and follow the correct path, he acted just as the Venerable Śāriputra did with the arrogant Brahmin—by employing the method of ritual purification to gather and transform him, ultimately causing that person to abide in the first fruit of the path.
Seeing this benefit, the Buddha said: "O Bhikṣus! You should wash yourselves clean according to the method of Śāriputra.

When the time comes for defecation, you should take a water jar and go toward the latrine. Once you have reached the room, place your robes to one side. Take fifteen lumps of earth and set them outside the latrine; alternatively, grind these lumps into powder, with each heap being about the size of half a peach. Place them upon bricks or on a wooden board near a flowing stream. The earth must be kept in a trough and prepared in advance at the latrine."

Furthermore, one must take three lumps of earth along with a cloth for wiping the body, and carrying the water flask, enter the latrine. The door must have a single leaf that can be bolted crosswise; once this has been done, or having wiped clean with a wooden stick or leaf, one should place the flask and the earth in their designated spots within the latrine, and then proceed to wash oneself clean.
Take three lumps of earth and wash them thoroughly with the left hand three times; then, holding the flask under the left armpit, push back the bolt with the right hand.
Return carrying it with the right hand, and squat down at the place where you washed your hands.

The elder places the empty water jar on his left leg and presses it with his elbow to take seven portions of earth; each one must be washed separately with the left hand, while for the remaining seven clusters, one should apply oneself with both hands to wash them together.
There remains one bundle used for washing the *kamaṇḍalu*; thereafter, he proceeds to the place for washing his feet.
Having washed his feet, he takes his robes and departs. Once he has reached the interior of his cell, he rinses his mouth with pure water.
The Buddha said:
"You bhikṣus, you must all perform the act of cleansing in this manner."
"If one acts otherwise, one incurs the offense of transgressing the Dharma.

Thus, the Buddha’s golden mouth clearly prescribed these matters of purity; yet some, harboring their own mundane intentions, have arbitrarily made alterations, employing bamboo tubes or wooden troughs, which fail to accord with refined propriety.
Although one may turn the mind toward purity and self-restraint, it is truly difficult to eradicate defilement.

This was because the regulations established by Śāriputra had not yet reached the eastern lands; this was likely due to the negligence of the translators rather than the fault of the practitioners. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus entered the latrines according to their seniority in the summer retreat, even while they were in the process of relieving themselves.
The Buddha said:
"In this place, one should not follow the order of seniority by summer retreat; whoever arrives first must enter first.
However, as for the places for washing hands and washing feet, these must indeed follow the order of seniority."
If one acts otherwise, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma (*dharmātikrama*).
Furthermore, one should not intentionally linger in the latrine area, as this also incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
The details are fully explained in the fifth fascicle of the *Vinayakṣudrakavastu*, in the *Śaucavidhi-sūtra*.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who silently entered a latrine; one already inside had his body exposed, which caused him to feel shame. The Buddha said:
"When wishing to enter a latrine, one should snap one's fingers, cough, or make a sound by treading on the ground."
"If one enters silently, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma; because there are no door-panels, it is necessary to install them.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who defecated and urinated beneath flowering and fruit trees. The Buddha said:
"One must not defecate or urinate beneath flowering or fruit trees."
"Should anyone violate this, they shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
However, there is no fault if one is beneath a thorn bush.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu, having consumed ghee and being overcome by thirst, went to consult a physician.

The physician instructed him to eat *āmalaka* fruits—which are the *yugan* (余甘) found in the region south of the Ling Mountains. When first eaten, they are somewhat bitter and astringent; however, once one drinks water following their consumption, a delicious flavor arises. Because this effect occurs immediately upon eating them, they are named "Remaining Sweetness" (*yugan*).
The old term "āmalaka fruit" is an error.
The Buddha said:
"There are five kinds of fruits:"
1. Harītakī (formerly transcribed as *hālílè*, which is erroneous);
2. Vibhītaka (formerly transcribed as *bǐxīlè*, which is erroneous); 3. Āmalaka;
Fourth, *marica* is black pepper; fifth, *pippalī* is *kōjō* (vinegar made from fermented soybeans), formerly referred to as a type of *pippalī*.
These five fruits may be eaten at will, whether at the proper time or not, and whether one is ill or healthy.
As the Blessed One said:
"In border regions, leather bedding is permitted.
However, in the Middle Country, Upānanda immediately prohibited it, yet he allowed it once again within lay dwellings.
The Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One:
"Bhadanta, regarding the regulations concerning leather, you have permitted sitting but not lying down; to what extent, then, should one sit?"
The Buddha said, "As far as the seat where one sits. [The questioner asked:
"If lying down is not permitted, up to what point should one lie?"
"It refers to a place where one might sleep.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus used lion skins to make sandals; they put them on and went to King Prasenajit’s camp, which caused the herd of great elephants to become terrified.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "O Bhikṣus!
You must not use the skins of superior elephants, superior horses, lions, tigers, leopards, and the like to make leather sandals; to do so constitutes an offense against the Dharma."
These types of laces should also not be used.
In making leather footwear, one should not have lacing at the front or back, nor should they be made as long boots or short boots.
One who wears such footwear commits an offense of transgression against the Dharma.

"Bhadanta, as the Blessed One has said:..."
"Regarding the statement, 'One does not make leather sandals from the hide of a superior elephant,' if there were other hides,
such as those of dull-witted elephants or horses, would it be appropriate to make sandals from them?
The Buddha said:
"It is not fitting.
"What is the reason for this? "It is because he possesses the power of his tusks."
“Venerable Sir! If the hide of a superior horse is not used for shoes, could one make shoes by combining the hides of other inferior horses?
The Buddha said:
"It is not appropriate.
"What is the reason for this? "Because he possesses valor and strength."
“Venerable Sir! If one does not make shoes from lion skin, tiger skin, or leopard skin, would it be permissible to make shoes from other such skins as these?”
The Buddha said, "It is not permitted; these also possess the strength of claws and fangs.
[The questioner asked: "May the hides of these various animals be used to make footwear?"
The Buddha said, "It is not appropriate;
in the Middle Kingdom there were originally no boots or shoes, and for this reason we have only the name 'xie' (shoes).
Thus, after the World-Honored One had established the training rule, a hunter who had conceived feelings of reverence and faith presented a bear skin as an offering to the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣu did not accept it and immediately informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"It is rare to find a hunter who is both respectful, faithful, and honest; you should accept it. Place it at the head of your bed; bear skin is powerful and can make the eyes clear."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu whose eyesight had lost its strength; he went to consult a physician, who replied, "You may use bear skin to make footwear."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“As the physician has stated, one should use bear skin for footwear.
If it is too thick and cannot be obtained, even a single layer may be used; place it upon another hide with the fur facing toward the body, and wear it as you please.”
“Venerable Sir! Just as elephant and horse hides are impure, are their flesh, sinews, tusks, and bones also impure?
The Buddha said:
"All of these are impure.
As the Blessed One said:
"One should cause a water filter to be kept."
Regarding the question, "How many kinds of strainers (*cīvaraka*) are there that a bhikṣu does not know?
the Buddha said: "There are five kinds of strainers: [1] the *daśāpatta*, [2] the *daśāpuṭa*, [3] the *daśāvastra*, [4] the *daśāpuṭavastra*, and [5] the *daśāvastrapuṭa*."
First, as for the *fangluo* (square filter): if it is for regular use, one requires three feet, two feet, or one foot of silk.
For use by the Saṃgha, it may be made from two pieces of cloth, according to the size required at the time.
Those who make the nets must use silk that is fine and dense; only when insects cannot pass through is it fit for use.
If the material is coarse or thin, it is fundamentally unserviceable.
There are those who use inferior silk, loose gauze, or ramie cloth, who originally have no intention of protecting the insects.
The second is the *dharmakalaśa* (dharma-flask) and the *yīnyáng-bíng* (yin-yang flask);

the third is the *kamaṇḍalu*, which should have its mouth tied with silk and its neck with a fine cord; when it is submerged in water, pull it until half of the mouth emerges, for if it is completely submerged, the water will not enter.

When drawing water after waiting for it to fill, one must still inspect for insects. It is not only the *kuṇḍikā* (water jar); rather, for any vessel with a wide mouth—be it a bottle or a jar, regardless of size—one should cover the opening with silk and tie it securely with a thin cord. Taking water at any time in this manner is extremely convenient and eliminates the need for a separate strainer; this is of profound importance.

Fourth, regarding the style of the *catur-kośa* (four-fold strainer), this did not originally exist in the land of China (*Dongxia*). As described elsewhere, it is simply a small, round cloth strainer; although its function is largely the same, it is not the original form. Fifth, as for the "corner-strainer" (*vastra-koṇa*), take a piece of fine silk about one span square.
It may be tied to the mouth of a jar for drawing water for use, or it must be used when placed inside a bowl to filter water; it is not merely a corner of one's *kāṣāya*.
This [filter] is both dense and greasy; how could it possibly be fit for straining water?
It is used only because those who have long been lost in their direction require someone to point out the way.
Nevertheless, all such filters are currently in use in the West.
The Great Master, out of compassion, even prohibited the eating of meat to save all living beings; how could one who kills with great cruelty ever attain Buddhahood?
Even if you must briefly leave the monastery, you may take a net, along with a fine cord and a jar for releasing captive creatures.
If one does not carry [the scriptures], it is not only that one disparages the Buddha's teaching, but how else could one instruct and train one's disciples?
The practitioner should reflect on this and especially strive to preserve and protect them for the benefit of both self and others.
The Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One: "Bhadanta,
is it permissible to go toward another village, city, or monastery beyond five krośas without a water filter?"
The Buddha said:
"It is not permitted.
If you go there, provided that your perception of whether it is water or a filter is complete, you may go even if [the filter] is lacking."
“Venerable Sir! Is it possible to cross rivers and streams without a water-strainer?
The Buddha said:
"No. You may use it as you see fit at any time.
"Venerable sir!"
"When crossing rivers or mountain torrents, after having observed them once, how many times must one apply mindfulness? "Upāli!
If one goes with the current, it takes one *krośa*."
If another river comes, one must further observe it as it flows upstream;
observing it accordingly, one drinks the water that does not flow, and observing it accordingly, one uses it.
“Venerable Sir! May water that has already been filtered be drunk without being inspected?
The Buddha said:
"One must examine it before it may be drunk. "Venerable Sir,
can water that has not been strained be drunk if one examines it?"
The Buddha said,
"If one observes that there are no insects, there is no offense in drinking or using the water.
Then the Venerable Āniruddha, observing the water with his divine eye, saw clearly within it immeasurable sentient beings.
The World-Honored One said:

"One should not examine water with the divine eye. However, there are five kinds of pure water that are fit for drinking: [1] water from a stream, [2] water from a pond, [3] water from a well, [4] water from a rain cloud, and [5] water from a spring."
First, purity by an individual;
second, purity by the Saṃgha;
third, purity by means of a water-strainer.
Fourth, purity of the well;
fifth, purity of the spring.
Furthermore, there is the purity of the light-sign.
Regarding "purity by an individual," it means knowing that the person is trustworthy and will certainly not give water containing insects to others.
Regarding "purity by the Saṃgha," it means that the official in charge maintains a conscientious attitude and exercises supervision.
Regarding "purified by a filter," this refers to cloth or silk that is so fine and dense that insects have never passed through it.

Regarding "purified by a well or spring," if one has never recalled or seen insects in this well or spring, there is no fault in drinking from it even without inspecting it at the time of consumption.

Regarding what is called "purity by the appearance of light": whether water has been filtered or not, or if one harbors doubts, if one observes it during the day and then drinks it at night, there is no fault whatsoever as long as it remains until the appearance of light.
At that time, the bhikṣus became weary from observing the water for too long. The Buddha said:
"One may observe the water for as long as it takes six ox-carts to pass by, or one may examine it with careful scrutiny from the moment its clarity is perceived."
If a bhikṣu drinks water containing living beings while perceiving it as such, he commits a pāyattika offense.
If he drinks water containing living beings while suspecting it to be so, he likewise commits a pāyattika offense.
If there are no insects but one perceives them as such, one incurs a *duṣkṛta*.
If one suspects that there are insects when there are none, one incurs a *duṣkṛta*.

If there are insects but one perceives them as being non-existent, there is no offense; this is the explanation according to the Sarvāstivāda school. However, in cases of mere doubt, it likewise incurs the primary offense (*mūlāpatti*).

The origin of the tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*) arose by the side of the river Varuṇā. Because of this, the Blessed One, for the sake of the community of bhikṣus, ordained that they should chew tooth-sticks.
At that time, the bhikṣus began to chew them in exposed places and on paths where people were passing to and fro. The Buddha said:
"There are three matters that should be done in private."
First, defecation; second, urination;
third, chewing the tooth-stick.
"None of these should be kept in a public place.
At that time, the group of six monks chewed long tooth-sticks.
The Buddha said, "There are three kinds of tooth-sticks:"
That is to say: long, medium, and short.
The long is twelve finger-widths; the short is eight finger-widths.
That which is between these two is called medium.
At that time, after the bhikṣus had finished chewing their tooth-sticks, they did not know how to scrape their tongues; consequently, they still suffered from bad breath.
The Buddha said, "One must scrape the tongue. For this reason, I permit the making of a tongue-scraper, which may be made of brass, copper, or iron.
If one has no [tooth-stick], one should break it into two pieces and rub them against each other to remove the sharp edges; then, bending it, one may scrape the tongue.
Whenever discarding a tooth-stick or a tongue-scraper, one must wash it with water and make a sound by coughing or snapping the fingers to alert others.
One may discard it only in a secluded and unclean place.
If there is little water, one should wipe it away with dust and soil before discarding it.
To act otherwise incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.

Regarding the *Jñapti-caturtha-karman* for Contravening and Annoying the Community: At that time, the Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One, saying: "Bhadanta!..."
The Venerable Chanda had committed numerous offenses and did not confess them according to the Dharma. Desiring his benefit and for his peaceful dwelling, the bhikṣus said to him:
"Venerable one!..."
"Since you have committed an offense, you should confess and repent according to the Dharma.
Chanda replied, "You yourself have committed an offense; you should repent according to the Dharma."
Why is this? You all were born into various lineages and various families, yet because our World-Honored One has realized Great Enlightenment,
you have all come together to rely upon one another and have gone forth into homelessness.
"Having spoken these words, you have contravened and disturbed the communal teachings; how should the bhikṣus proceed?
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "O bhikṣus!..."
One should perform the *karmavācanā* to rebuke that Chanda;
if there are others of a similar sort, all cases should be handled according to this precedent.
Having performed the preliminary formalities (*pūrvakalpa*), one performs the *jñapti-karman*:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This bhikṣu Chanda has committed an offense himself, yet he does not confess it according to the Dharma.

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha grant permission; the Saṃgha shall now reprove the bhikṣu Chanda for his refusal to comply with the community's instruction.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Next, perform the *karmavācanā*:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu Chanda has committed an offense himself, yet he has not confessed it according to the Dharma."
When the community of bhikṣus, desiring to bring him benefit and for his peaceful dwelling, exhorted him in accordance with the Dharma, he obstinately rejected the instructions of the assembly.

"Venerable sirs, if you approve of the censure of the bhikṣu Chanda for his refusal to comply with the community's instruction, remain silent;
if you do not approve, speak. This was said a second and a third time.
“The Saṃgha has finished censuring the bhikṣu Chanda for his defiance of the community’s instruction.
Since the Saṃgha has granted its consent by remaining silent, I now hold it to be so.”
When the bhikṣus had finished performing the *karmavācanā* and censuring him, Chanda then thought to himself:
"Because of my own transgression, I have engaged in verbal exchange with those people, as it is said in a verse:
'All wise people Skillfully guard the four kinds of speech.'"
"Observe those birds of the mountain forests; though they can speak, they are bound within cages.
Having said this, he remained silent and spoke no further words.
Later, at another time, he committed an offense again, and the bhikṣus addressed him, saying:
"Venerable one!
Since you have committed an offense, you should confess it according to the Dharma.
He remained silent and continued to harass him through his silence.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do, so they informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said: "O bhikṣus!..."
Having performed the formal motion (*jñapti*) and the fourfold proclamation (*karma*), he rebuked that Chanda for his silent harassment.
Having completed the preliminary procedures, he made the formal motion as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu Chanda has committed an offense himself but does not confess it according to the Dharma.
Because the other bhikṣus wish for his benefit and for him to dwell in peace and happiness, they say to him:
"Venerable one!..."
"Since you have committed an offense, you should confess it according to the Dharma.
He remained silent, silently causing distress.
If the Saṃgha deems the time right and grants permission, may the Saṃgha authorize that the Saṃgha now reprimand the bhikṣu Chanda for silently causing distress.
"Thus it is announced.
"The formal ritual (karmavācanā) shall be established according to this announcement.
At that time, after the bhikṣus had performed the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) against that Chanda, he again committed offenses.
When the assembly of bhikṣus addressed him as before, that Chanda would either speak or remain silent to cause them disturbance and confusion.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"This Chanda has disobeyed and vexed the community's instructions; he incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If he disobeys an individual, he incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense."
Having turned his bowl upside down, the Venerable Upāli addressed the Blessed One with a formal motion (*jñapti*): "Bhadanta,
there is one named Subhadra of the Licchavis who, having been deceived and deluded by evil associates, has slandered Sthūlanandika as having committed a *pārājika* offense."

"May those who are capable of compassion please take pity on us.

"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
That Subhadra, having been deceived and deluded by evil associates, has slandered Sthiramati with a groundless *pārājika* offense."
For this reason, the Saṃgha performed the *pātra-nyubja* (turning-over-of-the-bowl) karmavācanā against that Suvīra.

“O bhikṣus, once you have performed the *utkūla-pātra-karman* against that Suvīra, you may go to his house to receive food, and even preach the Dharma to him; in all such cases, there is no offense.”
Regarding the formal procedure for admonishing harsh speech, the Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One: "Bhadanta,
suppose there is a bhikṣu who has committed many offenses, and a bhikṣu who is his friend, wishing to bring him benefit and cause him to dwell in peace and happiness, says to him:"
"Venerable one!
You must confess the offense you have committed according to the Dharma. He then replied:
"I myself shall know those who have regrets.
He further spoke these words:
"Venerable friends!"
Do not speak even a little to me, whether good or bad; nor shall I speak, whether good or bad, to you, venerable sirs.
Venerable sirs, please desist!
"Do not exhort me, and do not speak of me.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do, so they reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"Perform a formal admonition (praty-ājñā).
When they were being formally admonished, he stubbornly persisted and would not relinquish his position. The bhikṣus then informed the Buddha, who said:
"Perform an admonition by means of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations)."
The *khaṇḍika* (wooden gong) is struck as a preliminary rite: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu, [Name], has committed numerous offenses. When the bhikṣus, in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, offer formal admonition to him regarding the Sūtra of the Precepts spoken by the Buddha, he is of a malicious nature and does not accept their words of admonition, speaking as follows:"
“Venerable sirs! Do not speak to me even the slightest thing, whether good or bad.
I, too, shall not speak to you venerable sirs anything, whether good or bad.”
"Venerable sirs, please stop! Do not admonish me, do not speak against me.
Even when the bhikṣus attempted to exhort him separately, he remained obstinate and would not relinquish his position.
He says: "I declare this alone to be true; all else is false.

If the Saṃgha deems the time right and is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha grant its permission that the Saṃgha now admonish this bhikṣu [Name], who is of evil character and does not accept advice, by means of a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman).
The motion is thus made.
Next, the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is performed: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has committed numerous offenses. When the bhikṣus, in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, formally admonished him regarding the Sūtra of the Precepts as taught by the Buddha, he did not accept their counsel and spoke thus:
"Venerable sirs!..."
Do not speak even a little to me, whether good or bad; nor shall I speak, whether good or bad, to you, venerable sirs.
Venerable sirs, desist!
Do not admonish me, do not discuss me.

The bhikṣus then gave him a formal admonition individually; yet during this individual admonition, he remained obstinate and refused to relinquish his position, saying, "What I say is the truth; all else is false."
“The Saṃgha now proceeds to admonish this bhikṣu [Name], who is of evil character and does not accept counsel, by means of a formal motion followed by three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman).
If the venerable ones consent to admonishing this bhikṣu [Name] for being of evil character and not accepting counsel, let them remain silent; if they do not consent, let them speak.”
"The second and third times were spoken in the same manner.

Then the bhikṣus, having received the Buddha’s instruction, admonished him in accordance with the Dharma.
At that time, this bhikṣu remained as stubbornly insistent as previously described and would not relinquish his position.
The bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"This bhikṣu has committed an offense; it should be understood as explained above."
When the Saṃgha was performing the formal act of admonition against the bhikṣu Chanda—who had been rebuked for speaking of desire, hatred, delusion, and fear—he slandered them, saying:
"The Saṃgha possesses desire, hatred, and delusion."
“The assembly should perform the *karma* of censure and prohibition; it should be performed in this manner:
‘Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
When the Saṃgha was giving a formal admonition to this Bhikṣu Chanda in accordance with the Dharma, he spoke as follows:’”
“The Saṃgha possesses desire, hatred, and delusion.
The Saṃgha now rebukes and restrains Chanda:
“You should not speak such unrighteous words.”
"If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha permit that the Saṃgha now rebuke and stop the bhikṣu Chanda from speaking what is contrary to the Dharma.
This is the formal motion."
"The formal act (karmavācanā) is established according to the motion.
Then, the Venerable Upāli, who was acting as one of "the insane," requested the World-Honored One, saying:
"O Virtuous One!"

For example, the bhikṣu Skandaka suffered from the disease of insanity; its onset was irregular, and during the poṣadha ceremony as well as other formal acts (karmas), including the pravāraṇā, he would sometimes come and sometimes not.
At that time, the bhikṣus considered this to be a formal act of separate residence (*pārivāsika-karman*), but the procedure was not valid.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:
"O bhikṣus, you have performed the *unmattaka-karman* (the rite for one who is insane) for the bhikṣu Sīghra."

If there are others of a similar kind, they should all be dealt with according to this precedent; it should be granted in this manner.

“Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This bhikṣu, Sīghra, suffers from the disease of insanity;

its onset is irregular. Regarding the poṣadha and other formal acts (karmas), even up to the pravāraṇā, he sometimes comes and sometimes does not. This has caused the other bhikṣus to regard him as one who is living apart.”

"Thus it is announced.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This bhikṣu, Sīghra, suffers from the disease of insanity;

its onset is irregular. Regarding the poṣadha, other karmas, and even the pravāraṇā, he sometimes comes and sometimes does not. This has caused the other bhikṣus to regard him as one living apart [from the community]."
The Saṃgha now grants the *unmattaka-vidhi* (the rule for those who are insane) to Sīghra, so that his coming and going shall not be obstructed and he shall not hinder the performance of the Dharma.

if they do not consent, let them speak.

“The Saṃgha has already granted the *unmattaka-vidhi* (the rule for those who are insane) to Sīghra, such that his coming and going shall not be obstructed and he shall not hinder the performance of monastic affairs.

Once the Saṃgha has completed the ritual for the monk Sīghra regarding his insanity, it may perform the poṣadha, all other karmas, and even the pravāraṇā; do not harbor any doubts.

Furthermore, regarding the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for one who is not insane: there was once a bhikṣu named Sīghra who, being deranged, mentally disordered, and tormented by intense suffering, frequently violated the dharmas of a śramaṇa in his conduct. He committed impure acts; saliva and spittle flowed from his mouth, his eyes rolled back, and he appeared as if in deep sleep. Others, seeing him, falsely accused him, saying, "He deceives me."

"Venerable Sir!

The preliminary procedures should be understood as being in accordance with those above.

If the Saṃgha deems the time right and grants its consent, may the Saṃgha permit that the Saṃgha now grant the bhikṣu Hāsita the *vinaya* for seeking the essential nature of his offense.
"Thus it is announced.
Next, the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is to be performed according to the announcement, up until: "I now maintain it thus.
The Buddha said:
“O Bhikṣus! Having completed the formal procedure for that one who seeks the nature of his offense, I shall now declare the rules of conduct you must observe.

You must not grant others the going forth; you must not confer full ordination upon others; you must not act as a preceptor; you must not keep a śrāmaṇera. You should not be appointed to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs; if you were previously so appointed, you should relinquish that office. You must not censure other bhikṣus, nor cause them to be reminded of their broken precepts, wrong views, faulty deportment, or improper livelihood. You must not perform the *poṣadha*, nor the *pravāraṇā*; you must not perform a *jñapti*, a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, or even a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, nor recite the Prātimokṣa.”
If there is no one to recite the precepts, the precepts must still be recited.
This applies to the bhikṣu who is seeking out an offense.
Should anyone fail to act in accordance with what I have taught, they shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma.

When the Venerable Śrīgupta was being falsely slandered by the bhikṣuṇī Kalyāṇamitrā with matters that were untrue, he was subjected to interrogation by the bhikṣus regarding those matters; at the time of this interrogation, he became ashamed and abashed.
Then the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You bhikṣus should grant the *smṛtivinaya* (the verdict of mindfulness) to Sthiramati; if there are others of a similar kind, you should grant it to them in this same manner."
Having spread out the seats, [he] knelt down with palms joined and spoke as follows:

"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! I, Śrīgupta, have been slandered by the bhikṣuṇī Kalyāṇamitrā with an untrue matter. When the bhikṣus interrogated me regarding this matter, I became ashamed upon being questioned."
I, [name], now request from the Saṃgha the *vinaya-smṛti* (recollection of the discipline). May the venerable Saṃgha grant me the *vinaya-smṛti*.
May those who are compassionate do so out of compassion.
The second and third times should also be spoken in this manner.
Next, one bhikṣu should first make the formal announcement (jñapti), and then perform the formal act (karman):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
This Bahula has been slandered by the bhikṣuṇī Subhaddā with an untrue matter, and he feels ashamed.
This Bahula now requests from the Saṃgha the *smṛtivinaya* (the verdict of mindfulness).
"If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and they grant permission, may the Saṃgha allow that the Saṃgha now grants the *smṛtivinaya* to Śrīguptaputra.
Thus is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Next, perform the ritual act (*karman*):
“‘Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This Śrīgupta has been slandered by the bhikṣuṇī Kalyāṇamitrā with what is untrue, and he feels shame in his heart.
This Śrīgupta now requests from the Saṃgha the *vinaya-smṛti* (recollection of the discipline); the Saṃgha now grants the *vinaya-smṛti* to Śrīgupta.’”
If the Venerable Ones consent to granting the *smṛtivinaya* to Śrīgupta, let them remain silent; if they do not consent, let them speak.
This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third times were spoken in the same manner:
"The Saṃgha has already completed the *smṛtivinaya* for Śrīguptaputra.
The Saṃgha has granted its consent, as indicated by its silence; thus do I now uphold this."

"Having selected impartial persons, one performs the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation): 'If, when a dispute is being settled, the great assembly is unable to resolve it peacefully, one should select from among the members those who are virtuous and impartial—such as ten, twenty, or more elders named so-and-so—and have them settle that dispute.
This should be done as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!'"

At present, there are disputes within the Saṃgha that cannot be eliminated; the Saṃgha now wishes to select from among this assembly several upright and impartial senior monks (sthavira) to resolve these disputes, hoping for their swift cessation.

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and they grant permission, may the Saṃgha allow that the Saṃgha shall now select a certain number of senior monks from within this assembly to settle this dispute, hoping for its swift cessation.
"Thus it is announced.
The formal act (*karmavācanā*) is accomplished according to this announcement.

Once the formal act has been performed, if such persons still do not cease their behavior despite having been expelled, one may further select a particularly impartial and upright senior monk (*sthavira*) from among them; in this manner, the procedure should be carried out.
The selection by a formal motion with a second (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*): "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Now a dispute has arisen within the Saṃgha; although impartial and upright persons were selected from among the assembly in hopes of extinguishing it, it still does not cease."
The Saṃgha shall now further select from among these individuals those capable of settling disputes, so that they may go elsewhere to effect their settlement.

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, let the Saṃgha authorize this: the Saṃgha shall now further select from within the assembly those capable of settling disputes, so that they may go elsewhere to effect their settlement.
"Thus it is announced.
"The formal act (karmavācanā) shall be completed according to this announcement.

Regarding the entrustment to the disputants with a *jñapti-dvitīya* [motion]: "If the dispute still does not cease within this assembly, one should take these disputants before another assembly to resolve the matter in accordance with the Dharma."
It should be performed as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
A dispute has arisen within this assembly that has not been settled for a long time."
In order to bring it to an end, the Saṃgha now wishes to entrust this bhikṣu [Name], the quarrelsome one, to that community [Name] so that he may be eliminated.

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and they grant their consent, may the Saṃgha permit that the Saṃgha now entrust this quarrelsome bhikṣu, so-and-so, to that group, so-and-so, in order to have him eliminated.
"Thus it is announced.
The formal act (*karmavācanā*) is accomplished according to this announcement.

If a dispute has persisted for a long time and cannot be extinguished, those who have formed factions should cast voting tallies (*śalākā*) among the great assembly. This should be announced as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
A dispute has arisen within this assembly and has not been settled for a long time. Now, for the sake of settling it, the Saṃgha intends to employ the voting tally (dharma-śalākā)."
"If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha grant permission; let the Saṃgha now distribute the dharma-voting sticks.
The formal motion (*jñapti*) is thus made. The ritual procedure (*karman*) is completed according to this motion.

Even after the formal ritual of casting voting sticks (*śalākā*) has been performed, if the dispute still does not cease, the method for settling the dispute among those who have formed factions is as clarified in the *Mahāvibhaṅga*.
Regarding the formal authorization (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) for establishing a pure kitchen, the Buddha said: "You bhikṣus should establish a pure kitchen.
At that time, the bhikṣus did not know how to establish a pure kitchen.
Furthermore, how many kinds are there?
The Buddha said:
"In total, there are five kinds of pure kitchens."
What are the five? First, acting with the intention to do so;
second, maintaining a common consensus.
3. Like a cow lying down;
4. at a site that has been abandoned;
5. performing the ritual according to the Dharma.

All of these are generally bound by the common rules, though they may also be separately bound on one side. Regarding the statement "one who generates the intention acts": this refers to a monk who is a builder, or perhaps a layperson, who at the time of first laying the foundation stones for a dwelling generates such a thought:
"Now, at this residence, I shall construct a pure kitchen for the Saṃgha."

Regarding the phrase "to hold [the agreement] together": it is like a bhikṣu supervising construction who, when first laying the foundation stone and about to begin the work, addresses the co-resident bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"Venerable sirs, you should know that at this dwelling place, we shall prepare a pure kitchen for the Saṃgha.
As for the expression "like a cow lying down," it means that the doors of the rooms have no fixed alignment and are situated in a state of disorder.

Regarding the phrase "abandoned places," this refers to empty and deserted locations; among these two, the latter is more commonly seen in practice. As for the other three dharmas, they are constantly operative in their respective locations—whether summarizing the entire monastery complex or specifically designating a single area—neither interpretation presents any obstacle.
For instance, Nālandā Monastery was generally designated as a kitchen.

Regarding the question of whether there were localized designations in the north, this was according to the intentions of those who preferred such arrangements; all were permitted to do so, as detailed elsewhere.

Regarding the phrase "binding by the assembly," this refers to the formal procedure (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) performed with the collective consent of the great assembly. One should thus establish the location for the binding; it must be a place free from obstacles or difficulties, extending throughout the interior of the boundary as well as a fathom (*vyāma*) of its exterior influence, to be used as a pure kitchen (*kalpiya-śālā*).
When the Saṃgha has given its collective consent, one should prepare the seats at this very spot, strike the *gaṇḍī*, and have a single Bhikṣu perform the *karmavācanā*:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
Now that the construction and repair of this dwelling place are fully completed, I shall demarcate within its entire boundary and extending one fathom beyond it as the external sphere a pure kitchen.

If the Saṃgha deems the time right and grants permission, may the Saṃgha allow it; the Saṃgha shall now, within this dwelling place where the construction is complete, demarcate the entire boundary and extend it one fathom beyond as the external sphere, establishing it as a pure kitchen.
"Thus it is announced. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Now that the construction of this dwelling place is complete, we shall demarcate within its entire boundary, as well as an area of one fathom extending beyond it, to establish a pure kitchen."
The Saṃgha has now completed the construction and repair of this dwelling place; it shall establish a pure kitchen within its entire boundary and extending one *vyāma* beyond the outer limit.
If the venerable ones consent to establishing a pure kitchen within this dwelling place, throughout its entire boundary and extending one *vyāma* beyond the outer limit, let them remain silent;
if you do not consent, please speak.
"The Saṃgha has completed the construction and maintenance of this dwelling place; within its entire boundary, including the surrounding area of one fathom, it has established a pure kitchen."
"The Saṃgha has granted its consent; by reason of their silence, I now hold it thus.
"If the Saṃgha has collectively established a pure kitchen, then at this residence two kinds of benefit and happiness are obtained:
first, storing [food] outside the boundary while cooking inside the boundary."
Second, there is no fault in storing [food] within the boundary and cooking it outside the boundary.
When first constructing a monastery, at the time of laying the foundation lines, one should place bricks or stones at the four corners of the monastery to establish fixed points.
At that time, if one has the capacity, one should perform the *karmavācanā* extensively; or at times, the great assembly may say:
"This monastery precinct, together with its external boundary, shall be established as a pure kitchen; we now maintain it as such."
"A second and third time he spoke thus, and it was thereby rendered pure.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Siṃha who wished to eat granulated sugar (śarkarā).

The Buddha said, "Whether it be the proper time or not the proper time, whether one is ill or not, you may eat it as you please. However, in the Western Regions, when granulated sugar is made, rice husks are always added; this is like adding milk and oil when making rock honey (phāṇita)."
The Buddha permitted the consumption of food outside of the prescribed hours in order to prevent coarse physical manifestations and to provide sustenance for the body on the path.
In the various islands of the Southern Sea, people boil tree sap into wine and then form it into sugar balls; these are eaten entirely at improper times, which accords with this principle.
In the eastern lands, molasses and sugar may be consumed even if it is not the proper time for eating.
Why is this? The sugarcane itself is a medicine for the proper time, whereas its juice is for the improper time.
Although rice and malted wine are permitted during the day, why should honey cakes be forbidden after noon?

While a detailed examination reveals this to be logically sound, in practice people act according to their own inclinations; thick, turbid fragrant decoctions certainly do not fall within the permitted limits, while honey-boiled yams are definitively subject to the prohibitions.
As the Blessed One said:
"O bhikṣus, you should wear robes made of cut and sewn cloth.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu obtained a heavy, thick woolen blanket; he then took his knife and needle and went to the daytime dwelling place intending to cut it into pieces.
The Blessed One, having arrived at that place, asked him:
"What work are you doing?
The bhikṣu explained the circumstances to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“O Bhikṣus! There are five kinds of robes that should not be cut into patches:
first, those of the *kūṭāgāra* (high-pleated) woolen rug variety;”
2. A thick cloak woven from wool; 3. A coarse and heavy padded robe; 4.
A sparse cloth with "sparrow-eye" patterns; the people of the Western Regions do not wear robes made of patched rags.
Fifth, it refers to cases where the material is so small that even after cutting, it is insufficient; for these five types of items, I now permit the bhikṣus to wear them as patches.

Among these five, excluding the fifth, if one substitutes a thick mat for the fifth, then all five would likewise be beyond cutting. As for those who claim that bedding may serve as the three robes (tricīvara), though they call this "deep reflection," it is truly nothing more than a mere conjecture.
The Vinaya states:
"Bedding refers to sleeping mats; how could these be cut and pieced?
They should be used as the three robes, but it is not permissible to cut or patch them."
This passage is explicit; fearing that some may still harbor prior misconceptions, I have briefly provided these annotations.
As the Blessed One said:
"O bhikṣus, you should not make use of the bedding and furniture of the Saṃgha without having placed a protective layer beneath them."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus used items such as those that were greasy, thin, or tattered as under-linings for the monastic bedding.
Then, during the first part of the day, the World-Honored One took up his robe and bowl and entered Vaiśālī to beg for food, with the Venerable Ānanda serving as his attendant.
The World-Honored One then saw a man whose entire back was black, and he addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Do you see this man's black back? Ānanda replied:
"I see it," the Buddha said. "In the past,
during the authentic teaching of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, this person went forth as a monk and used whatever poor-quality materials were at hand as a lining for the monastic bedding."
Due to the retribution for his past black karma, he fell into hell; furthermore, for five hundred lifetimes, he constantly manifested a black back.
Because of this fault, a bhikṣu should not use coarse, thin, torn, or greasy materials as an underlay for the Saṃgha’s bedding.
"If a material is thick, it should be used as a single layer; if it is inherently thin, two layers must be used.
If one does not do so, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who made a *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) from various colored materials and kept the loose threads attached.
At that time, the brahmins and the lay followers began to mock him.
The Buddha said:

Regarding bedding and mats, one should make them double-layered and dye them to change their color (*kāṣāya*). A very fine, deep blue is not permitted by the Vinaya texts; rather, they should be dyed with colors that easily soil according to the circumstances, as this is what the rules allow. Regarding "mud" (*mṛttikā*)—as explained in the *Guanglü* (Extensive Vinaya)—this refers to red earth or red stone, or simply mud itself; however, pure black mud or black dye is not permitted, for these are the garments of non-Buddhists. Alternatively, it may refer to the *gandha* color (Sanskrit: *kāṣāya*), translated as "red. In the third section [of the Vinaya], it must be cut and sewn into patches, with borders applied to all four sides. Bedding was originally permitted for use as a substitute lining or matting, fearing that the body might become soiled; therefore, its length exceeds the height of the person and its width is like that of a small mat. The specific measurements in cubits are detailed in the *Guangwen* (Extensive Text).
My original intention was not concerned with prostration; this has not been explained in detail, as it is fully contained in other texts.
As the World-Honored One said, there are eight kinds of benefits. What are these eight?
1. Benefits obtained from the realm;
2. Benefits obtained from established regulations;
3. Benefits obtained from reliance.
Fourth, the gains obtained during the rainy season retreat;
fifth, the gains obtained by the Saṃgha;
sixth, the gains obtained by the bhikṣus.
7. Benefits obtained from those facing one;
8. Benefits obtained from a fixed location.

Regarding "benefits obtained from a realm" (*dhātu-labdha-lābha*): this refers to having a fixed jurisdiction within a single realm, or within two realms, or within many realms. According to these distinct locations, whatever sustenance is obtained is shared among the resident monks according to their respective realm divisions.

Regarding what is called "the benefit obtained through establishing a regulation," it refers to when various bhikṣus—whether belonging to the same faction or not—collectively establish a formal agreement before entering the rains retreat, stipulating: "Within this certain village, street, or thoroughfare, such-and-such a household belongs to me, and such-and-such a house belongs to you."
If one receives an object when it is obtained, one should do so in accordance with the regulations, as detailed in the *Mahāvibhaṅga*.
The term "those who follow the faction" refers to those who are companions and followers of Devadatta.
Those who speak of not following a faction are the disciples of the Buddha.
This is because, according to their place of residence, one causes things to be judged according to that location.
Since the "middle" is neither of the two locations, it is therefore dispatched that the two assemblies share [the property] equally.

Nowadays, throughout the Western regions, there are groups of those from the Devadatta lineage who have left the household life; their ritual protocols are for the most part identical to the Buddha-dharma, and even regarding the five paths of saṃsāra, rebirth in heaven, and liberation, as well as the Tripiṭaka they study, there is great commonality.

He did not reside in a great monastery, but lived among the villages and hamlets, sustaining himself by begging for alms. He practiced pure conduct extensively, using a gourd as his bowl and wearing only two pieces of cloth that were the color of mulberry bark. He abstained from milk and curd, and frequently attended the Nālandā Monastery to study various scriptures.
He once questioned him, saying:
"Your methods and style are mostly similar to those of the Great Master; yet where you deviate into heterodoxy, you again resemble Devadatta. Are you not, then, of Devadatta’s lineage?"
He then replied: "The one from whom I am descended is truly not Devadatta.
This was merely a refusal and denial out of fear that others might despise him, refusing to acknowledge his subordination!

Although these practices largely resemble the Buddha-dharma, when their observances are gathered together, the holy regulations divide into separate paths; each follows its own practice and presents its offerings individually.

How much more so for the various other non-Buddhists who speculate on annihilationism or eternalism, falsely cling to spontaneity, vainly claim to have attained the One, and sit intermingled during meal times—customs that lack any sense of distinction.

Those who follow old precedents take this as a universal standard and infect one another, so that the Jing and Wei rivers flow together in the same wave. Noble guests must examine such corruption; it is most appropriate that those of exceptional conduct sit separately on their own mats.

Regarding "benefits obtained through dependence," this refers to obtaining benefits by depending on men, women, or paṇḍakas while observing the rains retreat; those who obtain benefits based on this are so described.
Regarding "benefits obtained during the rains retreat," this refers to the material gains acquired during this summer retreat, which are to be distributed according to the donor's instructions.

Regarding the gains obtained by the Saṃgha, this refers to those that are determinate and without specific allocation; that is, when a donor brings forth an object specifically intended as a gift for the Saṃgha, no distinction is made therein, such as:
"This is for those who have completed the summer retreat," or "This is for those currently present. In such cases, one should inquire of the donor regarding the object.
The "benefit obtained by a bhikṣu" refers to that which is determined through a formal allotment; whoever resides in this particular room or courtyard shall receive its benefit.
"Benefit obtained face-to-face" refers to the material goods acquired directly from those present before one's eyes.

Regarding the sites where benefits were obtained through fixed locations: these refer to the eight places where the Great Master conducted his teachings throughout his lifetime; these are collectively known as the Eight Great Caityas.
First is the Place of the Buddha’s Birth, located in the Lumbinī Grove at the city of Kapilavastu.
Second, the place of attaining Buddhahood: at the Bodhi tree, upon the Vajrāsana, in the Dharmāraṇya of Magadha.
Third, the place of turning the Wheel of Dharma: at the Deer Park in Ṛṣipatana, near Vārāṇasī.
4. The place of parinirvāṇa was between the twin śāla trees at Kuśinagara.
5. [The place of the first turning of the wheel] was within the Bamboo Grove on Vulture Peak Mountain at Rājagṛha.
Sixth, he was in the High Hall by the side of the Monkey Pond in Vaiśālī.
Seventh, he was in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, at Śrāvastī.
8. The place where he descended from heaven was the village of Pāṭaligāma.
Of these, the first four places are called fixed locations, while the latter four are called unfixed locations.
If there is a gift intended for a specific place of birth, that object should be offered only at that place of birth and must not be transferred elsewhere.

If one lacks the capacity to send it, an offering may be made at any one of the three [other] locations; the remaining three places should be understood by analogy with this. The other four *caityas* (shrines) are different from these.

Regarding the procedure for the formal motion (*jñapti*) concerning the belongings of one who has passed away: after the Venerable Upānanda had died, his estate was valued at three hundred million gold coins. Monks from the six great cities all assembled and said, "I also deserve a share of these goods."
The community of bhikṣus did not know what to do, so they reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"It should be given to a bhikṣu and to those who are in the five [permitted] states."
What are the five?
First, those who assemble when the *gandi* is struck should be given their share;
second, those who arrive during the recitation of the three invocations (*tri-śaraṇa*).
Third, he comes at the time for paying homage to the caitya;
fourth, he comes at the time for distributing voting sticks;
fifth, he comes at the time for making the formal motion (*jñapti*).
All these shall be distributed;
it should be done in this manner.
Having spread out the seats and struck the *ghanṭī*, once the assembly has gathered, have one *bhikṣu* perform the *jñapti-karman*.
When about to perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*), one should ask the nurse and those living together:
"Has this person never owed debts or goods to others?
Or has anyone else ever owed him a debt?"
Having made this disposition, he makes the formal announcement: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The bhikṣu Upānanda has passed away here. All his existing and non-existing clothing, wealth, and miscellaneous items are now being held in trust."

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha permit that the Saṃgha shall now collectively take formal possession of all the robes, wealth, and miscellaneous items—both those present and those not present—belonging to the deceased Bhikṣu Upānanda.
"Thus it is announced.
Once the procedure of the single announcement (*ekoddeśa*) has been performed, all bhikṣus currently within the boundary who are entitled to receive the property shall do so.

If the procedure is not performed, then all disciples of the World-Honored One currently residing in Jambudvīpa or in other locations have a share. This is the rule for distributing the property of a deceased bhikṣu.

Furthermore, it should be known that if one encounters a noisy assembly where it is difficult for everyone to gather, the procedure may be simplified by performing the initial and final rites alone; in this case, ten coins or five coins should be given to the head monk and the youngest monk respectively, which shall serve as the formal record of the transaction.

Having set aside the belongings of the deceased with a single formal motion (*jñapti*), if there are difficult circumstances during the summer retreat, one bhikṣu should be appointed to act as the custodian of the deceased bhikṣu’s robes and requisites.
Once the assembly has gathered, one should first ask:
"O [Name], are you able to serve as the monk who manages the robes and personal effects of deceased bhikṣus for the Saṃgha? He should reply:
“Yes. He then instructed a bhikṣu to perform a *jñapti-karman*:
“Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, is capable of acting as the custodian of the robes and belongings of deceased bhikṣus for the Saṃgha.

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and they grant permission, the Saṃgha should authorize this: the Saṃgha now appoints the bhikṣu, so-and-so, as the custodian of the robes and belongings of deceased bhikṣus.
"Thus it is declared. As the Blessed One has said:
"There is the discordant *karmavācanā* and the concordant *karmavācanā*."
What is a discordant *karmavācanā*?

It refers to when various bhikṣus perform a *karmavācanā* within the same boundary (*sīmā*), yet the assembly does not gather in its entirety; those who should grant their consent (*chanda*) do not grant it; and even though they have all assembled, those who should raise an objection do so and do not desist, yet the *karmavācanā* is forcibly carried out. This is called a discordant *karmavācanā*.
What is a *saṃghakarma* performed in harmony?

It refers to when the bhikṣus within the same boundary perform a *karma*, all of whom assemble together; those who wish to grant their consent do so, and those who ought to voice objections do so, ceasing immediately upon such objection. This is called a *saṃghakarma* performed in harmony.
The Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One: "Bhadanta,
how many kinds of persons are such that their words are not to be reckoned, and their censures do not constitute a censure?"
The Buddha said:
"There are twelve kinds of persons.
What are the twelve?"
1. Lack of shame; 2. Having flaws or rifts; 3. Ignorance.
4. Delusion; 5. Lack of clarity; 6. Inskillfulness in speech;
Seventh, dwelling outside the boundaries;
eighth, being abandoned;
ninth, speech lacking coherence.
10. Abandoning dignified deportment;
11. Losing one's original nature;
12. Granting training to a person.
"The detailed explanation is fully contained within the *Nidāna* and *Mūlakas*. "Venerable One!
How many kinds of persons must speak for their words to be worthy of being recorded as a formal censure (*nigarhaṇīya-karman*)?
The Buddha said:
“There are four kinds of persons. What are the four?
First, those who abide in their original nature;”
2. Being within the boundary;
3. Not abandoning one's dignified demeanor;
4. Speaking with sequential order.
