At that time, after the householder Anāthapiṇḍada had offered many robes and articles at the Jeta Grove, he addressed the great assembly, saying:

"All those who are disciples of the World-Honored One, who have attained perfection in morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—those who are the unsurpassed field of merit capable of consuming offerings and benefits—should receive these gifts of mine as they please."
At that time, those whose outflows were exhausted all said:
"How could we possibly manifest our own bodies for the sake of this robe?
Then, the trainees (śaikṣas) also had this thought:
"We still possess residual minor fetters that have not been exhausted; therefore, it is not appropriate for us to accept this gift.
Ordinary worldlings also speak thus:
"We are all bound by the constraints of full fetters; we truly lack such aspirations."
In the end, not a single person accepted these garments and requisites.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said to the bhikṣus: "Did you not have this thought?"
"Have you come to me seeking liberation and practiced the pure conduct?
"Indeed, Venerable Sir," he replied. The Buddha said:

“I now grant permission: for all those who have resolved to seek nirvana and come to my presence to practice pure conduct, I shall accept and consume all their offerings—be they robes worth a hundred thousand taels of gold, dwellings worth five hundred taels, or food and drink complete with the six flavors.”
"O Bhikṣus! You must know that there are five kinds of enjoyment:
the first is enjoyment as a master."
Second, enjoyment of wealth received from one's parents;
third, enjoyment with permission;
fourth, enjoyment of what is owed as a debt.
Fifth is the enjoyment by thieves:
the Arhats enjoy it as its masters,
while those in training (śaikṣas) enjoy it as the wealth of their parents.
Ordinary persons of pure virtue who constantly practice meditative concentration and recitation, and who do not break the precepts, are permitted to enjoy [the offerings];
those who are indolent and lazy enjoy them as debtors;
and those who break the precepts enjoy them as thieves.

I have never permitted a bhikṣu who has broken the precepts to receive even a single handful of food, nor have I ever permitted one to tread upon the ground within a monastery with the heel of a foot; therefore, I now authorize the bhikṣus that if they receive offerings, the Saṃgha shall divide them among themselves.
The Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One, saying:
"Bhadanta, as the Blessed One has said:..."

"If any bhikṣu has finished making his robes and the kaṭhina cloth has been removed, should he, regarding any one of the three robes, remain apart from it in a different boundary—except when authorized by the community—he incurs the offense of naiḥsargika-pāyattika."
"O Venerable One! To what extent does a bhikṣu on the road not yet know the boundary of the robe's domain?
The Buddha said:

"Just as when the Brahmin Jātimanta planted seven mango trees, each tree being seven spans apart, with flowers and fruit flourishing, the total distance between them was forty-nine spans; this is the measurement for the robe-cloth of a wandering bhikṣu."
“Venerable One! If one dwells within the boundary of a bhikṣu’s robe, how far does that extend?
The Buddha said:
"It extends for exactly one fathom all around; whether sitting, standing, or lying down, it reaches one fathom.
"Venerable Sir! Suppose a bhikṣu is lying down between two boundaries; how far does his robe extend?"
The Buddha said,
"As long as even a single corner of the robe has not been separated from the body, it is called 'not being separated from the robe.
The Venerable Upāli then requested of the World-Honored One:
“Venerable Sir!
How many strips does the *saṃghāṭī* robe have?
The Buddha said:
“There are nine. What are the nine? They are:
those with nine strips, eleven strips, thirteen strips, fifteen strips, seventeen strips, nineteen strips, twenty-one strips, twenty-three strips, and twenty-five strips.”
Regarding the three initial grades of the saṃghāṭī robe: the middle panel consists of two long strips and one short strip; it should be worn in this manner.

The next three grades consist of three long strips and one short strip; the final three grades consist of four long strips and one short strip. Beyond these measurements, any further addition of patches constitutes a "tattered rag."
“Venerable Sir! Furthermore, how many kinds of saṃghāṭī robes are there?
The Buddha said:
“There are three kinds:
namely, superior, middling, and inferior.
The superior is three cubits in height and five cubits in width;”
"The inferior [size] is two and a half cubits in height and four and a half cubits in width;
those within these two [measurements] are called medium. "Venerable Sir!"
"How many strips does the *uttarāsaṅga* robe have?
The Buddha said,
"It has only seven strips, with two long and one short section separated by the border."
"Venerable Sir! How many kinds of the seven-strip robe (saptaka) are there?
The Buddha said:
“There are three grades:
namely, superior, middling, and inferior.
The superior is three cubits; the inferior is each reduced by half a cubit; those between these two are called middling.”
“Venerable Sir! How many strips are there for the *antarvāsa* robe?
The Buddha said:
“There are only five strips: one long and one short.
“Venerable Sir! How many kinds are there of this?”
The Buddha said:
"There are three:
namely, superior, middling, and inferior."

The superior [length] is three or five cubits; the middling and inferior are as previously stated. *Saṃghāṭī* is translated as "repeated-layered robe" (*chóngfù yī*); *uttarāsaṅga* is translated as "upper robe" (*shàngyī*); and *antarvāsa* is translated as "inner robe" (*nèiyī*).

In the Western lands (India), the three robes are all sewn with leaf-patterned patches to form a continuous whole; only in the Eastern Xia (China) are they left open and not stitched together. Upon careful examination of the Vinaya texts, there is truly no provision for leaving them open.

[The Chinese practice] involves making long strips and loops that hang down outside the arms, leaving the chest exposed and never covering the shoulders—this is precisely what constitutes a violation.
Who can take responsibility for the transgression of wearing such garments?

As the practice continued for a long time, admonitions were rarely followed. Regarding matters such as the application of tassels and fastenings, and the protocols for wearing robes and garments, these are detailed extensively elsewhere.
The Buddha said:
"The *antarvāsa* (inner robe) is further of two kinds."
What are the two? First, two cubits in height and five cubits in width;
second, two cubits in height and four cubits in width.
This refers to the maximum measurement for a robe held in reserve; it is the minimum size limit for a robe, which covers the three wheels above and reaches down to cover both knees.

If one's forearms are long, this measurement will correspond accordingly; however, if one's arms are short such that it does not reach the knees, one should take the length of the forearm as the standard.

If a robe is exactly one cubit square, this constitutes the minimum measure for a "distinguished" (vikalpa) robe; if one does not maintain it as a distinguished robe, both constitute an offense of forfeiture and transgression (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).
"If it is wide but not full, or long but excessive, there is no need for further deliberation; one may simply keep and use it.

"If a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī, regarding robes, bowls, net-bags, copper cups, waist-bands, or any such individual requisites for the sustenance of a śramaṇa, should commit an offense involving forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika), then among these, the extra bowl should be forfeited to the Saṃgha."

One should relinquish it in this manner: first, a bhikṣu to distribute the alms-bowls should be appointed; if he does not possess the five qualities, he should not be appointed, and even if he has been appointed, he should be dismissed.
What are these five? They are:
attachment, aversion, fear, delusion, and the inability to discern between what should be done and what should not be done.
If one is otherwise than this, then one should be appointed.
Beginning from the spreading of the seats, up until asking:
"Can you, [Name], act as the distributor of the bowl for the Saṃgha that has been found guilty of an offense? He replies:
“Yes. Next, one bhikṣu should first make the formal announcement (jñapti) before performing the ritual act (karman):
“Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, is capable of serving as the distributor of bowls for transgressions for the Saṃgha.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, may the Saṃgha permit that the Saṃgha now appoint this bhikṣu, so-and-so, as the distributor of bowls for transgressions.
"The announcement is made thus.
"The *karmavācanā* is established according to the announcement," the Buddha said.
"I shall now explain the rules of conduct for a monk who is carrying out the distribution of alms bowls.
When the community is in harmony, that monk who is distributing the bowls should make a formal announcement: 'Venerable sirs!'"
"Tomorrow I shall perform the *pātra-cāraṇa* (the distribution of bowls) for the Saṅgha; each of you, Venerable Ones, must bring your bowls and assemble.
When the next day arrived and the entire Saṅgha had gathered, that bhikṣu stood before the Elder holding the bowl containing the transgression, praised its qualities, and addressed the Elder, saying:
"This bowl is radiant, pure, and perfect, fit for use; whoever requires it should take it."
If the senior monk accepts it, he shall take the senior monk’s bowl and pass it to the second senior monk; in this manner, it is passed on successively until the end of the row.
If the senior monk does not require this bowl, it should be given to the second senior monk.

When it is the second time that the robe is being offered to the second senior monk, if the first senior monk then requests it again, it need not be given at the first or second request; it should be given only upon the third request.
If the Sangha’s Elder commits an offense of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*), he must confess and repent.
This applies down to the lowest-ranking monk; if he is given [the robe] only after three requests, it should be understood that, according to the rule for the Elder, he too must confess and repent.

When practicing in this manner until the end of the practice period, the alms bowl obtained should be given to a bhikṣu who has committed an offense involving forfeiture. One should inform him, saying:
"This bowl is not fit to be kept as one's own, nor should it be discarded; you should use it gradually, and must always protect and maintain it until it breaks."
"If a bhikṣu who possesses a bowl subject to forfeiture does not act in accordance with these rules, he commits an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now set forth the rules of conduct for a bhikṣu who possesses a bowl subject to forfeiture."
When going on almsround, one should place the *āpattibhājana* (the bowl for transgressions) in a fine bag, and place the *dhāraṇabhājana* (the bowl for maintenance) in another bag.
If one obtains fine food and drink, it should be placed in the *āpattibhājana*, while coarse food is placed in the *dhāraṇabhājana*.
If one has committed an offense, the bowl should be set aside to one side; the vessel that is properly maintained may always be used for eating.
Whether washing it, drying it in the sun, fumigating it, or traveling on a journey, this offending bowl must be carefully placed away until it breaks.
If this bhikṣu possesses a bowl that has been subject to an offense and does not act according to the prescribed rules, he incurs a *vyatikrama* (transgression of the law).

Herein, we shall first discuss the procedure for relinquishing the bowl; if there are other matters such as surplus robes (*atireka-cīvara*) and so forth, one should relinquish these offending items to a person who clearly understands the Dharma, speaking thus:
"This is my property, which has become an object of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; I relinquish it to you, Venerable Sir, and you may use it as you please."

"A bhikṣu who has committed an offense involving forfeiture may be used as an intermediary; this 'intermediary' refers to one who has passed through either one or two *sūryodaya* (dawn) periods. One should take that object and return it to that bhikṣu, saying:
'Venerable one!'"
"You may use it as you please.

Next, that bhikṣu must confess all his *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses, *pāyattikas* for disrespecting instructions, and all *duṣkṛta* offenses involving improper means before a single bhikṣu in accordance with the Dharma, speaking thus:
"Venerable one, please attend to me!..."
I, the bhikṣu [Name], have committed a naiḥsargika-pāyattika offense, as well as a pāyattika offense for disrespecting the instruction, and various duṣkṛta offenses resulting from my expedient means.
I now confess my offense before the Venerable One; I do not conceal it.
By confessing and disclosing my offense, I shall find peace and happiness; by failing to confess and disclose my offense, I shall find no peace or happiness.
He asked, "Do you see your fault? He replied:
"I see it. "Will you be able to well protect all the precepts in the future? He replied:
"Very well guarded.
The second and third times should be spoken in the same manner.
At the end, one should say:
"Aukṣaka. He replied, "Svādu."
"Subsequently, the bhikṣu should either maintain and designate the object, or give it away to others; he must not harbor doubts.
Just as with this object, if no interval [of ownership] has occurred, even if other objects are obtained, they are all equally subject to the abandonment of the offense."

If a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī, regarding a bowl or a robe, commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense, and they do not relinquish that robe, do not create a separation between it and themselves, and do not confess and repent for the transgression, then upon obtaining another object, they shall all incur the forfeiture of the offense; this is because the continuity of the defilement from the previously committed object persists.

"If the robe has already been relinquished, if there is again an interval [of time], and if the offense has already been confessed and atoned for, one may obtain the remaining items without any transgression.
The Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One, saying: "Bhadanta!..."
As the Blessed One has said:
"A bhikṣu should possess thirteen types of requisites for clothing.
How, then, should these be possessed?
The Buddha said:
"One must recite each name individually to maintain the observance.
What are the thirteen?"
1. *Saṃghāṭī* is translated as the "double-layered robe.
2. *Uttarāsaṅga* is translated as the "upper robe.
3. *Antarvāsa* is translated as the "lower robe."

These three types of robes are all called *cīvara*. In the northern regions of Suli, many people refer to the Dharma robe as *kāṣāya*; however, this is merely a term signifying the color "red" and is not the terminology used in the Vinaya scriptures.
In the Middle Kingdom, all these are called *cīvara*.
Fourth, the *niṣīdana* is a bedding mat for lying down.
Fifth, the *nivāsana* is a lower garment.
Sixth, the *nivāsana* (lower garment).
Seventh, the *saṃkakṣikā*, which is the armpit-covering robe; its ancient name was *fubō* (shoulder-cover).

It is long enough to cover the right arm, yet it certainly does not conform to the true monastic regulations. Had it instead covered the right armpit and crossed over the left arm, it would have been entirely identical to the Buddha’s own design.

Furthermore, this tradition has long been practiced with the creation of *cīvara-paṭaka* (shoulder-covers), which, though involving great expense and complexity, have never been heard to conform to the middle way. Since they violate the regulations of the Sages, one should naturally reflect upon these faults; yet, even though the clear texts are before one's eyes, I fear that people are still unable to eliminate and reform them. "Reform" refers to changing the manner of covering the shoulders, while "eliminate" means simply to discard the *cīvara-paṭaka* itself!
The details are as found elsewhere.
Eighth, the *pāṭa-saṃkakṣikā*, the side-covering armpit cloth.
Ninth, the *kāyapracchādaka*, the body-wiping towel.
10. The *mukhaproñchana* (face-wiping cloth).
11. The *kṣapaṭikā* (shaving garment), which refers to the garment worn during shaving.
12. The *kaṇḍupraticchādana* robe for covering skin diseases such as scabs and sores.
13. The *vaiśvāsika* robe, which is the requisite garment for medicinal supplies.
The summary verse says:
The three robes and bedding; the lower garment and two types of upper robes;
the body-towel, face-towel, and shaving cloth; the bandage for sores and the medicine-money robe.
"These various robes should be formally maintained by reciting their names as one does for the three robes, saying:
'This bedding and matting, I now maintain; it has already been made into a robe and is for my personal use.'"
"A second and third time he spoke thus; the rest should be understood accordingly. 'Venerable Sir!
Aside from these thirteen requisites and robes, there is this extra robe; what shall be done with it?'"
The Buddha said:

"Regarding the surplus robes other than the thirteen types of robes, one should entrust them to two teachers or other venerable persons. One should hold that object and, in the presence of another bhikṣu, speak as follows:
'Venerable sir, please attend to me!'"

I, [Name], possess this extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*), which has not yet been formally assigned; it is appropriate that it be so assigned (the old translation "to recite the *śuddhi*" refers to the underlying intent).
I now perform this assignment before the Venerable One, entrusting it to the Upādhyāya as a deposit; I now hold it.
The second and third [times] were also spoken in this same manner. Here, it is simply stated that he entrusted [the robes] to his two teachers.

The meaning is that the robes of those teachers symbolize their freedom from attachment and the absence of the burden of personal possession; however, it was not necessary to request them to act as the donors.

The Vinaya text merely instructs that one should point from afar and then stop; it is not appropriate to announce [the death]. If the person dies, one may dispose of the remaining items as one pleases. There is only this single method for distinguishing the rules regarding clothing; there is no further process involving a series of transfers or any other actual occurrence.
Since there are other texts [to the contrary], this is not the teaching of this school.
Generally speaking, when one speaks of "entrusting," it is intended to clarify that the person in question is worthy of being entrusted.
The Buddha told Upāli:
"When obstacles and difficulties arise, there are six matters that can be accomplished through mental resolve:
first, the formal maintenance of the three robes;
second, the relinquishment of the three robes;"
3. The distribution of extra robes;
4. The relinquishing of special invitations;
5. The performance of the Poṣadha ceremony.
6. "Perform the *pravāraṇā*.
The Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One, saying: "Bhadanta!"
"Is it permissible to maintain an uncut robe?
The Buddha said,
"It is not allowed."
"There must be other circumstances under which this too would be permissible. "Venerable Sir!
May one wear an uncut robe and enter a village or city?"
The Buddha said:
"It is not permitted.
However, if there is a specific cause or circumstance, then it is permissible."
“Venerable Sir! May one wear an uncut robe when entering the dwellings of those who have left the home life among the non-Buddhists?
The Buddha said:
"It is not appropriate.
However, if that person goes outside, it is also permissible. "Venerable Sir!"
"How should one maintain the uncut robe?
The Buddha said:
"One should maintain it in this way, saying:”

"I, [Name], possess this cloth-material; I now formally accept it as my own, which is what I have long desired. It shall be made into a seven-panel robe with two long and one short section; provided there are no other circumstances, I shall wash, dye, cut, and sew it, and it shall be for my personal use."
The second and third times were also spoken in this manner.

The five strips [of cloth] are to be understood accordingly. If one has white silk or white cotton cloth intended for making the two lower robes, but due to urgent circumstances lacks the leisure to do so, even a piece of white cloth may be kept and maintained as such.
If the dyeing is uneven or streaky, it is appropriate to do so.
Furthermore, when maintaining the robe within the ritual enclosure (maṇḍala), one may hold the robe against one's own body; this also carries no fault.
It is well if one can recite the texts from memory; it is also permissible to read them from paper.

Furthermore, as for those among the śrāmaṇeras who wear the five-strip robe (pañcakaṣāya) merely as a casual garment, yet occasionally don it [as if it were their formal attire], this is a grave offense of excessive laxity.
"In the land of China, this custom has long been prevalent; do not allow this improper practice to be adopted. The following clarifies the abbreviated teaching.
At that time, the Buddha was staying between the twin *śāla* trees at Kuśinagara, the birthplace of the Mallas, on the verge of entering *parinirvāṇa*. He addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"I have previously expounded the Vinaya teachings for you in detail but have not yet spoken of them in brief. You should now listen to the abbreviated teaching, known in Sanskrit as the *Saṃkṣipta-vinaya*."
Furthermore, regarding any matter concerning which I have neither previously permitted nor prohibited,
if that matter conforms to what is impure and contradicts what is pure, it is impure and should not be practiced.
"If a matter conforms to purity and opposes impurity, this is itself pure and should be practiced accordingly.
[The monks] asked:
"For what purpose did the World-Honored One deliver this brief instruction when he was about to enter parinirvāṇa?"
He replied:
"After the Great Master has passed away, until the holy teachings have finally vanished, let there be no cause for non-Buddhists to raise this censure:
'Since the World-Honored One possessed all-encompassing wisdom, yet there were matters in the world that he neither permitted nor prohibited—how are his disciples to practice? "
This rule was established to preclude such objections and to examine the future benefits from afar.
Furthermore, it must be taught so that the śrāvaka disciples may dwell in peace and happiness, free from obstacles regarding their affairs.
“As the World-Honored One has said:
‘If a matter accords with the impure and opposes the pure, or accords with the pure and opposes the impure, one should practice it; yet there are those who do not practice it.
I do not yet understand what the meaning and intent of these words are.”
He replied:
"If there is a matter that the Buddha neither previously permitted nor prohibited, yet which now gives rise to worldly censure and debate, this is impure and should not be practiced."

What is this? For instance, in various regions of the Noble Land [India], people of all classes, both noble and humble, consume areca nut, betel vine leaves, and white lime, mixing them with fragrant substances to create a savory delicacy.
If this is for the purpose of treating an illness, with the hope of removing bad breath as prescribed by a physician, there is no fault in eating it.
However, if it is for the sake of coloring the mouth or reddening the lips, it constitutes an improper act.

Furthermore, the dyeing of robes with red earth was likewise neither prohibited nor permitted from the outset; however, because its current use is identical to the garments of non-Buddhists, it gives rise to secular slander and criticism. This indeed merits prohibition, for the principle is that the yellow robes of the Eastern Land (China) should not be used, as the circumstances here are the same.
Furthermore, there are matters that are neither permitted nor prohibited; if their use at present is not subject to public censure, using them constitutes no offense.
This is just as the Buddha spoke of three types of waistbands, while others are neither permitted nor prohibited.
Furthermore, when wearing various sashes tied around the waist, there is no shame if others do not see them, and thus this is also without fault.

Moreover, as the Buddha taught regarding the eight primary colors for dyeing cloth, three types are permitted to be used: namely, indigo, mud-color, and red; these may be identified according to their actual appearance.
"Red" refers to the bark of the Bodhi tree; however, as for other dyes derived from roots, leaves, flowers, or fruits, neither permission nor prohibition is granted.

Nowadays, we see some people using other red barks such as *khaṇḍa* and the like, as well as *nāgapuṣpa*, to dye their robes. Since contemporaries do not criticize this, there is no fault in its use. All of these are pure and permitted by the Buddha alone; he never mentioned the use of chopsticks.
The current practice is a relaxation permitted by the abbreviated teachings.
However, sitting cross-legged on high beds within the hall while eating is entirely contrary to what is allowed by the abbreviated teachings.
Yet, as this has been practiced for a long time, it is truly difficult to speak against.
Furthermore, as the Buddha said:
"There are three kinds of substances that may be used for washing the hands:
first, salty alkaline earth;"
"Second, dried cow dung;
third, cleansing powder.
This is the permission granted.
Such things as the nyagrodha tree, flowers, pods of the soap-berry, and bathing powder are all suitable for washing and bathing.
Since these are neither prohibited nor specifically permitted, and they are non-toxic and free of insects, there is no fault in using them.
"In such matters as these, one should practice through reflection.

Regarding this, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* contains a brief instruction within its rules on eating; those of former times did not call it a "brief instruction," nor were they familiar with its profound intent. However, as the text is very close to this [present version], I personally examined the Sanskrit manuscript of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* and found it to be identical to this *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* without a single difference. It is merely that because the translations of previous generations varied, the wording has become different.
I hope that future students will thoroughly examine and carefully contemplate the intent of the teaching, and must not merely conform blindly.
The Venerable Upāli requested of the World-Honored One: "Bhadanta!..."
"In total, how many dharmas are there that can encompass the Vinaya?
The Buddha said,
"To speak in broad terms, there are three such dharmas."
What are the three? They are the *jñapti* (motion), the *jñapti-dvitīya* (motion followed by one proclamation), and the *jñapti-caturtha* (motion followed by three proclamations).
To speak in detail, there are one hundred and one formal acts (*karmavācanā*).
“Venerable Sir! Among the one hundred and one *karmas*, how many of each type—*jñapti*, *jñapti-dvitīya*, and *jñapti-caturtha*—are there?
The Buddha said:

"There are twenty-two *jñapti-karman* (motions consisting of a single motion), forty-seven *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (motions consisting of one motion followed by one proclamation), and thirty-two *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (motions consisting of one motion followed by three proclamations).
What are the matters concerning the twenty-two *jñapti-karman*?"
1. The formal motion for instructing a person in private;
2. The formal motion for inquiring regarding obstructing factors;
3. The formal motion for the *poṣadha* ceremony.
4. A formal announcement that the entire Saṃgha has committed an offense during the poṣadha;
5. A formal announcement that the entire Saṃgha has doubts regarding an offense during the poṣadha;
6. A formal announcement during the pravāraṇā.
7. A motion regarding the fact that the entire Saṃgha has committed an offense at the time of performing the *pravāraṇā*;
8. A motion regarding the fact that the entire Saṃgha has doubts concerning an offense at the time of performing the *pravāraṇā*;
9. A motion regarding a dispute over an offense within the assembly at the time of performing the *pravāraṇā*.
10. The formal announcement regarding the determination of offenses within the assembly during the *pravāraṇā* ceremony;
11. The formal announcement regarding the dates of the Saṃgha’s summer retreat (*varṣā*);
12. The formal announcement regarding the preservation of the belongings of a deceased person.
13. The announcement regarding the person appointed to guard and maintain the requisites of a deceased bhikṣu;
14. The announcement for the removal of the kaṭhina robe;
15. The announcement for declaring another’s grave offense (sthūlātyaya).
16. The formal announcement regarding the giving of a robe to the Venerable Sthavira;
17. The formal announcement regarding open contempt;
18. The formal announcement regarding contempt under false pretext.
19. The formal motion for granting the training rules (śikṣāpada);
20. The formal motion for granting the suspension of the training rules (śikṣādattaka) to a family;
21. The formal motion for overturning the alms bowl (pātrāvakṣepaṇa).
Twenty-two: The Announcement of the Upside-down Bowl.
"Regarding the forty-seven matters of the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement), what are they?
First: the *jñapti-dvitīya* for establishing a small boundary (*kṣudra-sīmā*)."
2. The formal motion with announcement for delimiting the great boundary (mahā-sīmā);
3. The formal motion with announcement for delimiting the boundary where robes need not be kept within (a-cīvara-apahāraka-sīmā);
4. The formal motion with announcement for those unable to attend at the time of the *poṣadha*.
5. The *jñapti-dvitīya* (motion with one proclamation) for those who are insane; 6.
The *jñapti-dvitīya* for appointing a person to perform the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to admonish).
7. The formal motion with announcement (jñapti-dvitīya-karman) for appointing a person to distribute bedding;
8. The formal motion with announcement for designating a pure kitchen;
9. The formal motion with announcement for setting aside robes and articles to be made into the kaṭhina robe.
10. The *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for the person who spreads the *kaṭhina* robe;
11. The *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for the person to whom the *kaṭhina* robe is entrusted—the above constitutes the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for the appointment of all twelve types of persons;
12. The *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for the appointment of the person who distributes rooms.

Furthermore, Upāli requested of the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir,
among the one hundred and one formal acts (*karmavācanā*), how many involve the presence of consent (*chanda*)?"
"How many are free from desire? The Buddha said, "Upāli!"
"All possess desire, with the sole exception of the establishment of boundaries.
"Venerable Sir! Among the one hundred and one formal acts (*karmas*), how many are performed by the fourfold assembly?"
How many are performed by a group of five?
How many are performed by a group of ten?
How many are performed by a group of twenty?
The World-Honored One replied:
"A group of forty is required to perform the formal act for a bhikṣuṇī; to do otherwise would be a violation of the Eight Rules of Respect.
A group of twenty is required for the expiation of offenses of a bhikṣu."
A group of ten refers to the conferral of full ordination (*upasampadā*).
A group of five refers to the conferral of full ordination in border regions and the *pravāraṇā* ceremony.
A group of four refers to performing other remaining matters.
“Venerable Sir! As for what is called ‘karma,’ what is its meaning?
The Buddha said:
"The matter by which [an action] proceeds is called the cause; performing that action is termed *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act).
"Venerable Sir! I still do not fully understand the meaning of these words."
The Buddha said:
“If one performs a *karmavācanā* for that specific matter, this is a *karmavācanā* performed by means of speech based on the presence of the requisite conditions.
“Venerable Sir! [he asked.]
"What is the meaning of the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of intimidation)?

The Buddha said, "This is a name established based on the nature of the act. When this *bhikṣu* is prone to quarreling and strife, the *tarjanīya-karman* is performed upon him with the intention that he shall be struck with fear and no longer commit evil; therefore, it is called the *tarjanīya-karman*. One should understand all other *karman*s according to this principle."
“Venerable Sir! Regarding what is called the *Vinaya*, what constitutes its essence?
What is its object of focus?”
What is the basis? What is the causal equipment? What is the arising?
What is their intrinsic nature?
What is their karmic fruition?
Please explain these seven essential points for us.
The Buddha told Upāli: "The physical text of the sūtra constitutes its substance;

as it is taught, the practice of cultivation serves as its object of focus; the actions of body, speech, and mind serve as its basis; the formal ritual procedures (karmavācanā) it employs serve as its causal equipment; the confession of transgressions is called its origination; all existing offenses constitute its intrinsic nature; and rebirth in heaven and liberation constitute its fruit."
The Buddha told Upāli:

"These constitute the one hundred and one formal procedures (karmavācanā). If these legal procedures are maintained in the world, then it should be known that the Buddha-dharma has not yet perished from the world."
At that time, Upāli and the great assembly, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

Regarding the statement that there are "one hundred and one" such *karmavācanas*, this is merely citing a general figure; if one examines them within the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śīla* (the Great Vinaya), there are variations in their number. Thus, they are subsumed under their respective categories, and there is no contradiction or hindrance.

Furthermore, regarding whether a formal act (*karmavācanā*) is accomplished by a single motion (*jñapti*), a motion followed by one announcement (*jñaptidvitīya*), or a motion followed by three announcements (*jñapticaturtha*), it is appropriate to understand these according to reason with mutual flexibility and sufficiency.

Recently, having compared the *Karmavācanā-mūla* with the two hundred-odd fascicles of the *Mahāvibhāṣā-vinaya*, I have conducted this investigation at great expense of effort; may later generations not harbor any doubts.
